PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS. -- IF your hat blows off in the street follow lb -placidly and with dignity. Somebody else will chase it for MAME "Were you ever in love ?" Helen: "Yes, with myself." Mattie : "Well, you never had any rivals to worry about, anyway. FIRST BANKER: "What a breezy fellow your clerk is 1" Second Banker: " Yea ; but he's not responsible for any of the drafts." WOMAN : "How much for children's pictures?" Photographer: "Two dollars a dozen, madam." Worn : " Why—er—yes ; but I've only got nine." SHE : "The play was affecting. I was moved to tears." He "Very. I should have liked to see the woman ahead of me moved two tiers." "JANE," said a man, looking for his razor•case, "I have places where I keep my things, and you ought to know all of them." "Yes," she said, 'I ought to know where you keep your late hours." (,or OFF EASILY.—" When I asked for a rise, I told my employer I had grown grey in his service." "What did he say!" "He said if I had worked anywhere else I probably would have got bald." QUESTION OF THE DAY.—Little Ethel (on being reminded that the baby was born on Valentine's Day) : "Well, papa, I s'pose you're just dying to know who sent it ?"

RESTAURANT GUEST: "Everything you have brought me is stone cold." Polite Waiter: "Here is the mustard and pepper, sir." CONSOLING. —" I have cast my bread upon the water," the young housewife sighed, "but it does not return." Her better half strove to comfort her. "Perhaps," he suggested gently, "it has not yet been recognised as such." Boy: "Mr. Smitters wants to know if you'll lend him an umbrella. He says you know him." "You may say that I do know him. He will probably understand why you didn't bring the umbrella." THE OUTRAGEOUS PART. Ethel: "Jack was kissing me last night, when papa walked in the parlour." Gracie: "What did he say? " "He said, Sir, this is outrageous I " "And Jack?" "Jack said, Yes, isn't it? Kindly oblige me by knocking before you enter the next time." MR.. GREEN (to Johnny, who has been hiding behind the screen) : "There, I'll give you a shilling not to tell that I kissed your sister I Johnny: "Yes, but I saw you put your arm round her waist a-cuddlin' of her. It's worth :mother bob not to split on that." OVERHEARD AT A LONDON STATION. —Station Inspector: "I think some one will get into trouble on a^count of that train starting three minutes late." Collector: " Why ? Any of the passengers complaining?" Station Inspector : "No ; but the manager of the refreshment-room vows he'll make it hot far whoever is responsible. The passengers have had time to eat what they paid for." _ _ _

TENANT (to owner of jerry-built house): "Some of the plaster in my kitchen fell down last night, and I want you to replace it." Landlord: "What caused it?" "The man who occupies the floor above sneezed." Landlord: "Well, some people think because they pay forty pounds a year they can carry on Just-as if they lived in a Roman citadel !"

HER IDEA.—" I understand, madam, that you have a very old clock in your sitting-room?" ten- tatively said a well-dressed stranger who had knocked at the door of a farmhouse away back in the Allegash hills. "May 1 look at it? I am an antiquarian, and"—" You don't say so 1" ejacu- lated Mrs. Juckles, in surprise. "Why, I should never have taken you to be that old—you don't look a day over forty." SHE (who has just said no) : " I am sorry I can- not give you the answer you wanted, Mr. Spoona- more ; but it is for the best, believe me. Some day you will aik yourself what you ever ssw in me to attract your fancy? "—He "I have no doubt I will, Miss Psharpe. My friends have asked me that question a hundred times since I began paying attention to you." A Postn.—" He," screamed the park orator, "who puts his hand to the plough must not turn back." "What's he to do when he gets to the end of the furrer ?" asked the man in the .crowd.

To BE SOLD TOGETHER.—At Bury, in Lancashire they tell of a horse-coper who once offored for sale three awful old "crooks." The three stood close together, as though leaning against one another. An intending purchaser looked at them, and, turning to the attendant, said, "Trot out the middle one." "What," ejaculated the caper, "and let the other two fall down? Not me ! DISPENSED Wirm—Once when the late Sir Frank L )ck wood was attending a poltce.court, he noticed that the magistrates were performing their duties in a very expeditious manner, and com- mented on the fact to a superintendent of police. "Yes," answered the superintendent, who was pompous and not too well educated. "Their wor- ships always dispenses with justice very fast."

"WHENEVER melancholy seizes me, and I begin to despair of the human race," said the philoso- phical man who was frequently out of employment, "I just take the testimonials that my former em- ployers have given me and read their glowing description of at least one man who is thoughtful, Intrepid, modest, energetic, scholarly, and a man of action, honest and shrewd,' &c., &c., &c., and Immediately my faith in mankind returns."

LITTLE BESSIE, having been punished for mis- behaviour, slunk to the other end of the room crying. XV hen her sobs had subsided, her mother turned to view her repentance, but found her engaged in making faces at her. "Why, Bessie," said her mother, "how can you do so " Oh, mamma," answered the girl quickly, "I was trying to smile at you, but my face slipped "

DISTINCTION WITH A DIFFEHENCIL—He PM very ill and very ,Iross. His poor wife could not please him any way, and dayand night he worried her with complaining. A neighbour looked in. "I hear your husband is not well." "Indeed, no," she replied: "he's very bad." "I hope his ease is not critical," said the neighbour. "Worse than that," replied the poor woman, "it's downright abusive."

"FOOTSTEPS OF Spas "—A ventilated shoe has been invented in Cologne. A steel spring operates a bellows between the heel and the sole, and every step the wearer takes drives a stream of fresh air through the perforations in the inner sole every part of the loot. This should conduce to to the "airy tread" of which Tennyson speaks in "Maud." People who suffer from hot feet may now take steps to ventilate them. _

FILLING UP SPARE MOMENTS.—A clergyman who has a small farm, was walking round superin- tending, when he CAM 3 up to his ;Loughman, who was resting his horses. The clergyman said "John could you not bring an old sickle and cut away the weeds in this corner while you rest the horses?" John said :—" Master, couldn't you take a bag of them mixed seeds into the poolpit you, and sort 'em while they're singing?" John always breathed his horses as well as himself after that, with nothing 89. id. . .

, A CHANGE OF CLTIC.-A butcher in a small way of business was in the habit of sending his son out With a small trap to deliver orders. The lad was a caruisss driver, and one day he knocked down an ola !ady. A lawsuit followed, and the butcher had to heavy damages. Shortly after this the son was ti. • cause of another accident which had a similar resu,-. and the drain on the butcher's re- sources broug .-• him to the verge of ruin. A few days after the -ond case had been settled he was sitting in his eh 7 thinking over his hard fate, when a neighbour , me rushing in breathless, with the information t 00..., 'he butcher's wife had been run over by the carelei.., driver of a private carriage and was lying in the th, ottal with a crushed leg. "Thank goodness," exclai med the butcher, as if greatly relieved ; "my lucL.'s changed at last t" SERVED RIM RICIIT.—" We like your house," said the old gentleman who thought of renting it fer the season, to the agent, "but you say in your advertisement that you won't take people with children." "That's true," said the agent. "I can't really, air; they do so much damage.'" "I don't think you'd suffer much from mine," said the old gentleman. "I cannot make an exception, even in your ease, sir," returned the agent, With some irritation, and the old gentleman went away. A few days later the agent discovered that the old gentleman's children consisted of two unmarried daughters, aged thirty-eight and forty-two reopen- tively,

div.head: ILLUSTRATED FASHION S.
div.p: ILLUSTRATED FASHION S.

Zibeline is a material which is again popular this autumn season, and nearly all the new materials are of this order, very soft and silky and excellently suited for softly falling draperies. The roughish surface is covered with long silky hairs, but it must be granted that though the original effect of these is pleasing, they soon wear off and it is spoiled by the bare patches. Zibeline can be had in two colours shot which has a striking appearance, but the plain colours of a uniform tone are likely to be more popular, as they do not date the gown so much as the more fanciful varieties. Gowns of this material are trimmed either with guipure lace, appliquts in white cloth or richly tinted em- broideries. The simpler coats and skirts confine themselves to braidings of all kinds, and any amount of stitched strappings which always look smart and wear well. Much more durable and equally as effective as the rough surfaced materials are those of durable fine faced cloth, which make up into very useful and smart costumes. Indeed, nothing to my mind could be smarter for autumn wear than a soft deep tone of reddish brown cloth, with a collar and strappings of the fashionable richly tinted Persian embroideries in tapestry wools.

The comfortable coat shown above varies little in style from some which have proved them- selves good and useful friends in the past. It is made in frieze with the collar cuffs and pockets of a lighter tone of checked material. It is almost a saque, having only a slight pretention to fit at the sides, its looseness allowing it to be easily slipped on and therefore adding to its sphere of usefulness. Indeed the capabilities of such a wrap do not confine it to autumn wear only, but prove it to be a welcome addition to one's wardrobe all the year round. There is a great variety in the length and style of the latest coats, which fact must be a welcome one to those of us who find it a difficult problem to dress as nicely as we would like on the small amount of money which can be spared for our dress allowance.

div.head: cOSY GOWN.
div.p: A cOSY GOWN.

The cosy dressing gown sketched is of a simple design and yet is sufficiently ornamental to allow of it making its appearance at the breakfast table if necessary. It is made in a warm crimson flannel, the fichu and frills at the sleeves being of cream washing silk, the latter being finished at the outer edge with a hem-stitched border and only tacked firmly into place, so that they are easily de- tached when they require washing. The fulness at the waist is confined by a broad satin ribbon which is passed round the waist and tied in a bow in front. The edge of the skirt is made with a frill of the flannel itself as a finish. Only the bodice, which has some pretensions to fit, is lined, the lining stopping short a few inches below the waist. About ten yards of flannel are required for its manufacture, together with three yards of washing silk for the fichu, etc., and two-and-a-half yards of satin ribbon to allow of a sufficiently full bow and ends. With the long and probably very cold winter before us a gown like this would be found invaluable, and it is best to take time by the fore- lock and provide against contingencies by using the bright days still remaining in preparing for the lull ones to follow.

The blouse illustrated is of a simple, yet smart and fashionable style which recommends itself for early autumn wear. It is made with three box pleats down the front, after the principle of a Norfolk coat, while the fulness of the sleeves. . which confined by tucks at the upper part of the arms falls freely at the lower in the manner so much affected at present. The throat and wrists are finished by dainty turn-over collar and cuffs of lace, and a dainty bow of silk and ribbon band en .mite give the finishing touches. A blouse in one of the Paisley patterned materials with blue as the prevailing colour would look well with a collar and cuffs of embroidery and the bow and band of bright emerald green ribbon. The con- trast between green and blue is always a popular one, and seems particularly so at present, as many of the smartest gowns and most fashionable bits of millinery are expressed in these shades. Metallic looking green and blue wings trim green or blue straw hats with charming effect. The wings are placed towards the back of the hat with the tips pointing downwards or are placed on the outside of the up-turned brims of the tricorn hats. This way of arranging them is generally becoming, and gives a look of width to the face.

only an episode, and when Syron said it way woman's whole existence it showed how very little that poseur really knew about women. She enjoyed her supper, regardless of after effects in the way of ghosts. There was something reassurin about the frank manliness of the man opposite. He was not absurdly deferential, but he was evidently accustomed to good society. She wondered what his views were on the subject of money. He seemed to be very much bent on mak- ing the Railway Company pay damages. "I don't know that I care so much about the money," he said, in reply to her queries.

" Whereunto is money goody Who has it has much trouble and care, Who once has had it has despair, and so on. I had a little once, and it has gone. Now, lam content to grub along as you see. I get a horse, plenty of exercise, and my books in the evening. lam thinking of bringing out emenda- tions of Shakespeare come day. I wonder what Shakespeare himself would say to them." "He would probably ask you not to move his bones, in that fashion, Isabel said, as she got up to leave the room. Mrs. Pilbeam had departed, presumably unto her virtuous rest. "By the way, Mr. Hearne, what is Miss Summerby like?" Was it fancy, or did an air of constraint spread over his frank feattnes ? He seemed embarrassed for a moment. "It is an odd question," he re. marked, as if he were trying to gain time. "It is an odd question." "And one, odd as it is, which I should like to have answered," said Isabel. "Do you know, Mr. Hearne, I am inclined to think that there is a mystery bidden in this gloomy old house, and that I am destined to unravel—'
"For Heaven's sake," began Geoffrey. He stopped confusedly. " Yes?" she inquired with feminine pectins,.

city. "I was only going to add, don't run away with such an idea as that," he said. "Haven't you discovered that it is always better to take things as they seem—not to look beneath the surface?" " Howaloes that apply with regard to your. self?" asked Isabel, surveying him curiously. "You are apparently frank, and yet you evade my question." "There is nothing to evade in your question," said Geoffrey. "If you want to know anything, you had better ask Miss Summerby." "Women leap to conclusions," said Isabel, tak- ing up her bedroom candle. ‘‘l am a woman; I have arrived at a conclusion." "What is it?" asked Geoffrey, recovering him- self. "In the first instance, that you would make a very poor conspirator, and in the second—" She paused. "And in the second?"

"And in the second that the secret is connected with Miss Summerhy." It was a passing inspiration on the part of Isabel, but it told on Geoffrey. "Take my frankness for granted," he said, almost sternly, "but if you wish to remain her (pardon me for saying it), do not allow your imagination to get the upper hand of you." Isabel drew herself up haughtily, and with a bow was passing from the room, but Geoffrey detained her. "Won't you say good-night before I depart into outer gloom?" "It isn't gloom—it's moonlight," said the practical Isabel. Where, as Mr. Bob Sawyer would put it, do you hang out'?" "I am suspended in the tower," said Geoffrey, with his boyish laugh. "It is given over to me. No one else," with a resumption of his former stern- ness, "is allowed to set foot in it." Isabel went upstairs, feeling that c:dstence was again enjoyable. "I am not curious," she said (what woman will admit, even to herself, that she is curious ?), "but there is a secret somewhere, and I will match my woman's wit against Mr. Hearne's knowledge. We shall see who will win ; " and she again confronted the hearse-like drapery of her gloomy room. As she coiled her long hair in a picturesque arrangement for the night, she fancied she heard a sigh and saw a white face in the glass before her.

She went to the door. No one was there. "That comes of listening to ghost stories," she said." Did you see any one?" she asked Mrs. Pilbeam, who was laboriously proceeding towards the servants' bedrooms. Mrs. Pilbeam affected to laugh. "It's your nerves, Miss. Bolt your door and go to sleep. You'll be as fresh as a fiddle in the morning." She passed on with a jolly laugh. Isabel bolted her door. When she awoke the sun streamed brightly into the room. She jumped out of bed with alacrity. 'Now for Miss Summerhy. I must have talked a great deal of nonsense last night." Miss Summerby was a meek-looking, somewhat insignificant woman of about fifty. Her physique was not insignificant, but the apologetic manner in which she went about seeming to make excuses for existing, rather did away with the effect produced by her height. She was muscularly strong, and handled a heavy tea-pot at breakfast as if it were a feather. Her dress was of gorgeous hues, and but for her pale, pinched features and miserably worn look she might have passed for an attractive woman. She gave Isabel the impression that at some time in her life she had received a severe shock—a shock which she could not forget. And she never looked people straight in the face. Any remark she made appeared to be addressed to a crumb on the tablecloth or to a fly disporting itsell head downwards from the ceiling. She came softly into the room, in a noiseless way which was sug• gestive of list slippers, and received Geoffrey Hearne, who also appeared at breakfast, in a timid manner, as if she had done a sum wrongly and he knew it would not add up. "I am glad to see you," she said to Isabel, and !presented her hand in mid-air as if she expected ' someone to shake it.

------- Isabel took it. It felt like a piece of cold fried fish—plaice or cod. "Did you sleep well?" she asked, looking straight through the window into the distance. "Very well indeed," said Isabel, with a sidt I glance at Geoffrey Hearne. Geoffrey had bowed on Miss Summerby's entrance, without appearing to see the outstretched hand, whereupon Mist Summerby had hidden it somewhere in her dress, af if ashamed of it. Miss Summerby appeared at a loss how to con. tinue the conversation. A happy thought struck her. "Do you take tea?" she asked Isabel. Isabel admitted that she took tea. "Or, perhaps, you would like coffee?" in a dis• tressed voice.
Isabel preferred tea. "With sugar?" " If you please, Miss Summerby." "Ilud then," said Miss Summerby, despairingly, "there is milk. Do you take milk? Some people do take milk."

"If you please." Miss Summerby partially poured out the tea and then put down the teapot. "You must pardon mail I appear to be confused. I think ii is.one of my bad days. Don't you fancy so, Mr. Hearne ?"

"lam afraid it is," he said, kindly. "But never mind, Miss Suromerby, you will feel better presently. Won't you have some tea yourself?" "Well, I don't know," said Miss Summerby, holplessly. "Miss Archer hasn't had any "Pray don't think of mine," said Isabel, wondering when they would really oomateno• breakfast."

" Ah, but I must," said Miss Summerby. "Coffee, I think you said, Miss Archer ? " And before Isabel could intervene she had filled up the cup which contained the tea and handed it to Isabel with, the air,of one who has successfully accom- plished a somewhat difficult task. Just as Isabel put this mixture to her lips, Miss Summerby appeared to recall something. She pressed her hand across her brow and said feebly, as if all her struggles were about to begin anew, "Perhaps you take cocoa ?" "I loathe it," said Isabel, with a fervour which surprised herself. "I never drink it." "I don't either," said Miss Summerby, with an air of relief. "It always troubles me when I see the:different advertisements on the walls. I never know which to choose; they all seem to be the best. Some of them cannot be telling the truth. Can they, Mr. Hearne?" "I don't think they can," said Geoffrey, pleasantly. "Never mind, Miss Summerby. I think if I were you I would stick to tea." "Ala, yea," she said, hopelessly; "but you don't wake up in the night and wonder which is best. I' do. They all come and stand at the foot of the bed and bother me. Fry quarrels with Epps, and Epps will insist on my preferring his. Cadbury is so.unkind." _
• "But, Miss Summerby, you must not let them do that," he said, kindly. "I am afraid you get a little bit overwrought sometimes, and that makes matters worse. Why don't you take things pleasantly

wisih-,-yes,--she‘said, poising her teaspoon fn•Sizo with a brisker demeanour. "It is a great pity to be bypochondriacal. I shall feel better after breakfast. Would you like some strawberries, Miss Archer? Do have some more coco

_ She said this quite naturally, and without any appearance of effort. Isabel revived also, and took strawberries. Geoffray Hearne had previously supplied her with food. The substantial Pilbeam brought her cream to eat with the strawberries, and Miss Summerby, now that she had discharged her social obligations, began to feel better. "It is 40 difficult to remember, she said, apologetically, to Isabel. "No one seems to have the same tastes in this house." _

_ "I think mine are very simple," said Geoffrey Hearne, who had been eating his breakfast in silence. "Isn't it a pleasant surprise, Miss Archer, to come back to strawberries after they are all over in town?"

_ . " I hadn't thought about it, but I am showing a practical appreciation of them." "Some more cocoa ? " asked Miss Summerby, with the air of one who has at last succeeded in recalling something. "No, thank you," replied Isabel, consuming dry toast in silence, and wonderin,,o, if Miss Summerby was always like that. She afterwards discovered that she wasn't. _ .

The breakfast dragged its slow length along, but, like most things, came to an end at last. Miss Summerby rose, and Isabel stood looking out of the window, only to be recalled by Miss Summerby's inquiry as to what she would like to do. "I am going to lie down," remarked Miss Summerby. "Pilbeam will take care of me. If you ride, Mr. Hearne can show you round the estate." If you ride ! Isabel's pulses tinged with delight. Conscience, however, restrained her. If she toak Miss Summerby's money, it was time that she began to do something to earn it. "Thank you, I should like it very much," she said, "but cannot I help to make you comfortable, Miss Summerby?" "No, thank you, Miss Archer. Pilbeam ean do all that is necessary for me; can't you, Pilbeam ? " "Certainly, Miss," said Pilbeam, looking at Isabel as if she expected her to get on horseback at once. "There are two or three horses in the stable doing nothing," continued Miss Summerby. "Mr. Hearne cannot exercise them all. lam glad you ride. I forgot to mention it to Mr. Dabchick when he was here." Mr. Dabchick appeared to pervade space. Per- haps he was not real flesh and blood at all, but only a zhost from Kensal Green or Finehley, and shared those grim haunts of his partners with legal impartiality, flitting from the "marble moniment and geraniums" of Mr. Perkins to the severely simple "plain cross and lobelias" of the defunct Mr. Snook. Geoffrey Hearne came to Isabel's aid. He had a somewhat masterful manner of helping people in difficulties. "If you will entrust your. self to my care," he said, in a matter.of-fact way, "I will take you round. Have you good. hands ?"

He was not referring to their shape. Isabel divined he was already cogitating as to the mount she should have. What manner of man was this who was only the agent, and yet decided questions of such a nature?

"If you have a light hand," he said, "there is the Irish chestnut mare. She is as fidgety and im- pulsive as—as a woman, and wants watching." "Like most women?" queried Isabel, indig- nantly. "Not at all. I only wanted to make you under- stand what she is like. There is also a cow-like animal who is not thoroughbred. She is placid— very placid—but uninteresting. If you would like her, you have only to say the word." He paused, with his hand on the bell-rope. "She is far safer," he suggested. " Safer !" The blood of all the Archers mounted to Isabel's cheek. "Safer !" she repeated. "Do you imagine, Mr. Hearne, that lam afraid? I love horses. There is something in a wild breezy gallop which makes me almost delirious with delight, and then you offer me an arm-chair! Thank you, no. I prefer the chestnut.

'" The—the other is more amenable to —to reason," observed Miss Summerby. "Miss Twankey always rode her. She said she was so— so thoughtful—such a Christian disposition, going down the hill. When Miss Twankey married the vicar, he forbade her to ride any more, and I don't like to sell anything. You wouldn't like me to sell anything?" she asked Geoffrey, looking at a moth on the curtain-pole. "It is not for me to dictate to you," replied Geoffrey, "but I don't think I would sell any animal which had belonged to me." "Well, I'd better be going," said Miss Summerby, metaphorically gathering herself up. "Luncheon will be ready at two, Miss Archer, or three, or whatever the usual time is. Mr. Hearne, have you settled with Meares about his rent?" -

"We will take him on our way back. Is he to be made to pay up ? " " I—l think he may have a month longer," said Miss Summerby. "Itis so difficult to remember when one's rent is due. He may have forgotten it.*

div.head: TITE HOUSE ON THI HILL,
div.p: TITE HOUSE ON THI HILL,
G. B. BURGIN. (Author of "A Quaker _Girl," c6c.)
PART 11.

'lsabel was received at the House on the Hill by the fattest woman she had ever seen. The park gates were of solid unpretending stone. A long avenue of sycamores led up to the entrance of the gardens. To the left of the house and somewhat behind it were the stables and outbuildings. To the right and, indeed, on the same terrace, was a square tower with small arched windows all the way up. It was as rugged and barren-looking as the house itself, and without the slightest preten- sions to architectural beauty or style of any kind. Before she had time to notice any further details, the carriage stopped at the stone porch, and the fat woman curtseyed .at her from the doorway, whilst Kinipple became purple with suppressed emotion in the moon-light. "Miss Mary Pilbeam," said the fat woman, again curtseying. "Kinipple, see that John brings up those trunks at once," and she again curtseyed to Isabel. Kinipple sulkily motioned to his subordinate, with an air which said plainly: "See how she orders me about before strangers. I have placed my head beneath this woman's chariot- wheel, and verily she abaseth me into the dust." "Miss Summerby's compliments, Miss," said the obese Pilbeam, " and she has retired to rest, not feeling very well. She will be down as usual in the morning. Would you like to go to your room? Follow me, Miss." She led the way across the hall, up the old oak staircase. Departed Summerbys looked from the wall in all the glory of mail armour and un- comfortable helmets which strongly resembled a modern stew-pan. They all had the same appear- ance of not being able to sit down with Joyous alacrity when tired. On the first landing were worthies in the flowing periwigs of the Georgian era. They all had the same supercilious expres- sion of not having been introduced to one another. Some of the ladies looked very wild indeed, as if they did not relish the indecorous proximity of so many cavaliers. " Yes, Miss," said the portly Pilbeam, pausing for breath on the landing. "They were a fine lot —all Summerbys. There ain't many left of 'em. Miss Summerby's almost the last." "Are you Miss Summerby's maid?" asked Isabel, glancing round the room allotted to her. "Bless you, no, Miss. I am the—the house- keeper. All the old servants were sent away before Miss Summerby came. Miss Summerby won't have a maid. I help her a little sometimes, but that is all." The room was not cheerful. All the walls were wainscotted. There was a suggestion of sliding panels about them which made Isabel feel uncom- fortable. Over the old-fashioned wooden four- poster hung a heavy green canopy—a green which was almost black. Indeed, the four-poster only needed the addition of wheels to make a very presentable hearse. The bed was draped with green to match the canopy. Anything less inTit- fog as a place of repose could not well be imagined. bmaller-sized ancestors than those on the staircase were dotted about the room. One picture repre- sented a headless lady, carrying her head under one arm and a riding-whip under the other. "That was Lady Mary," said Mrs. Pilbeam. "She was a brazen hussy; she was, begging your pardon, Miss, for my free speaking. In the wars between the Roundheads and Cavaliers, when old Sir John, her husbing, was a-fighting for the king, she fell in love with a Roundhead, Rupert Lisle of Lee. 'A crop-eared knave,' Miss Summerby calls him though I always thought a knave was part of a church. But here's your hot water, Miss." "Tell me about Lady Mary," said Isabel. "There isn't much to tell, Miss," said the fussy Pilbeam, pottering about, as she laid out Isabel's things; "and supper will be ready directly. Howsumever, this Lady Mary (look at her face, Miss, under her arm—she's exactly like the mis- tress) took to gallivanting about the lane below with Rupert Lisle, and Sir John came back unex- pectedly and killed 'em both. They say she cursed all the Summerbys, past and to come, and the only way Sir John could find to stop her tongue was to cut her head off. Every night she goes, with her head under her arm, down into the lane below to meet Rupert Lisle. I saw a white- faced bullock there one night, Miss, and I nearly had a fit. But your supper will be cold. Can I do anything more for you? That little door leads into the bath-room. Miss Summerby's room is at the end of the gallery."

Left to herself, Isabel looked round with a momen- tary feeling of discouragement. "What is the matter with me?" she said. "This grim old house suggests nothing but graves. I wanted excitement —adventure—something fresh. I wonder if I have found it. It is but scant courtesy of Miss Sum- merby to leave me to be received by a hireling. But I am unromantically hungry, although I never eat supper. An unwonted supper and that grue- some bed will bring on nightmare. I shall dream all kinds of unpleasant things, and wish myself back in that humdrum holy of holies, Bryanston Square. Ah, no; even the House on the Hill, which, by the way, is only half up the hill, ix better than that. Now for supper.' She opened the door, and went slowly down the old staircase, hoping that she might not meet the ghostly Lady Mary, with her head a in St. Patrick when he swam across the Liffey. Mrs. Pilbeam was waiting to show her the entrance to the dining-room. Standing composedly by the fire- place was Geoffrey Hearne. Isabel must have looked surprised. "I am afraid it is awfully improper," he said. "What would Mrs. Grundy eay ? Shall I retire to the tower? Take my little porringer and eat my supper there,' as the poet so pathetically puts it. I daresay, as a sacrifice to the conventionalities, Mrs. Pilbeam will consent to chaperone us." "Certainly, sir," said Mrs. Pilbeam, smiling upon them with maternal benevolence. "Let them as thinks 'arm do 'arm, is my morter." And with this modern equivalent of Honi soit qui mal pense, Mrs. Pilbeam took up her position behind Isabel, as if she had settled the matter. "You will have to cut up my supper for me, Mrs. Pilbeam;" said Geoffrey. "I can't do it with this hand until the stiffness goes off." Mrs. Pilbeam was in her element. She bustled about, talking with the utmost loquacity. It appeared that Miss Summerby did not like men- servants in the house. There were four maids and a cook, over whom Mrs. Pilbeam wielded a rod of iron. Kinipple was not amenable to her authority, and yet her sway over him was absolute save for periodical symptoms of rebellion which she promptly suppressed. Already, Isabel detected symptoms of a comedy. She had entered a new world. Discoverers of a new world generally had to feel their way. She pictured to herself Mrs. Archer's horror at the sight of her daughter te3te-d-tE,te with a prepossessing young stranger. There was a daring novelty about this innovation which com- mended itself to Isabel. She had been so long victimised by the conventionalities that she re- solved to amuse herself during her stay at the House on the Hill. The materials for amusement were not far to seek. By judicious handling, they might be made to afford gratifying results. There was an air of hearty cameraderie about Geoffrey Hearne which 'pleased her. She thought how very differently he would have behaved when com- pared with that other man who sometimes occupied her thoughts, although she angrily endeavoured to bury him fathoms deep in the ocean of forgetful- ness. But he would not be buried altogether. He pretended to have been very fond of Isabel. She believed him, until she found that there were debts and rumours ot debts, and that he imagined she had the wherewithal to satisfy thosa debts. Of course, the man had behaved contemptibly; there was no doubt about that. Still, there was a lingering tenderness in Isabel's heart for her first love which would not be wholly eradicated. He had only acted in accordance with the instincts of his kind. Marriage now-a-days was purely a matter of L. s. d. All the old nonsense about love was as out of date as Theocritus. People could not go over England clad in sandals and sheepskins, and engage in poetic contests for a dinner. The climate would not admit of it. Isabel resolved to have nothing more to do with sentiment. To live her life and feel it in every limb, to make existence as breezy as possible—these were her aims. She did not intend to rust; she would not be senti- mental ; she would get a little healthy enjoyment out of life. If the wound she had received some- times hurt, she would hide it--cast the pain from her—confront the world with a smiling face. Why should she wear rue for an episode? Love was

div.head: DELAMERE CAMP.
div.p: THE DELAMERE CAMP.
Interesting Manceuvres on Friday and Saturday.

Saturday was tbe final day of the tin eortant mitts, y manceuvres on DtlameroForear,in which 1,100 troops inducing &detachment of Volunteers fro n Warringt have participated under Major-General Hallam Par , commanding the North•Maiern Military Distric%

The previous day had witregsed an interestine deve- lopment of the scheme, which consisted of an invasion of Cheshire and an attempt to strike a bl,,vr at Blanches ter and the Ship Canal. Recent operatione bad resulted in the withdrawal of the home defenders fr, m North- wich in a northern direction, and the occupation of toe salt town by the invaders. A detached force of the enemy encamped by the Liverpool Sanatorium at Bingswood were notified by thi G.O.C. Blue (invaders) that a convoy of supplies was bring sent from Chester by the train road through K 8.11 and Delamere to Nrrthwich, They were c,mmanded to meet the convoy at Kelsall and escort it as far as Oak- mere Park, where an esdort from Northwich would he furnished.

The home defenders had a flying force in the neigh- bourhood of Crowton. This torce received orders to attack and destroy the convoy if possible. The eneraF took up a position at the top of Eddisbury Hill, sendio.: forward scoutS, etc., and an engagement occurred at Plover's Moss. The Blue (invaders) did not push for- ward rapidly enough to secure the railway crossinet otherwise the Red would have cxperienced some diffi- culty in getting at the convoy, the progress of which they succeeded in arresting temporarily•

The Blue force conslsted of tw„o troops of cavalry, a battalion of infantry, four R.F.A, guns (15-pounders), and one company ot mounted ud,antry. The Red force comprised two troops of cavalry, Yeomanry details, t wo 13.F.A guns, and one company battalion of infantry volunteers.

Major Browne, of the Royal Warwick Ilniment, com- manded the Bed force, while Major A 0 Vincent, Royal Marine Light Infantry, was in command of the Btu • The umpires were :—Red : Colonel Courtenay (chief staff officer headquarters, Chester N.-W. diet act), wbh whom was Captain Neil Haig (adjutant a the Earl of Chester's Imperial Yeomanry Cayahy) ' - Blue : Lieuteuan -Colonel Wand (O.C, Royal- 9rtillery N.-VV. district), and Captain Bunter (adjutant let V.B.C.R ). . The operations on Saturchy er.mmeno,d with the pr sunaption that the invaders had &en badly worsted 1 near Warrington, and were in full retreat. The horn, defenders' flying force near Hartford was detailed t:. pursue them, and, if possible, cut it off from the mail. body of the Blue force, who were retiring on Birkenhead I under cover of their fleet in the Mersey. The G.O.C. Blue irstructed the 0.C., the el,tached Blue force, to abandon the convoy they w re escorting and retire on Eleisby. This they endeavoured to accom- plish, making ass of De!amere Forest to cover the r retreat. Thy were however, intercepted near King - wood, the Red artillery coming into action on Hey Cliff when the enemy came within range in the neighhrtv- hood of New Pale and Manley. The Blue force, rakmsi every advantage of !Acme walls and hedges as screens, erdeavoured thus stealthily to pass the cliff, but the home defenders' gun effectually held them in check.

_ The Red force was made up of a battalion of infal try. Volunteers, a company of mounted infantry, two troops of cavalry, two R.F.A. gusts, and a cyclist section (Volunteers). They were ander the command of Major Cox, of the 7th Royal Fusliorss Major Talbot-, Roysl Artillery, cemmanded the Blue force, which was corn- posed of the remainder of the troops. The umpires wer” Courtmay (Red), with whom was Major Burrard, R.F.A. ; Lieut-Col. Bland, and Major )xley, D.A.A.G. (Headquarters Staff), (Blue). On Friday there was a very enjoyable sing-song camp fire at the Kingriwood Camp. Major-General Hallam Parr presided. The piano for the concert was lent by the authorities of the Liverpool Consumptive Sanate- /lure. On Saturday all the Volunteers left the camp and entrained for borne.
The Warrington Volunteers, arrived home between seven and eight o'elock.n the evening

EMMANUEL CHURCH. Harvest thanksgiving services were held in Emanuel Church, Bold-street, on Sunday, when there were large congregations. According to custom the church was not decorated. Mr Callen,of Cheshunt Colleue,preached at the morning and evening services. In the afternoon a well-attended lower service was held, and an addrees was given by Mr Callon. The lowers were afterwards distributed amongst the poor of the congregation and , others. • ST. BARN/4XAS' CHURCH. The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with St Barnabas' Church were continued on Sunday. The Vicar (Rev J H G Hollingworth) preached at the choral celebration of the Holy Communion in the morning, taking for his text the words " When thou haat eaten and art full, beware that thou forget not the Lord thy God." In the afternoon a childr an's service was held, the preacher being the Rev A 'agile. The church was filled in the evening, when the pulpit was °coupled by the Rev F E Powell; who based an eloquent sermon no the words" Walk in the spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lusts of the flesh. If ye be led of the spirit, le are not under the law."—The colleotioas were en behalf of the choir fund. GOLBORNE-STREET BAPTIST CHURCH. Harvest festival services were held in the above Church on Sunday last, and were largely attended. In the afternoon the choir rendered a service of song "River Singers " to a crowded congregation. Mr Owen was conductor, and Mr Dawson, L V.C.M , pre- sidtd at the organ. The Pastor occupied the pulpit morning and evening,and at the later service the enamel was filled to overflowing. On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held, when about 300 people were present. An enjoyable pr,gramme was gone through, including selections by the choir, songs by Miss Mansell and Mr and Mrs Annan," and recitals by Mr Sanders and the Pastor. Miss Dolly Buokby gave several pianoforte selections and Mr Owen had °herrn of the programme. The total proceeds amounted to £l9. ST. MICHAEL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN. The harvest thanksgiving services were eontieued at St Michael's and All Angels' Churehoon Sunday. The morning preacher was the Rev ES 0 iver, B. A. ,curate- in-charge. The Rev C 8 Richards arieisted at the ser- vice. In the evening the Rev E 8 Oliver took the ser- vice and the Rev H S Chesshire, M.A., vicar of St. Catherine's. Tranrnere, preached. The servieea were well attended. The singing of the choir WRB exeellent. The anthem was " Blessed be Thou,Lord Ood of Israel " (Merit) The quartette, duet and solo singers were R Moulton. F Weinwright and Messrs Hobson, J Blundell, W Hnpwood, J Roberts, J Wood and W Wishlade. Mr Ground gave a much appreciated organ recital prior to the service. ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN. The annual harvest thanksgiving services were held at St. Paul's Wesleyan Church, Runcorn, en Sunday. There were Dirge congregations. The morning preacher was the Rev J B Foster whose eubject was " The well watered garden." In the evening the Rev A Wells, superintendent minister, occupied the pulpit. EP spoke on harvest lesions, taking for his text" He reserveth unto us the appointed weeks of harvest," Jeremiah v. 24. Harvest hymns were sung at both services. The anthem "Swell the anthem" was sung in the morning' The solos were taken by Miss Withington and Mr John Leathwood. At the evening service the anthems were " Praise the Lord, 0 Jerusalem " and "Oh clap your hands all ye penple." In the first the tole was sung by Mr E Kniveton and in the second by Miss Ta. lor. Mr G Bowyer presided at the organ. The church was very tastefully and artis- tically decorated; in fact, it was questionable whether on any similar occasion the tokens of harvest bad been arranged with better taste and effect. The general appearance of the church was most effective and the decorators are to be complimented upon the suncess of their work. At the entrance was a table upon which was arranged a choice coliection of fruit and vegetable., the words " for the harvest is foil" being shown on an effective background. Inside the church the pulpit attracted special attention. Its decoration was a verit- able work of art. Flowers, fruit, vegetables and ferns were skilfully employed in a scheme that was both ornate and tasteful. In the centre of an elaborate cloth-like piece of work hanging from the pulpit was a beautiful Maltese cross of white flowers, and on either side were charmingly designed shields. The organ was also effectively treated. The windows and pillars were decorated in excellent taste, and the generally pleasing appearance of the body of the church was enhanced by hanging baskets of flowers. Shields on either side of the church bore the mottoes " Seed time and harvest never all "and "The earth is the Lord's."

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

THE ACCOMMODATION AT PADGATE SCHOOLS. A meeting of the above mentioned Board was held on Wednesday at the Workhouse. Mr A Brookes presided, and there were also present :—Dr Murray, Messrs S Davies, .1 Billinge, James Robinson, G Pilling, Alfred Jolley, George Mather, with J C Sutton (clerk), and A Wright (superintendent of Pulgate schools.) At a meeting ot the Padgate Schools Committee held on the 23rd of September it was resolved that Mrs Sarah Jane French, el Padgate, be appointed additional teacher at a salary of £B5 per annum. The question of pro- viding additional accommodation for children was con- sidered. The matter was, after discussion, adjourned for six months. Mr A J JOLLEY moved the confirmation of the minutes. Mr S DkVIEi seconded and the minutes were agreed to. Mr A J JOLLEY said he would like to state that he re- gretted personally the decision of the committee with reference to the accommodation question but same action might be necessary 'to relieve the pressure at Padgete. The feeling of some members, although not formally expressed, was that if the need arose they might Rend some of the grewn-up Roman Catholic chil- dren to schools controlled by the Roman Catholio body. Father Wilson informed the committee that the charge would be about 61 weekly per child and a small addi- tional sum for outfitting the children when they left the school. He (Mr Jolley) thought the Board ought to ascertain the cost officially and he therefore moved that the Clerk communicate with the Leyfield Roman Catholic -School far girls at Liverpool and the Fulwood Roman Catholic School for boys at Preston and ascertain the terms upon which children would be admitted. The CLERIC. said it would be very desirable before ~ deciding upon any ecbool that a small deputation should 0- visit the place. There had been a great deal of trouble -. lately with regard to some sehools. Mr A J JOLLEY said his object was only to ascertain the terms. - : Mr PILLING said the Runcorn Board of Guardians, of which he was a member, seat ,ts Roman Catholic sabildren to Pantassph in Wales, and Bucklow Hall, near Roehdale. He had visited these schools and they were . well!manfteed institutione.Pantssaph was really a lovely place He believed the charge to the Runcorn authority was only five shillings per child per week. Mr Mather thought the Clerk ought to ask for terms from these schools as well. Mr JOLLEY agreed to this and the proposition was unanimously agreed to. —0.—..... Fatality at a Lodging-house. An inquest was conducted at the Police Station on Wednesday, by Mr S Brighouse, county Coroner, touching the death of Patrick Lamph, aged forty years, who was found dead at the foot of the stairs at Caveney's lodging-house, Ship-yard. on Sunday morning.—Alexander Algie said he had known the deceased for about ten years,and Lamph had always been of drunken habits. Witness last aw him alive on Saturday, about eleven o'clock when he left his work.—Margaret Caveney said the deceased asked for a bed at the lodging-house on Saturday night, and she let him have one. He was then drunk. Next morning she was informed that deceased was lying at the foot of the stairs, and she sent for the police.—Patrick Glynn, a lodger, said she heard a noise about midnight as though someone Was falling downstairs. The next morning he found deceased lying dead at the foot of the stairs Dr Smith said that death was due to a fracture of the base of the skull. A verdict of i• Accidental .death "was returned.

Warrington Savings Bank. A return relating to trustee savings banks con- tains the amount of business transacted during the year. From this we collect the following relating to the Warrington savings bank. In this bank therP were 12,894 accounts oven, against 12,636, with £352,323 apainst £353,463 owing to de- positors. The total invested with the Com- missioners for the reduction of the National Debt was £31.051, against £352,22; balance in the hands of the treasurer £3,451, against £1,702 amount of separate surplus fund in the hands of the Commissioners, £3,700. against £3,300, and other assets .£1,300 against .Cl,3oo.making the total assets 1358,402. against £359,224; expenses of manage- ment £892, against £859.

Volunteer Inspection Ball. Success attended the annual inspection ball in connection with the local Volunteer Battalion which Wag held in the Drill Hall on Monday even- ing by permission of the cowman ling officer (Colonel Ridgway). The band of the battalion was in attendance and played a capital selection of lisle The catering, which gave entire satisfac- tion, was entrusted to the sergeants. The room was crowded,and altogether about 300 persons were present. The M.C.'s were Sergeant-Instructor Ingram and Quartermalter-Sergeant Willeockg. Dancing was kept up until an early hour on the following morning.

The South Lancashire Tramways. The trial run in the Leigh district of the South Lancashire Tramway Company's trams took place on Tuesday night. The car, which contained Mr Hutchins, chief traffic manager, Mr Salter, chief engineer, Mr Adam, a director, and Mr Krauss, of Bristol, the contractor, and others, left the general station at Howebridge,near Leigh,at eleven o'clock, amid the cheers of an interested crowd, and pro- ceeded through Atherton to Hulton Four Lane Pride, arriving back at Howebridge at one o'clock. The run was successful, the only delays being through the bearings of a wheel getting over- heated. The car service commences in three weeks.

A defendant at Huddersfield oa Wednesday was said to he deaf. As a witness was giving evidenne,however. not in a very loud voice, the defendant interjected a remark in the nature of a correction, and the court aughed.

div.head: First Division.
div.p: First Division.
WARRINGTON'S SURPRISE PERFORMANCE.

After a narrow victory over Brighouse Rangers at War- rington the week before. the" wire-pullers " journeyed to St Melons to play off their League engagement with the newly-promoted "Saint." Hallam and Isherwood were still absentees from the Warrington ranks, but the team turned out as selected. St Helens were also compelled to experiment by plaeleg Foulkes at half-back. The game was expected to be closely fought. with the odds slightly on the side of the hontesters, but Warrington rose to the °elision, and won easily by 18 points to 5 points. Mr dreetcheen of Oldham was the referee. There would be about 2,000 spectators when the teams lined out as follows : St Helena : Hunter, full back ; Bacon, Doherty. Barnes, and Livertage,threequarters ; Foulkes and Kennedy, half- backs ; Briers. Thompson, Carney, Green, Lee, Maguire. Prescott and Mooney. forwards. Warrington: Knight, full back ; Fish. Hoakenhall, Dickenson. and Harris, three-quarters ; Burgess and Edmunds, half backs ; Boardman, Morrison, Taylor, Roberts, W Swift, Jolley. Forster, and 'Edmondson forwards. Warrington started against the breeze and even play followed untie Green changed the venue with a long punt in touch. Wftrringten broke up the scrummage, and Forster got hold off-side and ran to the line before the whistle soun dad. The home team forced Warrington back slowly but surely with the aid of the touch line, until Foulkes kicked rather too strongly and the be I went in touch behind the goal line Warrington rallied and rushed down the field. Hunter mulling Dickenson's kick. Harris picked up and passed to Bdmondson, who was pulled down at the corner. Warrington maintained thell attack, Bdmundsinassed te Fish who euccumbea to numbers on the line after a tricky effort. Again the ball came out on the visitors' side and Fish ran down to the corner, whence he unexpectedly screwed the ball woes the goal to Harrie,who took it first bounce and ran round the posts without opposition, the Saints all having run arrest to intercept the wile Fish The latter added a goal. Warrington were now showing fine form, the backs giving St. Helens a lot to do. Harris intercepted once and looked a scorer when Hunter brought him down The home for- wards raised the hopes of the locals with a fine dribble which beat Knight, Edmunds going down and saving pluckily. Play was still in the Warrington half when Burgess got away from the scrummage, and gave Harris a timely pass. The wing man broke away and leaving his pursuers doubled Hunter and scored behind the posts after a brilliant run Fish again kicked a goal. The Saints. seemed quite nonplussed by the smartness of the visitors, who had vastly altered their tactics from the previous week and played the open game to perfeetioe. after Harris's second try there was a little ill-feeling shown and Edmunds retali- ated noon Lee for an unnecessary tackle. The referee sent both men off the field. Hoakenhall goidg half. Pi h centre,and Forster wing on the IVarrineton side. For a time St Helens showed better form, while Warrington "fell off" Doherty got away but was grassed near the line by Harris. Scrum- meges near the line followed and Foulkes ran in rather easily. Barnes adding a goal. From now to the interval the .ers had rather the best of matters, Barnes trying at goal again from Doherty's mark, but being unsuccessful' Half-time : Warrington 10 points, St Helens 5 points. Barnes re-started and with a fine kick found touch near the Warrington line. The attack was soon repulsed however and Warrington went to the other end where Liversage saved near the line. Warrington attacked hotly. Forster dropping at goal and coming Very near Pieces,. A brief visit to the Warringten half was made by the home forwards, who were always energetic. Ferster cleared and passed to Fish who ran half the length of the field, punted, and then upset Hunter near the goal a fine piece of work Hoek enh oil got possession from the pack and ran for the line with Dickenson and Harris in atter:clan". Just when a transfer was expeoted he swerved aud beating flunfer scored behind the posts, Fish kinking his third goal. Warrington were far too smart for the Saints and while scrummaging at the quarter line, Burgess passed out to Fish who dashed through the home backs and soored at the come-. On this occasion he failed at goal. There was only one team in it to the close and Dickenson would have scored, but Boardman's pass was badly judged. Final : Warrington. 3 goals, 4 tries (18 points) ;St Helens, 1 goal, 1 try (5 paints).

div.head: RUNCORN V. HUDDERSFIRLD.
div.p: RUNCORN V. HUDDERSFIRLD.

Played at Irwell-lane on Saturday before a good attend- I ann. both teams being strongly representative. The visitors wen the toss and Runcorn started from the town goal. Jones broke up a good combination.transferring play to the visitors' 25. Off-side play gave the home tern a good chance. but Jolley missed' the opportunity by bad fielding. Shortly after Kitchen got away butLarrard passed for ward when there was a good (Mance of breaking away. Flanigan made a good attempt to get through but failed, Jolley also having a futile shot at goal. Runcorn continued to press, and a score seemed immi- nent when the ball was kicked into touch. Dribbling tactics by the visitors gave Runcorn an anxious time, but the danger was cleared by the sterling work of the home backs I Houghton repeatedly found touch when pressed, and cleared I his lines repeatedly in tine style. Runcorn still maintained the upper hand, and after an exciting time Richardson scored after two or three magnificent attempts Farmer failed at goal. After this reverse the visitors played keenly but good com- bination between the Runcorn backs prevented any scoring. Half time, Runcorn, a try. Huddersfield, nil. On restarting liteadohongh saved a dangerous forward rush by kicking dead Runcorn still attacked strongly Kitchen and Larrard event sally clearing. The visiting backs played strongly after this and the homesters tied some little difficulty in maintaining their lines intact. Shortly after Jolley had to retire the visitors, during his absenee, straining every nerve to effect a score. At a critical moment Jolley reappeared and the whole eomplexien of the game was altered, Runeorn gained the upper hand and maintained it from some loose work in front of the visitors' goal Woods slipping in. Farmer failing to convert. Final: Runcorn a goal and two tries ; Hudders- field nil.

div.head: WALFORD v WIDNES.
div.p: WALFORD v WIDNES.

On Saturday Widnes journeyed to Salford, where the best game they have yet provided resulted in a victory for their entertainers by five points to nil. The teams lined up as fellows :—Salford Smith, Riley, Tom Williams. Bell, and /orris ; Lomas and Davies ; Tunny. Rhapps. J Brown. Heath, Shaw, Buckler. and Shore. Widnes : Tilley: Hughes, Whelan, Brown, awl Cohen; Lalley and Taylor; Aspey. Curtis, Power. Riley. Rigby. Leyshon. Webster. and Lynch. Referee. Mr B Ashton, Oldham, Some 6,000 specta- tors were present when Lomas opened for the homesters. the Widnesians, whe had the choice, electing to play down the field with the advantage of the wind. Sevecal serim- mages were fought in the vicinity of the Widnes goal. Widnes made a rush into the Salford territory, but there was little difficulty in staving off the danger. Dan Smith made a valiant attempt to open out the game Tilley, despite the attentions of several of the home players was pro- minent with a strung punt, which placed Salford on the de- fensive. Up to qusrter-time there was no scoring, though both sides worked hard from a scrimmage near the centre. Lomas received possession, and was only tackled on the line. Tom Williams and Lomas were prominent with smart work. and their efforts were for a long time unrewarded. Then clever passing between Williams and Lonaas resulted in the latter cleverly scoring, but the same player failed to convert. At this point play was going In faYour of Widnes. From a tree klek for off-side Salford relieved. Widnes repeatedly placed themselves on the attack by sending into touch, Tilley, their fall back, being an adept in this re- spect. There were so many packs that the game was very slow, and unfavourable comments were made by the specta- tors against the new rule abolishing the punt out from touch. Prom a drop out Salford again attacked warmly, but Tilley cleared. Brown made a desperate effort to get over for Widnes, but failed. The visitors continued to press, but the home defence was excellent. Just before the interval was reached Williams saved a forward rush which looked very dangerous. Half-time Sal- ford, one try (three points) ; Widoce. nil. In the second half, although Salford had had rather the better St the play, the visitors quite held their own, and Lemas's try was to some extent one cf those individual efforts for which the Cumberland man is so well known. At the re- start the crowd, which had increased, were at once treated to a series of exchanges by the backs, and some scrimmag- ing. From one of these Talley broke away and ran to the quarter fag, where Davies overhauled him. Cullen and Tilley were to the front in the defence, and the home lot were held until Norris broke away with a short run. A punt Into touch by Tilley brought the necessary relief, and a free kick by Widnes caused the home full back to reply ia similar fashion. Smith and Hughes exchanged without result, and Lomas filled to break through. Here Tilley made a blunder by passing to Hughes when the lattsr was net looking, and lost ground. Whelan, however, with a fine run, penetrated to within a few yards of the Salford goal

A meeting of the Northern Rugby League Committee was held at the Exchango Hotel, Manchester. on Tuesday even- hag. Mr Collins (Rochdale) presided. The Hull Club lodged a complant regarding T W Newlove, who had signed on for Normanton. It was alleged that the payer named had by doing so cornmitted a breach of League Rule VT. In the match St Helens v Warrington the referee, Mr McCutcheon. had omission to send off the field Lee, of St Helens. and D H ficimunds of Warrington for fighting: A fortnight's suspension was passed on Edmunds while the ex- tent of Lee's punishment was a month's abstention from play Abusive 'language wee laid to the acsount of Holliorake, of Todmorden, by t/r Kilner, and the player in question was suspended up to and including October IS. There were several impositions made for late start& Hull Kingston Rovers were fined 6s for this offence at Halifax,and Wakefield Bs in their match with Halifax Reserves The biggest fine of all was that of Brighouse who were mulcted ins sum of 40s for late start at Warrington. At Stockport. South Shields arrived behind time, and had to pay a penal y of 105 while Holbeck and Moreoambs were called upon to pay 'Ts 6d. The explanations of late starts by Idle, at Hudders- field, and that of Castleford, at Barrow were accepted.

WARRINGTON " A " DEFEAT wERNEFE.

Warrington "A" had Werneth for their opponents on Saturday, the match being played on the Wilder:spool enalosursa before a fair attendance. The visitors were strongly represented, several playe: a who lid duty for Oldham last season. Including Thomas, the county full-back, turning out. D Isherwood. the popular first team captain, figured in the Warrington three-quarter line, and played a capital game throughout. The teams were as follows :—Werneth : full back ; Brierley, Thomas, Taylor, and Price, three- qoarters ; Baldry and Belfield, half backs ; 3tubbs, Roscoe, Porter, Cockroft, Todd, South worth and Ronkh awe, forwards Warrington, Fillingham, full back ; Watkins. 13ro :ks, Isherwood, and Bailey. three-quarters ; Clare and Duckworth, halfbacks: Ashton, Harmer, Meaoock.Fairhurst Warburton, &film Wen, and Brady, forwards Fairhurst kicked off with the wind in his favour and the Warrington- fans at once attacked. A forward drit,ble relieved the visitors. Duckworth dribbled away, but, overran the ball when he had almost a clear field. A fine breakaway by Thomas. the old Oldham back looked like a certain seore.but Watkins saved splendidly. le. hot attack by Werneth resulted In a minor, Isherwood, Brooks, and Bailey each tried to get away. but the tackling was too keen Give-and-take play followed, until Thomas, by failing to drop a goal, caused another tonoh down After a spell of midfield pl .y. Isher- wood picked up in the loose, and eluding the opposing backs, got over the line amid loud sheers. He also added a goal. At the interval Warrington were leading by 5 points. After the interval play was very uninteresting, neither si .e put- ting much energy into their work, At length Fillinscham being tackled on his line kieked the ball into Brierley's bands, and the last-named player got over easily The kick at goal was abortive. There was no further scoring and time arrived with the result -Warrington 1 goal 1 try (5 points), Werneth I. try (3 points). WIDNES " A " v SALFORD "A." The Widnes second team opeuel their season on Saturday with a visit from Salford "A," whom they beat by two points to nil. Barber captained the Widnesians, tut lost the choice of ground. Widnes initiat .d the operations. and from the return the visitors worked their way by stages to the home 25. A fine passing bout enabled Barber to get going and he was well down the visitors' half before he was grounded. The Salford back section played with admirable spirit and made many sterling attempts, but these were discounted effectually by good, keen and effective tockling by the Chemicals. Suitt before half-time a grand effort was made by Barber. which fully deserved a score The second half was very similar to the first, the game being vigorous and well contested In the opening stages Salford had slightly the advantage, but later on Widnes asserted them- selves, and a goal was kioked, giving them a final lead of two points

div.head: Another Success by the Apollo Choir._
div.p: Another Success by the Apollo Choir._

At Tyllesley Kisteildiod la-t Saturday the War- rington Apollo Male Voice Choir, under the con- ductorship of Mr Harry &Trey carried off the first prize, value £lO, for the best rendering of the test piece " Wyr Phitistia " (Valiant Warriors) from "David and Goliath" (D Jenkins). Tne adjudicator was Mr J I Jones of Liverpool. His adjudication on the Apollo Ch,tir was :—" This choir are a fine body of singers, voices equal all round. The in- tonation, balance, tone, tune, expres-ion phrasing was splendid and without further comment this choir unioubteely deserves the prize." The posi- tions of the choirs were 1, Warrington Apollo, 2, Medium Welsh Choir, 3, North Manchester, Our readers are reminded that the Apollo Choir will give their second annual concert in the Parr Hall on Monday evening next. A splendid programme has been arranged, the following being the artistes: —Miss Ethel Parr, Miss Annie Dennett, Mr Harry Berrey (conductor of St Helens Prize Choir), Mr R Hamblett. Mr Topping, Mr Wilson Blackledge ;humorist), Mr Harry Berrey's operatic company (sixteen voiles) and the Apollo Male Voice Choir.

How little position and wealth of themselves bring happiness has never been more exemplified in the case of anyone than Queen Marie Henriette of Belguim, who died suddenly at Spa at the end of last week. Born at Pesth, on August 23rd. 1836, she was the daughter of the Archduke Joseph. Palatine of Hungary, and Marie Duchess of Wurtemburg, and at the age of seventeen was married to Leopold, Duke of Brabant, first by proxy at Schonbrunn and then personally at Brussels. She was very beauti- ful and, through imbued with all the haughtiness

div.head: LATE QUEEN OF THE BELGIANS.
div.p: THE LATE QUEEN OF THE BELGIANS.

of the Hapsburgs, by her grace and vivacity won the hearts of the Betgian Court. At the time all looked bright for her, and it seemed as though the gipsy's prophecy of her unhappy life was not to be realised : but soon it began to work itself out in the most literal fashion. First came the death of her brother-in-law, the Archduke Maximilian, who had been made Emperor of Mexico by the Powers, but had no easy throne, which came to an end by revolution; and then tke troubles she had passed through bereft the Empress Charlott,e, Maximilian's wife, of her reason. It was about 'this time that her consort became King of the Belgians, and four years later her heart was almost broken by the death of her dearly loved son, the Duke of Brabant, the heir to the throne, at the age of ten. Ip 1875 her eldest daughter, Princess Louise, married Prince Philip of Saxe-Coburg, and was driven mad by the union under circumstances too painful to dilate upon. In 1881 her second daughter, Prin- cess Stephaine, married the Crown Prince of Austria : and all the world knows the terrible tragedy of hieyerling. Then the widowed princess insisted upon marrying Count Lonyay, and was consequently estranged from her family. So estranged indeed are all the family that there have even been painful scenes in the death- chamber itself. For many years Queen Marie Henriette has lived a most retired life; and since her severe illness two or three years back it has simply been a case of awaiting the end, which came so suddenly and peacefully at last Rumour is naturally always rife about such an important parti as the heir-apparent to an European empire, and nobody's name has been so frequently coupled with eligible princesses as that of the Crown Prince of Germany: but hitherto all such gossip has proved to be groundless. During the last few days, however, the German papers have been most persistent in declaring that the Crown Prince's engagement will not be long postponed: and the young lady to whom they join his name is Princess Alice of Albany, one of the most thoroughly English of all our princesses. She is charmingly pretty and is a great favourite not only with our
PRINCE OF GERMANY AND PRINCESS ALICE OF ALBANY,

WHOSE ENGAGEMEIT IS SHORTLY EXPECTED IN GERMANY. but also with the German OWD royal family, Emperor and his Consort : and such a union would be highly popular on all sides. Princess Alice is. of course, the daughter of the late Prince Leopold., the Duke of Albany, whose early and tragic death was such a sorrow to the late Queen. Since then his widow has made her home in England at Claremont Park, Esher, and has brought her two children up in thoroughly English fashion, sending her son to Eton until he became Dukeof Saxe- Coburg-Gotha two years ago. The Duchess of Albany, who is a sister of the Queen Dowager of Holland, however, continued to reside in England with Princess Alice in the neighbourhood where they are so popular. The mother and daughter are staying at present at the Villa Ingenheim, at Potsdam. and the Princess Alice visits the Kaiserin at the Palace daily. The Crown Prince is known to be very favourably disposed towards England—.

Drury Lane always gives the theatrical world a big sensation every autumn: and as a rule, its drama takes its tone from the topics of the time. Hence this year it is most fitting that The Best of Friends should deal with the lately concluded wax in South Africa, and various phases of the social relations involved. Naturally it is as full of tableaux and sensations as ever, if not a trifle more so, with a great mechanical contrivance to rescue the heroine at the critical moment. The whole play is typical of Drury Lane, and Drury Lane at its best: and Mr. Arthur Collins and Mr. Cecil Raleigh, who work so well together as producer and author, have to be heartily congratulated upon the success of their united efforts. They have a knack of getting hold of an idea of the moment and working it up to suit the popular taste in a marvellous manner, combining it with the most lavishing expenditure in production and the most extraordinary sensa- tions in mechanics, to give the whole realism, Puck as can be got at no other theatre. The greatest tableau of the play is "The Last Kopje," which is a most impressive sight and brings home some of the situations in the late war very vividly. There are, also, Boer spies and agents, treacherous and.

_ PERSONS CONClu.n...— . THE -RY LANE DRAMA, " THE REST or FRIENDS." gallant Britons and Boers, and many other familiar figures in the popular eye. In fact, Mr. Raleigh; has done for the late Boer War in The Best ofi Friends what Messrs. Conquest & Pettit did at Druryi Lane many years ago for the Zulu War with The Queen's Colours. It may not be history, but it Is a vivid picture of the times making facts realised by its realism. The centre) figure of interest is Mrs. John Wood, the doyenne of the stage, who, has a very good part in the new drama and met! with a great reception on the first night. The, production, as usual, reflects the utmost credit on the management and all concerned. Paris, the home of agitations and sensations, has found its latest cause for controversy and excite- ment in the recall of the Due de Montebello from St. Petersburg. where he has represented his country for nearly twelve years. All sorts of stories, piquant and malicious, are on the tip of every Parisian tongue, to account for this most unexpected and surprising action on the part of the new French Government, who are said to, have been actuated .by the pettiest of motives in the matter. The fact remains that it is mainly thet. Due de Montebello, who has engineered the Franco- Russian eutente cordial', through his personal popu- larity at the Court of the Czar, who is so great; a friend that he stood godfather to the Duke's latest born, when he was visiting Compiegne last year. The fact is that at that very time the Ambas- sador to St. Petersburg gave the gravest offence .to the more bourgeois members of the French Cabinet by his absence of friendly social relations with them,so much so that no quarters were allotted to him at Corn. THE 1,. piegne and he THE TRENCH AMBASSADOR AT found the great- Sr. PETERSBURG, WE) Tus eat difficulty in JUST BEEN RECALLED, getting a peed-a- • terre for the christening ceremony! Thus relations became very strained; and, while the Duke was said to have lost the confidence of the Quai D'Orsay, he on his side found himself unable to see eye to eye. with the Republican Government on many matte. Hence his recall by M. Delcasse from an originaHy petty dispute. After a series of secretaryships, he was first appointed to Munich and Brussels, ' and between eleven and twelve years ago, was sent as Ambassador to St. Petersburg_ 1 His tenure of office has been marked by most important results; and his recall is consequently regarded as a poor return in many quarters.

div.p: „ live in history. ,he is a first-class cruises of 14,200 tons, with a speed .)f 22-4 knots, and a complement of 840 men. Com- missioned at Portsmouth on March 24th, 1898, by Captaiu C. G. Robinson. in September, 1899, she was taken over by Captain Percy Scott and started for the China station. At Capetown she was stopped on account of the war; and it is now history how Captain Scott improvised mountings and ran big guns up to Ladysmith. Proceeding on ,her way, the 7errible reached Hongkong on May Bth, 1900. in time to ' take part in quelling the Boxer rebellion, landing men and. guns for the storming of Taku and the relief of the Legations. Then her crew managed to raise the dredger, Canton, Ricer, which was sunk by a typhoon in November, 1900; and while at Hong- kong they set up a world's record with their shooting, making wonderful practice owing an invention of Captain Scott, who is a brilliant inventor in conection with gunnery; and then they established a marvellous coaling record, which will stand for a long while. Truly a great commission and worthy of the finest traditions of the British Navy!

No much so, in fact, as to excite considerable jealousy in his own country; and with the fair sex he is very susceptible. Recently there was a stupid canard about coupline the Prince with an American lady; but that wakeaken for what it was worth. It is more than likely, if not absolutely certain, that he will marry an English princess; and it would be no matter for surprise if the German papers were correct in their surmise about pretty Princess Alice of Albany. Such a union would be hailed with real pleasure in England.
