MR. BALFOUR made a Withdraw or graceful speech at Had- Dissolve." dington which, while it contained very little of political iaterest, was none the less a rather interesting personal revelation. The remark that, whatever may happen to himself er his party, the Premier of these islands is quite certain to be a Scotsman was amusing, and can displease no one but a certain politician from Bir- mingham. More serious was the dissertation on party government. Mr. BALFOUR thinks that this political system succeeds only when the differences between parties are real but not fundamental. They must be real, otherwise politics become merely a heated struggle between the ins and outs; while, in his view, they cannot be funda- mental without endangering the public peace. This is highly characteristic. Mr: BALFOUR fails just because he refuses to believe that his onpon- eats really are in earnest about fundamental principles. He is convinced, for instance, that the opposition to his Education Bill is factious and insincere. It is rather a pity that he was at Haddington on this particular afternoon. If he had chanced to be at Leeds instead, when 80,000 people assembled on Woodhouse Moore, he might 11 have changed his mind. Working men do not give up their half-holidays, and pay their fare by special train, to voice an insincere opinion. Neither do Trade Unionists combine with Liberals and Free Churchmen to utter a mere party cry. The West Riding believes profoundly in its School Boards, and it does not wish to see them displaced by an undemocratic authority, which will represent nobody and control nothing. Nor is it prepared at this time of day to abandon the :ancient principle of "no taxation without representation." If Mr. BALFOUR can organise an equally enthusiastic and unanimous mass meeting in support of his bill let him persist with it. If not the only honourable course is to accept the alternative of the Leeds resolution—" withdraw or dissolve." This Government was elected by a trick on a wholly irrelevant issue. It has no man- date whatever to destroy our present educational system and to build another on sectarian founda- tions.
IN the last of the No Popery—Dr Clif- ford and Lord Halifax. series of letters contri-

buteu by Dr CLIFFORD to the "Daily News on the subject of the Edu- cation Bill, he brought a serious charge against Lord HALIFAX and the English Church Union. Practically it amounted to this—that he and those members of the Church of England who worked with him had made deliberate attempts to subject their Church to the domination of the Pope and the Church of Rome. Lard ITALIFA.x and Mr HILL, the lay secretary of the English Church Union, repudiated the charge as "abso- lutely untrue," and challenged Dr Clif- ford to produce proofs of the accuracy of his statement. This the Doctor found no difficulty in doing; for he was able to cite passages from speeches delivered by Lord HALIFAX which, if interpreted in the plain sense of their words,could mean that and nothing else. They were passages in which Lard HALIFAX expressed his earnest de- sire for the "union of Christendom" and "the restoration of unity with the members of the Church abroad, East and West alike, but above all with the groat Apostolic See of the West " ; and asked whether there is a"single instructed Christian who would not prefer LEO XIII to the Privy Coun- cil;' and "welcome with his whole heart any advance on the part of LEO XIII. which might facilitate the renewal of those relations between I:England and It erne which bound St. Augustine, the first Archbishop of CANTERBURY, to St. Gregory the
Great and the venerable traditions of the Romani
Church." Lord HALIFAX may give what explana- tion he likes of these words of his, but plain Englishmen will interpret them to mean that he would like to subject the English Church to the

Papacy, and that is a thing they will not submit to. If a large section, as is alleged, of the Church of England agree with Lord Eamrax,then English- men who value their freedom and prize their liberty are bound to resist a measure like the
Education Bill, which will give opportunity and power to those clergymen to train the minds of the children of the country in these pernicious doctrines.

In the absence of a reply from Lord Halifax to Dr. Clifford's vindication, Mr Hill wrote a letter in which, finding himself unable to contradict or disprove the specific charges made against his patron, he sought to minimise their effect by abus- ing Dr. Clifford and praising Lord Halifax lo this letter he spoke of the "large-hearted toler- ance "of Lord Halifax "for such men as Dr. Clifford." What impertinence! Who is L3r3 Halifax that he should exercise " tolerance" towards Dr. Clifford ? If great Britairt were polled it would be found that for one man or woman that kn3ws and respects the former there are a thousand by whom the latter is loved and r3vered. Within the narrow bounds of the

div.head: English Church Union, Lord Halifax may be
div.p: English Church Union, Lord Halifax may be

worshipped as a little Pope. But Dr. Clifford name and reputation as an eloquent advocate el political and religious liberty and justice, as a champion of the weak and oppressed, as a fearless foe to tyranny and wrong, are known all over the Empire. But even if it were not so—if Lord Halifax were famo•is and Dr. Clifford obscure-- where is the ground for tolerance on the part of the one towards the other Dr Clifford is checked by no bonds such as the Establishment enables the
Slate to impose on the Church of which Lord Halifax is a member. In his largo freedom he call pity the President of the English Church Union, whose aspirations for union with Rome sr°

baulked by the decrees of Parliament. Fro' Lord Halifax and his followers he has nothing to ask and nothing to gain. His rights and his liberties were won for him more than a centurf ago by men who repudiated the tenets and re" sisted the pretensions of the Lord Halifaxes of their day. It is not, therefore, tolerance or tolera- tion that he asks; that is already his legal and unchallengeable right. It is justice, or, rather,the prevention of flagrant injustice, such as the passing of the Education Bill would inflict on him and other Nonconformists. It is for the fall freedom, the complete equality, which the bigotry and selfishness of the Church have checked and mut"' lated, that he is fighting so bravely; and he claims and demands them, not "with bated breath and whispered humbleness" as a concession or a boons but as a right. Let all true Britons, all "Go' Englishmen," as Milton .called the stalwarts of his day, rally to his side!

Iris an interesting rumour De Beers and which ascribes to the Taxation. Treasury the intention of suing the great DE BEEus diamond monopoly for the income-tax which it has never yet paid silica its foundation. The million or so which plight be raised in this way would be some little help towards paying for the war, especially if the other South African mining companies were treated la like manner. It was at aDE BEZELS' shareholders meeting that Mr RHODES explained that the Unime

Jack was their greatest asset. It is an asset that must be paid for. If this news be true then we' may hope that the Colonial Office will really saddle the Transvaal mine-owners with e considerable share of the debt incurred by in a war which they provoked, and froM which they alone will profit. It is said thfo Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is thinking of fixing this sum at £loo,ooo,ooo—about half the cost of the War. It would not be an excessive proportion; and the mineslare well able to pay. In 1899 Mr. Hays 11.A.3t- moNo, the expert of the Consolidated Goldfielda Company, calculated that as a result of the war the mines stand to gain a sum of 2t millions per annum in increased dividends. Every penny of this would be unearned profit. Why, in the name of justice,should a gang of cosmopolitan financiers, already rich beyond the dreams of avarice, be allowed to pocket this money quietly ? It has been earned by the price of our soldiers' lives and the nation's sacrifices. It is ill-gotten gain at the best. But assuredly the BESTS, the EmsrEnts,the JOELS, the ALBUS, and the GOERTZS have rie moral right to it. This sum alone would almost suffice to pay the interest on a Transvaal war loan of 100 millions. We need not scruple to claira it. Large as the sum is, moreover, it will be greatly increased when the new reefs which have been discovered are in working order. But let us have a care how we impose this taxation. It la all very well to make our claim for a war debt. But we have no right to treat the Transvaal as a tributary State, which can be bled for our benefit- If we try to tax South Africa from London we shall fail, as GEORGIE 111. did in America. Taxa- tion and representation must go hand in hand. We may imagine that the burden falls merely on a few financiers. But South Africa as a whole has a claim to the fruits of the mines and, we shall find that the colonists will be solid against any attempt to levy tribute through an autocratic dictator. The moment taxation begins on any large scale we are bound to concede representa- tive government. Even a millionaire has a right to appeal against an assessment on his property- There are grave possibilities of future trouble ia this difficult situation.

The short but emphatic Memorandum issued by Lord Roberts with reference to" ragging" in the Army closes the unpleasant incident of the ill- treatment of Lieutenant Gregson at Windsor by his fellow-officers of the 2nd Life Guards. The results of that incident have already been unfor- tunate enough to warn others against a repetition The victim of it has been allowed six months' leave, and will on its expiration be transferred to another corps, one captain has been core - polled to resign his commission, and several lieutenants have suffered the penalty of having their leave stopped for some time. The pritc- tice of " ragging " must, the Commander-in-Chief declares, be put down; and he lays particular stress on the fact that officers who show zeal and love for their profession deserve all honour and every en- Couragement. That " keenness " was the crime which led to the "ragging" of Lieutenant Gregsoll, is practically proved by the emphasis which Lora Roberts lays on this point, and it is considerablY to the discredit of the whole of the officers of the 2nd Life Guards that thous should be the regiment which has been the cause of the Issue of the Memorandum under notice. Tile Commander-in-Chief has s!iewn—both in this matter and in the Army Order dealing with musketry training issued last week—that in regards the future of the Army as in the hands. 01 the officers. Lord Roberts did his early soldiering e the in a school where keenness and efhcloneY Wer

only paths to promotion for the unknown young man. Unfortunately the Army at home is not as the Army in India was, or is; but just as Lord Roberts succeeded in infusing the Artillery—to take an example—in India with his own enthusiasm, and producing results in artillery practice the efficiency of which astonished the authorities at home, so he may rouse the officers here to a better sense of the responsibilities of their profession, and make the British Army what it should be—the best in the world.

At the present moment the fate of "Table Tennis" seems to be trembling in the balance. Is the game to have anything like the vogue it en- joyed last winter, when the miniature net was set up on every parlour table, and young and old de- voted themselves to the study of volleys and returns? The manufacturers, of course, hope for the best; and "Ping Pong " sets, and all the paraphernalia of the game, are beginning to be prominent in the shop windows. The two Associa- tions which aspire to rule the game, and are not willing to coalesce into one authority, have been holding their annual meetiu gs,discussing suggested alterations of rules, and acting in every way as if ping-pong, or table tennis, had not only another season of great popularity before it, but , were as certain of immortality as chess or draughts. At places where tournaments were held last winter there was also signs of activity, and fresh competitions are being announced for local or pro- vincial championships. These matters, however, are only machinery; the future of ping-pong de- pends solely on the attraction it possesses for those who play it. It is undeniable that there was a great falling-off of the interest in the early summer, and that where public tables have been kept open their use has steadily diminished up to the present. Now is the time, if at all, for a re- vival of practice. The next week or two will prob- ably show whether the game is to be regarded as a permanent social institution, or whether it will sink merely into a pleasant little pastime useful for keeping from mischief the inmates of the nursery.

For a moment it seemed as though the Irish Land Question were in a fair way of settlement. Influential landlords Lords Mayo and Castletown, the O'Connor Don and Captain Shawe-Taylor were working for a compromise and a round table conference. Mr. Redmond, Mr. T. W. Russell and Mr. O'Brien were only too ready to join it But the real chiefs of the uncompromising land lord caste, Lord Abercorn and Lord Barrymore will have nothing whatever to do with the scheme It is to be feared that the struggle, aggravated by Mr. Wyndham's revival of the Coercion Act, will now proceed to its suicidal conclusion. It is an ugly propect Coercion simply removes the ordinary safeguards of freedom, and subjects the majority to the mercy of removable magistrates of the landlord class, packed Protestant juries and Sergeant Sheridans. That hero is not yet for- gotten. A London policeman named Rolls has just been tried for an unsuccessfal plot against a citizen, and convicted of perjury. Sheridan succeeded not once but four times. Ile had accomplices. One of his innocent victims died in gaol, others lay there for years. And yet Mr Wyndham steadily refused to put him on his trial. That contrast is not lost upon the people of Ireland. They ask why police-perjury is punished in London and protected in Ireland. It is this sort of partiality which is fatal to our administra- tion. We refuse Home Rule. We refuse to settle the Land Question. Our one important device is coercion and more coercion'.

A significant more has just been made by the Cheshire Lines Committee, which, desirous of ex- tending the traffic between ;St Helens and South- port and having no direct line between the two places, has allied itself with the tramways coin- panies which connect St Helens with Knotty Ash Station, from which point the Committee has a direct line to Southport. Intending visitors to the" Eastbourne of the North " from St Helens can therefore go direct by tram to the station and thence by rail in an expeditious manner. This is a most commendable piece of enterprise on the part of the Railway Company, and one which should arouse much interest in this part of the county, seeing that South-West Lancashire is fast being covered with a perfect network of tramlines and light railways. The Cheshire Lines Committee's smart move may cause other companies to follow suit, greatly to the benefit and convenience of intending travel- :ors. A new era in the method of getting quickly from one place to another seems to have dawned, and the inhabitants of this busy, crowded part of the County Palatine will feel grateful for the allur- ing prospect opened up by the enterprise of the Cheshire Lines Committee.

Warrington and District Teachers' Association. A meeting of the vVarrington and District Teachers' Association was held on Saturday, in the Heath Side Boys' School. Mr WFt Stansfield, 8.A., presided over a fair attendance. Messrs Unsworth (president), Morgan (ex-president) and Bradley (secretary)attended aq a deputation from the South East Lancashire District Union to press the claims of that Union on Warrington Teachers. Each mem- ber of the deputation proved eloquen; and convinc- ing in advocating Federation,with the result that it was unanimously decided that the Warrington Teachers' Association become affiliated with the South East Lancashire District Union. A discussion on the local aspects of the Education Bill, was ow- ing to the lateness of the hour, adjourned, after some instructive remarks on the question from Messrs Stanfield, E Wallington and Upson. Mr George Snarplas of Manchester was nominated for the vice-presidency of the National Union of Teachere,and four new members of the Warrington Association were elected.

, MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN. On Saturday afternoon a sailors' and workers' garden party was given by Mr J T Rodgers, of Liverpool, in splendid weather. Games and sports were held in the Mersey Mission Recreation Field, Holloway, which was gaily decorated with bunting After games of football, &c., the sports commenced. The events included a flat race, kangaroo race, three-legged race, blind jockey race, skipping rope race for ladies, &c. A substantial tea was after- wards provided at the Institute. ' There were more than 600 present. After tea, Mr Shaw, missionary, Runcorn, presided, Captain WC M Kinnon, of the ship Belford, distributed the prizes to the success- ful competitors, after which Captain H H Dexter, of the Samaritan, entertained the party with some gramaphone selections. Mr !Shaw proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr Rodgers for his hospitality and generosity This was seconded by Captain Kinnon, and carried wish acclarnation,three hearty cheers being given. A vote of thanks was passed to Captain Dexter for the gramaphone enter- tainment. The proceedings, which had proved most enjoyable,concluded by the singing of the Doxology. INTERESTING LETTER TO THE CHAIRMAN OF THE URBAN COUNCIL. The following letter has been received by Mr S Taylor, J.P., chairman of the Runcorn Urban Dis- trict:Council,idated, 22nd August,--" Tubbalf ion, Bengal, India, to the Chairman of the Urban Dis- trict Council. Dear sir,—l received with pleasure yesterday the Coronation letter and postal order forwarded by you on behalf of the inhabitants of Runcorn as a Coronation gift to ten members of his Majesty's forces belonging to Runcorn who had been on service in South Africa. lam sure it does great credit to the people of Runcorn to think of those who are thousands of miles away from home fighting for King and Country; and I can assure you I deeply appreciate their kind gift. We all herd out here with regret of the illness of His Majesty the King the night before Coronation day but were glad to hear later that His Majesty was progressing. I should very much have liked to have been in Runcorn for the Coronation celebra- tions but shall keep the letter as a souvenir. Hoping you are in good health, your obedient servant, Geo Percival, (Sergeant, 2nd South Lanca- shire Regiment).

The Thelwall Nuisance is still productive of ani- mated debates in the Rural District Council Cham- ber. On Tuesday the matter engaged the attention of the Council for a long time, due probably to the fact that it was a wet day. As the chairman re- marked" It is a wet day. gentlemen, and we may as well discuss this matter in here as be outside" (Laughter.) Such a remark may be humorous but it is certainly not business. This, however, aptly illustrates the attitude of the Council when the subject is to be discussed Usually, there are plenty of more or less humorous remarks respecting Mr Naylor, the nuisance; and things in general. Of course it may be pleaded that something is required to enliven the monotony of investigating a nuisance which has occupied the attention of councillors for upwards of font years. But it may justly be urged in reply that a matter of such gravity does not admit of levity, however much the tempation may be to indulge. The fact is that the Council, being sick of the whole matter, is inclined to let the nuisance go on in its own sweet way irrespective of conse- quences. This is neither right nor proper. If the nuisance had existed from time immemorial it is no reason why it should continue for ever. What the Local Government Board will decide when it receives Mr Naylor's reply to Dr Adams' report, is hard to say. The easiest way out of the difficulty for all concerned would be a Local Government Board inquiry.

Mr Hough, it is pleasing to record, has been offici- ally appointed to the position of assistant clerk to the Guardians and the Rural District Council. Mr Hough is to be congratulated on his appointment, and it is to be hoped that it will materially improve his prospects in climbing up the ladder.

The oldest debating society in the town has now fairly commenced it Winter Session. Mr Douglas Moore the energetic secretary to the Brunswick Mutual Improvement Class will be only too pleased to see at the weekly meetings any who will not be afraid to splinter a lance in defence of their belief. A capital programme has been arranged and anyone with Wednesday evening to spare could not do better than attend these meetings.

A FLOATING -MORTUARY SUGGESTED.

Mr E S Turner, General Manager of the Weaver Navigation,Northwich, wrote acknowledging the receipt of the Clerk's letter of the 10th just and stated that he would lay it bef we the Executive Committ le on the 25th. Meantime he wrote to pint out that the Weaver Trustees have no buildings along the lower portion of the navigatioo from Winnington to Weston other than the lock and bridge tenders' houses and the bridge hot at the bridges across the Navigationtwhich as the Council would readily understand are in constant use. He might also say that the trustees were entirely ot the view of the Council that it was not healthy for &cora- posed bodies to be placed near to dwelling houses and that if suitable accommodation was not to be found that it should be provided by the proper authority. He was unaware whether the Council was the proper authority but he feared the trustees would be unable for the reasons above given to help the Council in the anatter. If the Council had any specific suggestion to make in the matter he would be glad to have it in time to lay it before the committee with the previous letter. It was resolved on the proposition of Messrs. S Wood- ward and Mclntyre that the Clerk write to the Weaver trustees stating that a floating mortuary would be the best thing to cope with the present state of affairs and asking them if they would assist the Council in the pro- vision of one and allow facility for the moving of such a mortuary.

THE BUCKLOW ORPHANGE,

Mr Edwards .-presented the report of the committee appointed to visit thelPantasaph and BucklowOrpbanage They were received by the lady superior and conducted over the place everything being found to be most satis- factory. They had eleven girls there who were being thoroughly trained for domestic service. Tnese children were not restricted from going to any place not con- nected with the Roman Catholic faith, the Superior telling them that all they wanted for them wets respect- able hemes• On the 19th they visited Bucklow where they had two boys. These were trained to a trade such as shoe making, tailoring, carving &c. Mr Wright seconded remarking that it was a pity that the Church of England had not similar institu- tions. The Chairman said that one good feature of such homes as Bucklow Orphange was that if s boy had any particular trait it was carefully developed. Such in- stitutions turned out good men and were a blessing to the country. cMr Gleave supported, paying a high tribute to the work of the institution, and the report was adopted.

div.head: VACCINATION ACT.
div.p: THE VACCINATION ACT.
Exemptions at Widnes and Earlestown. Magistrates and the Law.

At Widnes, on Tent to lay, John Marshall, Oakland-st., a waterman by occupation,applied through Mr Poole for a vaccination exemption order. Applicant briefly stated his objection, which did not amount to a tangible one. Mr Neil asked applicant to listen to him,for a minute." I see you are only young, and perhaps you will not quite remember the epidemic some year.; ago."—ipplicant : Ne.—Mr Ned : You don't see or hear of people having smallpox now?—Applicant stated that doctors would not gualantee the lymph pure.—Mr Neil : The lymph is pure by Act of Parliament.—Applicant : As God made children man cannot mend them.—Mr Neil : Tnen you don't believe in science P—Applicant : Yes ; but they cannot mend God's handiwork.—Mr Poole (addressing the bench) : Is not that a conscientious objection P—Mr Brown : Then we have no option but to grant it. The Rev James Sutcliffe, Coogregational minister of Golborne, applied to the Newton magistrates on Thurs- day for a vaceinatien exemption certificate in respect of his chtld.—The Clerk (Mr Greenall) : You conscienti- ously betieve that vaccination will be prejudicial to the child's health P—Mr Sutcliffe : Yes—The Chairman (Mr Gillespie) : What are your objeCtions to it. —Mr Sutcliffe.—l think that the risk is greater than the prevention. I have known cases where trouble has arisen from vaitcination.—Mr Gillespie: You have not convinced us as to the ground of your objection, and unless you do we cannot grant the order.—Mr Sutcliffe : I personally object to it very strongly indeed, and I sweat that I believe it will be prejudicial to health. dow is it that the Government does not order children over seven years of age to be revaecinated,w hen the vaccin ition is stated to have lost its effect ?---The Chairman: this is not a case of revacci- nation.—Mr Greenall : They were not ordered to be revaceinated.—Mr Gillespie : I advise you to get the opinion of some medical men on the subject, and ascer- tain whether there is any danger in vatAnation, You have only given us your opinion. If an attack of small- , pox creaks out you would be the first to have your child vaccinated. We shall refuse the certificate.—Mr Greenall : You cannot do that, sir. If he swears you must grant it.—Mr Gilespie : We cannot refuge it, but I should strongly recommend you to think the matter over, and take the opinion of some medical person. The Chairman refused to sign the certificate, and passed it to Mr Unsworth to sign.

FAILURE OF A ST MELEES GLASS MERCHANT. At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court on Wednesday, Walter Samuel Hadley, a glass merchant of the Hard- sbaw Brook Work9,S; Efelens,came up for public exami- nation. The statement of affairs shows liabilities of £1,312, and assets of £sB2,leaving, a deficiency of £730. —The bankrupt who was examined by tbe Official Re- ceiver, said that up to 1895 he had been assistant mana- ger in a glass works at Sutton, receiving a salary of £6OO per annum. The company went into liquidation, and be then started in partnership with a Mr F W Sef- ton, and traded as Hadley. Sefton, and Co., at Man- chester, as glass merchants, silverers, and bevellers. Be borrowed £4OO from a friend to put iota the business. That partwrslaip was dissolved in November, 1900, because it did not seem sufficiently prosperous to keep both the partners. The bankrupt re- ceived his £4OO back, and the continuing partner, Mr Sutton, arranged to pay the liabilities. In January, 1901, the bankrupt commenced business at the Hardsbaw Brook Works, but owing to high prizes of materials and adverse circumstances generally the business proved un- remunerative. The public examination was adjourned to the 23rd October. Mr Tickle, solicitor, St Helens ap- peared for the bankrupt. Mr Tranter (Tranter, Dolby, and Co.), accountants, Liverpool, is the trustee.

div.head: CHILDREN'S FANCY DRESS BALL.
div.p: THE CHILDREN'S FANCY DRESS BALL.

Presentation of an Album to the Mayoress. The Mayor and Mayoress (Hr. and Mrs. Charlton Parr) were pleasantly reminded on Thurs- day of the children's fancy dress ball which they gave in the Parr Hall on New Year's eve, for they were presented with a souvenir of that interesting event. The present took the form of a large album, handsomely bound in French morocco, and contain- ing 327 portraits of children in the fancy dress costumes which they wore on the occasion when they were the guests of the Mayor and Mayoress at the Parr Hall. The portraits, which were all cabinet size, had been mounted by Mr. Birtles, and the names of the guests with the characters repre- sented,had.been neatly limned underneath each por- trait. The album was embellished on the outside with the Borough Arms, blocked in gold, and the title page bore the follawing inscription :—" To the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington (Mr. and Mrs. J. Charlton Parr) from the guests at the Fancy Dress Ball, Parr Hall, December 31, 1901." A large number of subscribers and young people assembled in the Town Hall on Thursday afternoon to witness the presentation. The duty devolved upon Miss Irene Roberts daughter of Councillor William Roberts, to make the presentation. She did so in the following words; I have much plea- sure in asking you to accept from the guests of the Fancy Dress Ball given by you this mementol of the very happy event. (Applat.se.) The MAYORESS, in accepting the gift, said: I cannot possibly find words to express my thanks for this beautiful present. I can only say we shall value it very much. It is a very happy day for us, and we are very pleased to think we were able to give pleasure to so many young people. We thank you very much indeed. (Applause.) i fhe MAYOR said : The Mayoress s quite over- whelmed with the kindness and beauty of this pre- sent. She and I enjoyed the evening which lei to it immensely, and we were very pleased to see so many happy faces around us. I hope it will teach the younger generation to know us better, and, if I may say so, to love us better. We shall be more than rewarded for the effort we made for your pleasure on that occasion. (Applause.) A large number afterwards inTected the album nd light refreshments were served in the entrance hall.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.

ASSAULT WITII A POKER. AT EARLESTOWN. At Newton Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Ellen Hopkins, of Vista-lane, Earlestown, was charged with assaulting Elizebeth Marsh. She was further charged with assaulting Theresa Taylor. Defendant pleaded not guilty to assaulting Marsh, but ad- mitted the other charge.—Elizabstb. Marsh said that on the 10th inst defendant and her husband were quarrelling in Vista-lane. Defendant then struck complainant on the head with a poker. —For the defence, Mrs Hopkins said that it was complain- ant's mother who hit her, and not defendant.—For the assault on Elizabeth Taylor she was fined 2s 61 and costs. and was bound over for six months for the assault on Marsh. ALLEGED WOUNDING AT NEWTON. At the Warrington Occasional Coast on Monday, before Colonel Ridvvay, a woman named Blanche I Kelly was charged with unlawfully wounding Mary Kenny, at Hazel-grove, Newton-le-Willows. —Margaret Carlon stated that at midnight on Friday she heard a noise and on looking out she saw Mrs Kelly strike the complainant on th 6 head with a bottle. Witness went downstairs and found Mrs Kenny bleeding from the head. Complainant was quite sober. Previous to seeing Mrs Kelly strike complainant she saw her carrying a bottle behind her baek.—A police inspector stated that the wound on Kenny'a head was three inches long, contused, and lacerated,and penetrated to the bone. She was taken to Dr Valentine and the wound was dres,ed. It would be quite a week before she would be able to appear. Accused was remanded until Thursday week. MR. PETE CURRAN AT EARLESTOWN. On Monday evening a meeting of gas workers and labourers, under the auspices of the Gas Work- ers and Labourers' Union, was held in the District Schools, Earlestown,when an address was delivered by Mr Pete Curran. Dr W Latham presided. In the course of his address Mr Curran said that the chairman had spoken about the law being against trades unionists. What could they expect? They who voted for Co!. Pilkington could not expect him to vote for working men. Out of the 650 members of Parliament they had only eleven who claimed to represent labour. Whilst in that position they could not expect laws to be made for the benefit of the working classes. Almost every law on the statute book had been placed there with the idea of Iputting property first and humanity afterwards. They wanted to reverse that, and would have to revolutionize the present constitution of Parliament if they wanted humanity first and property after- wards. He understood that Earlestown was part of the constituency that Mr Woods was going to fight, and urged them to support the cause of labour as opposed to capital. Mr Curran also advised the non-unionist members of the audience to join the society, so as to bring about a proper and more noble condition of affairs for labourers in the dis- trict. (Applause.) KEEPING UNLICENSED COACHES AT EARLESTOWN. At Newton Petty Sessions on Thursday, before Mr Gillespie and four other magistrates, Samuel Walton, of Cross-lane, Earlestown, was prosecuted by the Inland Revenue for keeping unlicensed carriages at his establishment. Mr J W Knowles, who defended said that Mr Walton had had a stroke and was unable to appear. He pleaded not guilty. Mr St. Leger who represented the Inland Revenue, said that on September Ist, Walter Farmer, Excise Officer, called at the defendant's establishment,and there saw twelve conveyances, eleven of which were in use, while the other Was a new one. Walton had only taken out four licences in February last, and that leis seven coaches, which were in use that had not been licensed. The officer had previously seen all eleven conveyances in use in Earlestown.—For the defence,Mr Knowles said that the defendant was a dealer in coaches,and owing to the fact of his illness the coaches- that should have been sold were left on the premises. The other seven licences had since been taken out. The business was on sale.—The banch,after retiring, fined the defendant 40s and costs.—Mr Knowles said that the bench could not order costs, as it was a Crown prosecution, and quoted several cases.— The Clerk (Mr Greenall) overruled the objection. PIERROT CONCERT AT EARLESTOWN. The first of a series of pierrot concerts in aid of the funds of St. John's Church was held in the Town Hall Earlestown, on Thursday night. The Hall was fairly well filled and a capital programme was gone through. The proceeding were opened by a pianoforte solo " Tarantella " after which a quartette entitled "The dear little Shamrock " was rendered by Misses Skeet and Marsland and Messrs Foye and Johnson. Miss Skeet afterwards evoked loud applause by a delightful rendering of" Sweat Genevieve" whilst Mr Noah Johnson similarly pleased the audience with "Oh! Oh! hear the wild wind blow."Mr Fred Morgan,described as a Thespian •elecutionist and charaeter actor, gave recitations from various well known works which was followed by "Mr McG-regor's gathering" from Mr James Foye Miss E Marsland exhibited a well-trained voice in "The auld plaid shawl," whilst an agreeable change in the programme was provided by Mr J E Sykes in the form of a coon song with banjo solo, "The Soldiers chorus" by Misses Skeet, Marsland and Measrs Foye and Johnson brought the first portion to a close and after a short interval songs were rendered by Miss Marsland " Songs my mother sang" ' Mr James FJye, "The sailor's grave " ; "The Baudolero," Mr A Johnson ; "Come back to me," Miss Skeet; " The battle eve," Messrs Foye and Johnson; recitations by Mr Morgan and humorous songs by Mr Sykes, a thoroughly enjoyable programme being brought to a close by the singing of" Gocd-night beloved" by Misses Skeet and Marsland, and Messrs Foye and Johnson

div.head: ST HELENS CHILD BURNT TO DE&TH.:
div.p: ST HELENS CHILD BURNT TO DE&TH.:

• I& Brighouse, county bold the at St Helens Junction on Wednesday on the body of Jessie Hennigan, aged one year and eight months, daughter of ' Edward Hennigan, sheet repairer at the Lladon and North-Western sheeting sheds, of 16, Eliza-street, who died on Sunday evening from burns.—Mrs Sarah Traves , the child's grandmother, said that on Friday afternoon I, last week the mother of the child was out, and the child was in witness's charge. The child had been playing outsiae the front door for some time, when she saw the child's pinafore in flumes. She ran and extinguished them, but the child was burnt about the arm aad side of the taco. The doctor was called in and the child appeared to be going on well until Sanday, when death took place:—ln answer to the jury witness said she thought that a match had been dropped accidentally by Someone, and the child had tptai3d it. She did not see anyone pass who might have thrown a lighted matc.ti down.—Verdict " Accidental death."

div.head: LATE MR. JOHN CROSFIELD. --- His Interest in the Workingmen's Mission.
div.p: THE LATE MR. JOHN CROSFIELD. --- His Interest in the Workingmen's Mission.

Unveiling of an Oil Painting. By the death of Mr John Crosfield in December last, the Workingmen's Mission at Bank Quay lost its founder and greatest friend.lt was felt by those connected with the mission that some steps should be; taken to perpetuate his name and :the move- ment being well supported. it was decided to have a portrait of the late Mr Crosfield painted in oils and hung in the new schoolroom in Thewlis-street —a building which Mr Crosield himself provided out of his private purse. Mr Gallon, who bolds a position at Messrs Crosfield's works was commis- sioned to paint the portrait and his work, was un- veiled at a social gathering held in the schoolroom on Monday evening. The ceremony was performed by Mr Arthur Crosfield. The portrait was regarded as a faithful one ana Mr Gallon was warmly con-
gratulated on his success. There was a large attendance of friends connected with the mission. The chair WIS taken by Mr

Nathan Hough (president of the mission), and he was accompanied on the platform by Mr A II Cros- field, MrJ J Crosfield, Miss Crosfield, Alderman and Mrs Roberts, Mr Ashley and Mr Dale The proceedings commenced with the singing of a hymn, and prayer was offered by Mr Thomas Dale (superintendent of the Sunday school). Mrs Hannan's contralto voice was heard to advantage in the solo " Good-bye," and Mr Butcher followed with a violin solo, "San Toy," in which he was accompanied on the piano by his
sister. The CHAIRMAN, in calling upon Mr A 11 Crosdeld to unveil the portrait, said the first time he saw the late Mr Crosfield,3B years ago,the latter took him by _ . .
die- hand and addressing him as a young man said _ . . •
"Do lastly and right will follow." •(Appl'ause.) lie bad not forgotten_ that remark. Mr lioula pro-
- • ceeded to refer to Mr Crosfielors interest in the mis-

goo, and said the lives of some of those who had been influence by the mission would speak even more eloquently of Mr Crosfield's goodness than that building, which he erected, would. Mr Croi- field could always be approached in the cause of right and justice, It was a pleasure to him to help those who were in need, and well might it he said

of him " The steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord." It was one of the proudest experiences in his tlir Hough's) life to have been associated with Ir Crosfield in the work of the mission, and he was glad to think that the members of Air Crostield's
family were determined to continue the work of the
mission.

Mr ARTHUR CROSFIELD, on rising to unveil the portrait,had a cordial reception. He remarked that when his old friend Mr Nathan Hough asked him to perform that ceremony he had a good deal of hesitation in acceding to his request. He thought in the first place it would have been more fitting if someone not connected with the family should have unveiled the portrait. They all knew his father so well, and his character and principles were so familiar to them, that he would pass over recent history and deal with tbe earlier part of his life ; and just tell them a little that they might not be so well acquainted with. There was a fine line which said " Youth longs and manhood strives but age remembers." During the later years of his life his father was fond of telling them anecdotes with reference to his earlier days, and some of them had become household words with the members of the

--- family. His father was brought up in a very strict Quaker regime, and used to go the Friends' meeting house with the rest of the family in the days of his (the speaker's) grandfather, Joseph Crosfield ; and be believed his respected grandfather used to shock the family and some of the austere members of the Society of Friends on Sundays by producing during very long meetings a copy of Milton's" Paradise Lost,' and reading it to relieve the monotony of the service. (Laughter.) His father was sent to a Quaker school in York when he was about nine years of age,and if they had read the description of " Dotheboys Hall " they would know the rough manner in which the schools in Yorkshire were I conducted in those days. The pupils had to live on skim milk and dry bread,and the regime was calcu- lated to harden them, and it did harden his father, and, perhaps, it stood him in good stead in connection with his long commercial 'career. The winters on the Yorkshire plains were severe, and it was quite a common thing for the boys when their toes were blue with the cold to pull off their boots and stockings and run about in the snow to warm their feet. The lads bad a holi- day once a year, and that was at mid-summer. It was usual for. his (Mr Arthur Crosfielo'e) grand- mother to send his father a present at Chri trees, and on one occasion some mince pies were for- warded. It spoke rather well for the stamina of the family that his father managed to consume nine of them at one sitting. (Laughter.) There were one or two records of the same sort in the same school. Another lad at Christmas got a box of oranges, of which he ate 35, and he (Mr Arthur Crosfield) was afraid the consequences in his case were rather seriou., but in the case of Mr Crosfield the mince pies had no prejudicial effect whatever. (Laughter.) His father remained at York school for five years.

At this school they were very particular to-culti- vate as far as possible a taste amongst the scholars for natural history, and several of the scholars be- came eminent naturalists. That taste for natural history lasted with his father all hie life, and he (Mr. Arthur) often accompanied his father on expeditions in search of specimens. He (Mr Arthur) was not sure whether that had not developed another taste in him for attempting mountain climbing— (laughter)—which was sometimes considered a little foolhardy. On leaving York hie father pro- ceeded to a school at Glasgow where be remained for 18 months, and he always considered that the keen competition with the keen-witted gentlemen in the north further" stood him in good stead when he entered into business. In 1847 his father came to Warrington and commenced, in company with Mr George and Mr Moreland Crosfield, his long career at Bank Quay. All present knew how for many years he was immersed in business. He had many tastes and hobbies, and he took a special interest in art, music and education: He had a dislike for sectarianism in any shape or form, and he took a delight in knowing that the institutions in connection with their own workpeople were not of a sectarian character, but open to all. He had heard his father say more than once that nothing gave him more unqualified pleasure than the little expenditure he undertook in connection with that part of the town which bad been productive of un- mixed good and to himself an unmixed satisfaction. , He was glad to assure them that the sympathy of IMrs Crosfield would be continued in connection with the institutions. (Applause). He would now have the pleasure of seeing for the first time the oil painting, which was the work of Mr Gallon. (Applause). The portrait was then unveiled amid cheers. Alderman ROBERTS hiving been asked to make a few observations, said he didn't expect to be asked to take any part in the interesting proceedings when he came into the room, but, perhaps they had a ritht to expect him to say something as an old friend of the late Mr John Crosfield. He did not find it.an easy mottcr to say all he would like about him, but to have known him in- timately as a friend was not only a piece of good fortune but one of those incidents that did not happen too often in this life. There were two men who s'..ood out in his memory in connection with the large numbor of public men he hod known during the period he had occupied a more or less important position in public life. They had all passed away, but two of them had left impressions upon him, and he hoped upon his character that bad stood him.—and he bopPd the town—in good stead. He alluded to the late Mr John Gordon McMinnien and Mr John Crosfield. (Applause). He began his active ass'- elation with Mr Crosfield when he was 19 years of age, and that begat a friendship of a deep and sincere character which was a treasure house to him, and as long as his memory lasted it would he one of hie pleasantest reflections. (Applause). There was one characteristic of Mr Cros- field that entitled him, and those who bore hie name, to the gratitude of all their townsmen—his absolutfly unselfish devotion to what he believed to be the put lin interest. Me did not know that in thexe days they were worse than they were 30 or 40 years ago or longer, but it was a fact that the proportion of men who had leisure, ability, and wealth who gave any portion of them to the public service was far more limited than it (moil,: to be. (Hear, hear ) In every one of these particulars Mr Crosfield's life was an example—on example which should have many mcre imitations than it had. (An- plauqe.) Another characteristic was his downright straightforward way of sayinc, what he meant. There were times when people thought he etrad on the severe side, but hie coaduct was more a mannerism than any- thing else. Etc had an absolute horror of anything that favoured of hypocrisy or cant, or that which was not absolutely clean and rtraierfirwarci. His nattier' ten- dency was to ray exactly what he thought, and ex cress his ideas as strongly as his language would permit him ; in fact, in all his dealings with his fellow men, in every one of the r.umerous walks of life, both as master and friend, and making allowances for the frailties common to all of them, no one tried more honestly or more con- scientiously to do what he believed to be his

' duty, with • full tense of his responslbility to his fellow men and his God. (Applause.) The rortrait which they had unveiled, and which Was to find a place on the walls of that building which Mr Crosliqd provided, would be an incentive to many wbo entered to attempt as far as they possibly could to walk in the light of him whose lineament they saw on the walls. (Applause.) A programme of a miscellaneous character was after- wards submitted. During an interval light refreshments were handed round. Several musical items were given and Mr 11 M Ashton contributed humorous readings. The duties of accompanist were performed by Mr F AtkinEo3.

div.head: NOTES ON LAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON LAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
[By °voila.]

The drooping spirits of the Warrington supporters will, no doubt, be revived by the result of Saturday's match at St Helens. Prior to this encounter Warring- ton have been' severely trounced by Swinton,while they only got the better of Brighouse by a solitary try after a game of the most tiresome description. Last week the prevailing opinion was:that the game and the Warrington Club were both going to the dogs, while chances of suc- cess at St Helens were almost too remote to be contem- plated. This despondency will, however, by now have given place to a more cheerful and optimistic frame of mind in the great majority of cases, for Warrington showed on Saturday that they could rise superior to circumstances, new rules, and the St Helens Club all combined

I was surprised at the number of Warringtonians who made the journey to the glass and pill centre on football intent. There was quite an imposing array of Warrington 'buses at Boundary-road, while the special also brought a good number. The balance of the visit- ing crowd were cyclists. A week s reflection must have encouraged these enthusiasts to give Warrington oae more chance' and they will probably be pleased with themselves for having refrained from sending in their season tickets after the Brighouse burlesque.

From the kick-off Warrington showed that they not only meant to win but that they had profited by the lessons of the previous encounters. Touch-kicking was alright for clubs with poor backs, but for Warrington it was both infra dig and idiotic. These seemed to be the conclusions which had been tome to judging by the run of the play. If St. Helens had had their own way the game would have been fought out in the neigh- bourhood of touch-lines and the result would probably have been a pointless draw. Warringt4ln's notion was to keep the game open and they succeeded admirably by avoiding the touch-line as they would the plague— unless defending—which was not very often As a matter of fact Warrington played last season's football and played it rather well, with the result that they ran up a score of 18 points to 5, which fairly represents the game.

Play had been in progress about ten minutes before one got the idea that Warrington were going to be masters of the situation. Edmondson and Fish both came very near scoring but the latter was particularly we-watched. Presently he ran down again, only to meet a regular covey of • Saints "in the corner, They were all there, or as close as they could get and just prior to meeting their embrace Fish screwed the ball across dm field with a wonderful left-foot kick and then ran into the saintly throng. The ball bounced near the goal where Harris alertly secured and' ambled round the posts, what time the aforesaid Saints helplessly were looking on. Fish emerged from the crowd of captors in nice time to place an easy goal. That try and the way it was obtained merit a special par !

Another five minutes had barely elapsed before the score was doubled. Harris was again the scorer, he having received from Burgess beyond the centre line and beaten off all opposition en route for the goal posts, which he rounded after a very fine run The necessary goal was added by the obliging Fish, as usual. St. Helens, in a minority of ten points, now made efforts of a desperate character, and managed to force War- rington back to the line. Here there was a tight scrum- mage or two, and.Foulkes took advantage of a loophole in the Warrington defence to slip over the line. Barnes kicked a goal and halved the adverse margin.

1 Prior to this " Little Tich " got mixed up with two big St Helens forwards and as the injustice of the case impres Jed him forcibly he hit one man as high up as he could reach—somewhere about the collar stud I think it was. Referee M'Cutcheon was so shocked at the affair that he sent both combatants—Edmunds and Lee—off the " acid. It struck me that this was doubly hard luck for the diminutive Warrington half back, who had played a smart game. In consequence of this incident Fish went centre. put Forster on the wing and Hockenhall behind the "serum" Warrington seemed slightly disorganised for a while and there was no more scoring before the interval. •

There Was not much chance for the homesters after this, for Warrington had the breeze behind them on resumption, and though Barnes placed the ball in touch near the line when re-starting, the Saints we^e quickly repelled. The Warrington backs soon found their feet again, and after Fish had brilliantly led his men to the home quarter, Hockenhall cleverly bluffed the Saints and placed the ball behind the posts once more, Fish kicking his third goal. The effort on Hockenhall's part was a particularly smart one, If he would give his mind to the work. I am confident that he would make a better half back i than three. quarter. Beforia the close Fish scored his first try of, the season, racing through the home backs in characteristic fashion, but groundin too far out for another goal. Thil was the total of St Helens' mis- fortunes, and Warrington retired winners by 3 goals 4 tries (18 points) ; St Heleas, 1 goal 1 try (5 points).

From the spectators' point of view the game was worth watching, play being pretty fast right through. Warrington's efforts were directed towards keeping the ball on the move, and their superiority behind soon told. St Helens resorted a lot to the touch-line but beyond gaining ground which was quickly lost they profited none by these tactics. Saturday's display con- vinced me that a fast, open game can still be played between teams possessing any scientific knowledge of the game and a few capable exponents, notwithstand- ing the touch-line. But how often shall we see teams willing to play the gamei thusly ? It suits7Warrington well, and by sticking to open play they should get quite as many points as last season.

By virtue of a smart win over Huddersfield on Sat- urday Runcorn are still at the head of affairs. Will they be so still after the match at Warrington to-day ? That is the question of the hour in both towns, and Warring- ton way there is plenty of confidence that a check will be administered to the Linnets. Edmunds received a fortnight's suspension on Tuesday for his bout of fisti- cuffs at St Helens, and the vacancy will be filled by Duckworth. The necessity for the change is to be regretted, but more unfortunate still is the absence of Isherwood whose knee has given trouble again, After his fine display for the "A" team on Saturday we were all hoping to see him in his old place against Runcorn, but Fate has cruelly decreed otherwise.

The team will therefore be :—Knight, full back ; Fish, Hockenhall, Dickenson, and Harris, three-quarters ; Burgess and Duckworth, half-backs • Boardman,Taylor, Morrison, Edmondson, W Swift, Jolley, Roberts, and Forster, forwards.

' Warrington's policy against Runcorn should be the same as against St Helens—open play with plenty of passing amongst the backs. The team has two excel- lent wings and they ought to be given any amount of work and opportunity. The thing t ) avoid will be punting into the hands of Houghton and Jolley, who are admirably suited by the new rule.

Warrington Reservists and the Drink, Two local reservists just returned from the front bad an unpleasant experience in Manchester on August 2Gtu, which caused one a month's detention in the hospital, and the other two months' imprison- ment in gaol. William Campbell, labourer, Latch- ford, and James Butler, iron worker, Warrington, were paid off from the Lancashire Fusiliers at Bury on August 26th, and visited Manchester. Here they admitted getting druck, and Butler told the City Stipendiary et the Min- shall-street Court on Thursday morning that his friend, without the slightest provocation,kicked him on the knee, and afterwards rendered him un- conscious. lle remembered nothing more until next morning, when he discoyered he was in the Manchester Infirmary suffering from a dislocated shoulder blade, displacement of the right knee cap, a sprained ankle, a punctured wound in the head, and two black eyes. lie was afterwards taken to the Crum Campbell, who waspsall Infirmary., charged with assault sind inflicting grievous bodily harm, said be could give no explanation of the oc- currence. They were both drunk. He was sent to prison for two months.

div.p: ME EXAMINER FRIDAY SEPTEMBER 26 1902

delay, give his ideas permanency ot paper. . . . The bath is a luxury in which he indulges every :morning, and invariably on Thursdays just before enter- ing the pulpit. A sound body is necessary for a sound mind, and both for a good sermon, is his creed. He does not smoke or take stimu- lants of any kind. Exercise is taken as regu- larly as his dinner, when weather permits. There are few people about Hampstead who have not seen him, umbrella in hand, taking his constitutional between the hours of twelve and two. Latterly Dr. Parker has lived much in the open sir when weather permits, and has his study in his garden.

div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
TUB POLICY OP " PASSIVZ ERSISTAPICZ."

The final result of the appeal which the National Free Church Council has made to its eight hundred constituent local Councils on the question of passive resistance to the education- rate (in the event of the Bill being passed) is awaited with the keenest interest. The General Committee of the National Council meets on October 6, when the Rev. Thomas Law, the secretary, will submit the returns from the local Councils. In the meantime the campaign of protest is being carried on with undiminished enthusiasm and determination. The education question will figure very prominently in the coming municipal elections. Many Free Churchmen have resolved to vote only for those candidates who will pledge themselves not to put the Bill into operation. There is a growing feeling, even in quarters favourable to the Government, that the Bill will not pass into law.

div.head: PETER PICKLE AND MINISTERS' COURTING.
div.p: PETER PICKLE AND MINISTERS' COURTING.

Peter Pickle continues his frank and enter- taining papers in the Free Church Chronicle. In the October number he writes quaintly on the text: "Study to be quiet," and puts in a plea for sweet-voiced parsons. "Mr. Jewett, in his memorable address on preaching delivered at Cardiff eighteen months ago, commented on the absence of the wooing note from our sermons. He might have added that the wooing note, even if present in the substance of the sermon, will not be heard if it is not also present in the preacher's voice. I know many ministers who have excellent wives, and lamperfectly certain that they did not employ their pulpit tones in their courting. If they had, they would still have been bachelors." This is pleasant fun. Who is Peter Pickle? A FREE CHURCH "PARISH MAGAZINE."

It is announced that Mr. Joseph Hocking has written a serial story for the Free Church- man for 1903. This magazine has an extensive circulation as a localised magazine among the Free Churches and Free Church Councils, as it seeks to serve their needs in an especial manner. Our Anglican brethren have for many years used parish magazines with great effect. They are usually very well conducted, though, alas, not unfrequently marred by envenomed attacks on Nonconformity. The Free Church- 2nan seeks to counteract the influence of the parish magazines, but there is nothing of the bitterness of sectarianism in it. I am told that among the contributors to the number for January next, which is now ready as a specimen number, are Dr. Parker, Dr. Horton, Mrs. L. T. Meade, Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., the Rev. Bernard J. Snell, M.A., B.Sc., and others. Mr. Snell has a special gift for addressing children and the conductors of the Free Churchman have been fortunate enough to secure Mr. Snell as the writer of the children's page.

div.head: REV. CHARLES WILLIAMS.
div.p: REV. CHARLES WILLIAMS.

We regret to hear that this veteran Baptist minister is at present indisposed. Though loosed from his church at Accrington, Mr. Wil- liams has given himself no rest. His recent labours among the churches, first on behalf of the Twentieth Century Fund, and later on behalf of the Baptist Missionary Society. have been very abundant and have told severely on his strength, and he has cancetieil all his engagements. We hope that a complete rest will soon thoroughly restore him. Mr. Williams is a close friend of Dr. MoLareia of Manchester.

div.head: REV. G. CAMPBELL MORGAN.
div.p: REV. G. CAMPBELL MORGAN.

Mr. Morgan has been conducting well at- tended services at the Westminster Congrega- tional Chapel. This huge building, which seats 3000 people, is a standing problem t;o_London Congregationalism. Since the days of Samuel Martin it has never been more than half Mled. Some people are daring enough to hope that Mr. Campbell Morgan might be persuaded to take it in charge, as a mission centre, and revive its glories. The district is enormously difficult, but not too difficult, it is believed, for Mr. Morgan. But would the Americans, who love and prize him, consent to give him back to tho country from which they took him.

div.head: "THE NEW FRANCISCANS."
div.p: "THE NEW FRANCISCANS."

In the meantime, the Rev. R. Westrope, who has just retired from the pastorate of the chapel, is trying to establish an order of New Franciscans, whose aim would be to promote simplicity of life and justice in social relationships. Mr. Westrope has been fortunate enough to win the support of Mr. Price Hughes. Everyone knows the invaluable work which the Sisters of the West London Wesleyan Mission have done, but up to the present Mr. Hughes has failed to secure similar service from men of social position and privilege; and yet the special work of men is as greatly needed as the special work of women. It is not generally known that it was at the suggestion of Dr. Horton that the officers of Westminster Chapel invited Mr. Westrope to the pastorate.
FORWARD MOVEMENT IN LONDON CONGREGATIONALISM.

The appeal for funds for equipping Clare- mont Church, Pentonville, as the first of the London Union's mission centres, has resulted In contributions of over £2OOO, which, with Mr. W. H. Brown's promise of £4OOO, brings the fund to within £2OOO of the £BOOO which is being expended on the building, it is hoped that the outstanding £2OOO will have been pro- mised before the opening of the mission on October 2, as to open free from debt would give an impetus to the Forward Movement.

THE NEW LIFE OF DR. PARKER. The new biography of the famous preacher, written by his friend, Dr. Adamson, and pub- lished by Messrs. Cassell, gives some interesting personal particulars. Dr. Parker's rising, time of meals, work, exercise and leisure are all regu- lated in such a manner that no time is wasted, and one seeking him at any quarter of an hour sould tell exactly where to find him, and what he would be doing. . . , There are not many days in which he doss not spend six or eight hours in bard study, these being fre- quently extended by a sadden insisitatioss deeming upon him. whom he must. withor.k
