div.head: STRICKEN WINDER.
div.p: THE STRICKEN WINDER.

Miss Macdonald, called the stricken winder, liveat 134, Murray-street, Maryhill, Glasgow. Her experience Is one to call the colour from the bravest cheek. Sleep- ing by tier fireside, tired with work,she awoke to a new world. She had, forgotten how to use he,' limbs. True. they moved : 'but they would not move as she wished them to ! Her story has interested and puzzled medical men, and she was told by the best authorities that the cause of her misery was creeping paralysis and that she would never be able to move as long as she lived. How she bore her trouble and how only three boxes of Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people gave her back her lost power are best told In her own intelligent words. " I am a wool and elk-winder. I was paralysed, and the doctors said I should never be able to move for the rest of my life. The pain which I endured, week lifter week, in mr left leg and down my bsek, I can hardly describe. As the paralysis crept npward. I found that the power had gone out of my left arm, and I aeon ex- perienced the greatest difficulty in speaking. My eyes became sunken, and my cheek-bones began to stick through. Four times was lin the infirmary. I was dismissed hit the professors and decors as incurable. Misery made me hysterical ; I laughed and cried with- out reason. Hearing of cures in cases ac bad as mine through Dr Williams' pink pills I gave them a trial." She jumped up and walked round the table. " See ! That is what the taking of three boxes of them has done for me ! or two yens I was bedridden. Now I can go to the door and get an airing, and the district nurse said at her last call that I was so well that she would require to knock rty name off her book. My appetite is so good that I weary for my food ; lam putting on fiesh fast, the pain is quite away from my ankle. I can move my legs—indeed, walk on them, as you saw, without the aid of crutches ; and the power is back in my left arm and fingers, so that I can thread a needle, sew and knit." That Miss Macdonald 9houln be thus cured after the best medical science had given her up is no new experi- ence. Many " hopeless failures" and even a number of men discharged from the Army as incurables, have been made well and active by Dr. Williams' pink pills. Why ? Because they give new vitality—new blood, which is new life and casts off disease. Lonometor ataxy, palsy, Brieht's disease, consumption, and other diseases that are incurable by ordinary medicine, they have cured, the lesser ailments of every day—rheuma- tism, St. Vitus' dance, anemia, hysteria, lumbago, the bacbaches of women and girls, spinal weakness in men old before their time—all have yielded to the same remedy.

div.head: Councillor Bennett and Conservative Working
div.p: Councillor Bennett and Conservative Working

Men. On Saturday a meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Conservative WorkinelMens Federation was held at the Manchester Conservative Club,Councillor Arthur Bennett (Warrington)presidiug.—The Chair- man'drew the attention of the meeting to the educa- tion and Irish questions. He said the irreconcilable attitude of the opponents of the Education Bill clearly proved that they sought to wreck the measure altogether, and some expression from that committee was most desirable.— Councillor Starkie (Rochdale) endorsed these remarks, and to test the feeling of the committee moved the following resolution :—" That this executive strongly condemns the factious onposi- tion now waged in Radical quarters to the Educa- tion Bill, considers the wilful misrepresentation made with reference to it by certain Nonconformist divines, and their advice to repudiate payment of rates, a disgraceful stultification of their sacred calling, offers to the Right Honourable A J Balfour its hearty support of the Bill as it now stands, and trusts that on the re-assembling of Parliament be will resist any further encroachments upon the principles of the proposed measure, and carry the same to a successful issue.—After some discussion the resolution was carried.— Mr Oldfleld (Altrincham) sieved :—" That this com- mittee hails with satisfaction the timely steps for the suppression of the pernicious action of the United Irish League, which has again sought to re- vive the hateful system of intimidation ef all law abiding and loyal citizene who refuse to subscribe to its decrees, and tenders to the Right Hen. Geo. Wyndham, M.P., its earnest support in his en- deavour. to rescue that country from the machinations of Fenian intrigue under- lying the poliey of the Irish Nationalists." Mr Letts (Newton Heath) seconded and the resolu- Von was carried unanimously —lt was further re- solved that the Federation take steps during the ensuing autumn to arrange a political campaign in conneetion with the clubs and associations affiliated 80 that the persistent misrepresentations of the Radical party may be met and refuted, it being felt that counter agitation on the part of the Conserva- tive party was a necessity if it was to continue in Its present favour with the electorate, now greatly deceived by Radical emissaries."

IHE JOURNAL FOR THE DEAF contains in its last number a complete description of a borne treatment for deafness and ear diseases by means of external application, which has been repeatedly successful in restoring hearing in cases pronounced in- curable by the usual methods. Another special fesi`urs is the enclosure of a Report Form by means of which anyone can obtain full particulars and free advice as to the use of the treatment in their own case. To obtain s free copy of the " Journal," with report Form dud a " Supplement," illustrating upwards of forty cases cured during the past month, it is only necessary to address The Secretary, Drouet Institute, Regent's Park-road, London, N.W:

Warrington P.S.A. Society. An open meeting of the above-named society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Sunday, there being a large attendance of members and friends. The Brick-street choir gave a caetata entitled" Quicksands," which was ably rendered and thoroughly enjoyed. The connective readings were delivered by Mr A. Perkins, and the soloists were Misses Gallop, Hill and Lewis, and Messrs Lightfoot, Shaw, and Jolley. Mr W Barton con- ducted the cboir,aad Mr Toeskinsen was the accom- panist. A collection was taken on behalf of the society's funds. he Liverpool and Manchester Electric Express. ' Considerable progress has been made of late in the matter of providing capital for the Liverpool and Manchester Electric Express Railway, anA it may be expected that before long an official announcement will be made as to when the con- struction of the new railway will be commenced. Outside the provision of the capital nothing remains to be done in connection with the line. The plane are all ready, and tenders can very quickly be obtained, in the meantime the engineers are very busy on the new London to Brighton and Dover mone-railway, and there is little doubt that it will be proceeded with during the next session of Pariiament. It is not quite certain that the same thing will happen in the case of the proposed Glasgow and Edinburgh line. Unfortunately the delay in getting to work on the Liverpool and Man- chester line is likely to affect the success of these other schemes, for Parliament is sure to demand some evidence of the succees of the Liverpool and Manchester line before allowing the construction of ethers in different parts of the kingdom, and that success csozotibo demonstrated forlseme time yet.

div.head: I LIBERALS AT WALTON I LEA.
div.p: I LIBERALS AT WALTON I LEA.
Mr. A. H. Crosfield "At Home." -- A New President of the Liberal Association Elected.

Walton Lea has seldom been the scene of such an animated spectacle as was witnessed there on Saturday afternoon. With his usual thoughtful- ness and coneideration for the Liberal workers of Warrington,Mr. A.H.Cresfield invited them anditheir wives and lady friends to an "At Home." The invitation was very generally accepted, and a com- pany of considerably over 1,000 persons proceeded to Walton Hall. Omnibuses were provided for the conveyance of the guests to and from the house. The vehicles were rapidly filled, and as the weather continued fine, a number preferred to walk rather than wait for a 'bug to return. On arriving at the hall, the visitore were graciously received by Mr Arthur Crosfield and Miss Crosfield.. The privi- lege was granted of an inspection of several of the principal rooms, the furnishing and embellishments of which were greatly admired. The visitors were at liberty to enter the conserva- tories and greenhouses and saunter about the grounds. The flowers were hardly at their best, but there was much to delight the eye, the vineries especially being a great attraction. The grounds looked trim and neat, and a miniature fountain around which gentle sprays were playing, height- ened the effect Selections of music were played by Messrs Croafielel'e band and dancing was engaged in on the green sward alees and chorusen were sweetly sung by the Warrington fale Voice Choir under the direction of Mr IV H Payton, Mae. Bac. Mr Frank Hickman presided at the piano. During the afternoon Mr Birtles photographed the large company on the lawn. Tea was partaken of in a large marquee. The catering was in the hands of Mr James Evans who is to be congratulated upon the excellent arrangements made. The afternoon was pleasantly whiled away and prior to departing several eneeches were delivered and Mr C B Parker, of Penketh, was elected president of the Association. It will he remembered that at the last annnal meeting of tha Association Mr Ziba Armitage was invited to take the position, but he found himself unable to occupy it. MR, CROSFIELD AND CURRENT POLITICS. MrenoeFestrep, who heel a hearty reception seid : —ln the first place may I say what very great pleasure it gives my sister and myself to meet so many of our friends. We are deliehted to see you and if Mrs Croefield herself is not here to-day 1 know you will understend nntler the circumstances Ithe natural reason for her absence. She is with us in thought—(cheers)—as Ole is in synanathy with all the best causes which my dear father had at heart in the town. (Cheers). Now this is not an occasion for what is popularly known as" stump- ing," but still I have a duty which is as pleasant as it is important to perform in pronosing to you the name of a gentleman who is now prepared to occupy the position vacated by our late president of the Liberal Association. I will say I do not think it would be easy to over estimate the great gain to our party and the great advantage we shall have in the guidance and leadership of Mr Charles Parker. (Loud cheers) Having had some oppor- tunities of ascertaining the opinion of different see- tions of the Liberal Party, I know the very deepl satisfaction which is felt at his having consented to take this position, and lam warranted in assuring him that he will receive the backing of a solid an I united peeve (Cheers.) You know the pre-eminent' Iposition he occutniee in the industry with which he I is connected. On political matters we may hear something from him this afternoon, but we already know that he is a sane and a sound Imperialist, and there is all the difference in the world between that and the arrogant jingoism and reckless earth hungeethat would ecize every square inch of terri- tory from the Eqnator to the Poles. (Hear, hear.) In home affaita I know from the letters Mr Parker has written me how keenly alive he is to the ter- rible question of overcrowding in our cities,the un- wholesome and shocking density of slum popula- tion in this country; and we may be sure he will insist on the urgent need for reforming this by 'taxation of site values—a measure in my humble opinion of infinite importance —and in other ways. I knew that he regards the physical health and well-being and the intellectual equipment of the nation at large as to say no more, an indispensable preparation for the great commercial international struggle we have to face in these days in the iii- mediate future. (ilear,hear.) Welyadiea and gentle- men) we regard this as the best kind of patriotism (Cheers.) On the other hand, legislation which proposes to sacrifice the best interests of education to the prejudices and privileges of any one sect or which adds to that terrible sub-stratum f society what is called the" submerged tenth," by pushing into the social malbelge those who now stand trent- bling on the brink—legislation of this kind such as the Government's Education Bill and the Corn Tax we regard net as natriotinne but a muse spurious Icounterfeit of the real article. (Cheers) _

, We have admired Mr. Parker's letters en the Education question, a question on which with his experience and his ability he is entitled to speak with great weight, and we may congratulate him on the juncture at which he is about to assume this influential position. (Rear, hear.) The politi- cal omens are favourable for us more favourable than they have been for twenty years past. (Cheers.) Things are going very badly with our Tory friends, and the next time that we assemble at a gathering of this sort it may be to write an epitaph, if not upon an already doomed ministryc at all events OR some of their attemnts at re-actionary mischievous legislation. Speaking of epitaphs I ara reminded of a story which perhaps you will let me tell you before moving my resolu- tion. It is a tale of a Quaker ancestor of mine, once a familiar figure in • Sankey-street and on wkom another Quaker, a very intimath acquaint- ance was calling one day. Bre turned to my rela- tive us he was about to leave and said, " I've written thee epitaph." This he proceeded to recite and it rail as follows : Reader, if read thou mast "

you will observe that in those days also educational attainments left a good deal to be desifed—and in order that I may not interrupt myself too often, let me anticipate the allusion in these lines to a bye-gone industry in the town. NOW I think wholly extinct. Some of von may have heard that there was a time when dip candles (laughter) were made there. Well then I will give you the lines as far as they went:

"Reader, if read thou east then read and know The ashes of a soap amt camile maker lie below ; (laughter) In this, his trade, be beat all brother chips Bare Price & Co., bat they ne'er dealt la dips. Of impudence he had the most, abundant share . . '

Hie faults were many and his virtues rare. . . (laughter) That is as far as our friend got in this his first attempt to recite these lines. As a Quaker my ancestor was a men of peace, be even men of peace have a bit of the old Adam (laughter) about them and sometimes indulge in what is called " Righteous indignation." And se if tradition may be depended on the exit of that candid friend was more speedy than dignified. That is where the analogy with the present situation comes in. What is this Education Bill as introduced by the Government but a monstrous affront to the good sense and prudence St the whole country (cheers), and is not this and the re-actionary taxation they have introduced calculated to bring about in no very distant future an exit of this Government which will be of a very undignified description. If I say any more you will accuse nte of getting on the stump, so I have now great pleasure in preposinetoi.youjthat Ale Charles
Parker be elected president of the Liberal Associa- tion, a resolution which I will ask Councillor Tinnion to second and Councillor means to support, (Cheers.)

div.head: HUSBAND WHO FLIRTED.
div.p: THE HUSBAND WHO FLIRTED.
Singular Case of Family Neglect at Warrington.

Severe Penalty, At the Warrington Police Court on Monday, Thomas 1 Cotton, Williamson's-square, Church-street, was i summoned for neglecting la'e five children.—Mr Browne I prosecuted on behalf of the N•S P.O.C. and said the case ! had been under the observation of Inspector Hackett 1 for over two year,. Prisoner had been prosecuted betore on the information of his wife, but when the woman eloPeared in the witness box she absolutely I " tamed round " from her previous allegations against the prisoner, and they were compelled to withdraw the case. In his (Mr Browne's) opinion the woman ought to be charged with the de- fendant, becluse when Dr. Peacocke examined the Wl- drsn h. found them In a terrible condition. It was only fair, however, to say that Mrs Cotton s :id they had got into that state in consequence of her having to go out to work because her fleabane would not do so. He was a bricksetter'a labourer and could earn Sid or 61 an hour. The complaint of the wife was that he would not work but would " toff up as a swell and go aboat with other girls, representing himself as a single young man." She had caught him no a number of occasions going with single girls, and when the first prosecution was instituted a girl was brought forward to whom deferdant was supposed to be engaged. He dressed himself up inefread of working and that was where the eeriest canoe le. Neighbours had been exceedingly g col in giving the children food. The wife was not entirelv free from blame, but the Society in London for some reason only ordered a summons against the defen- dant. TR three months all he gave his wife was 20s and 12s. He was not a drunkard ; the neglect was due pure and simply to dressing up and walking about instead of working— Dr Peacocke said he visited defendant's house on Septem her 9th and found the children in e verminous state. John, aged 16 months, was in an advanced stage of tuberculosis. There was no fool in the house, which was in a filthy condition, the floor upstairs being thick with dirt. He attributed that to the neglect of the wife i who told him she had no time to look after the children 1 as she had to go out ta work.—Elizabeth Mary Cotton, wits of the defendant, said her husband could earn from 25e to 30s a week, aceording to the weather. From March up to the present time she had bad one full week's wages from him. He would go out in the morn- ing and come in at night and say he could not get work. IFle /said he bad had a bad foot during the last seven weeks. He would not go to work, making all sorts of excuses. The children had no food except that which she worked for and the neighbours provided. Her husband said she must aleo provide him with food when he was not working. During the last seven weeks he gave her about £2. Since Dr Peacocke visited the house the child John had died. The reason that she could not attend to the children was that she had to go out and work. Defendant went mat at week-ends " dressed up." On one occasion she met him with a woman ; of cnurse she thrashed the woman. (Laughter.) Defendant passed off as a single man. During the last six weeks, however, be had not acted in this was', and he said he would try to do better. —Mr Bane. school attendance inspector, said he had had occasion to visit the defendant's house. The children wet., very much neglected, and the woman Was seldom at home when he called. A girl aged eight years bad to earn money by washing steps.—P.C, Clough said he viaited the house on the 11th inst. Oae of the children was then lying very ill in a basket. Mrs Cotton said defendant had not given her any money for several weelea. Defendant said he had a lead foot and had not been able to work. Witncs4 knew defendant dressed up and walked about with young girls, passing off as a single man, and that his wife harl to work very hard washing and cleaning. She had to keep the house going and keep defendant in addition.—lnspector Hackett said he had had the case under observation for two years and had paid fifty visits to the house. The woman was generally out working when he called. Witness was Sure that if the woman received wages regularly there would be no crime for complaint.—Defendant said he always gave his earnings to his wife. He bad had a bad foot for seven weeke and had not been able to work. He made a start last week and cal Saturday gave his wife 24s 81. He had never walked one with girls since the first presnoution was bilriTht against him.—The Chair- man said the bench thought the case was one of very Pross neglect on the part of the man and he would be oommitted to gaol for three months with herd labour. If he name before them again he would receive the full penalty.

The Lifeboat Saturday Movement. On Tuesday evening a meeting of the Council which was elected to make arrangements in con- nection with the Warrington Lifeboat Saturday movement was held ih the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, under the presidency of Mr Henry Thornton. The Secretary, Mr W H Drinkwater,was also present, but there was only a small attendance. Letters of apology for non-attendance were read trim several gentleman. ,The secretary read several circulars showing what had been done in the shape of a demonstration in other towns, and suggestions made by the organizing secretary of the movement. !The queetion of having a lifeboat and crew to take part in the proposed local demonstration was dis- cussed and the expenditure reviewed. Some dis- cussion took place as to whether a demonstration should be organized, but it was the general feeling that they had been approached too late in the year for a practical demonstration. After some discus- sion the meeting was adjourned until Tuesday next, and the matter was left in the hands of the secre- tary and treasurer (Mr Bradshaw), who promised to see the Mayoress with reenact to a meeting of adies. Mr Thornton was thanked for presiding nd:the Mayor for allowing the use of the chamber

matter, and there was no doubt that the Non conformist had a standpoint to judge the quee- tion upon, and it was a very imporatant one. To them it was a very serious one and that was 1 that they declined to have their chddren educated in religious prineiplea to which they were resolutely op Dosed. (applause.) That was an important point. 'There wee one point which had not received sufficient attention in Warrington. The Liberals had left the Free Churches, the Nonconformists, too much to fight the- educetion question. It was time the Liberals of War rington took up their pesition, enunciated clearly, and forced to the front this fact—that in educational matter they must eo in far efficiency, They would never get proper efficiency with denominational schools. He bad stated before in Warrington, and he spoke from an ex- perience of 25 years of managers of denominational schools—he did not make any difference in this matter between church and chapel as it was always the same-- that wherever they had education under the control of the denominations they always had it subordinate to the denomination. What they had to determine was that their children should have the beet education it was coesible to get, and to secure that it was necessary they should have the education under their own Centro! and pay for it themselves, The Education Bill proposed that the public should pay for education but that °there should manage it. He accepted the position of president of the association with a great deal of hesitancy because his time and energies were lergely taken up in connec- tion with industrial thines,but if he wanted any encour- agement he saw it in the earnest, strong,aed determined Liberals he saw before him who had fought in the Warrington elections for many years. Let them all bind themselves together, put aside personal questions, and each do his Of her part to carry firward the cause. The wanted the Liberal Aseoestion of Warrinston to be broad-based and thoroughly democratic —that each one should take his or her pert and that each one should have the pleasure of paying for it. He did not think it was a good thing for a Liberal Associa- tion or any ether association to depend on one or two. Let everyone give co the association according to their ability no that they would have a broad based associa- tion. He wished to thank those who in such kind terrns had proposed him, and those present who had so kindly carried the reselution and placed him in the position of president. (Applause.) SPEECH BY COUNCILLOR W. PIERPOINT.

Councillor %Yuman PIEMPOINT said it seemed to him like old times to see such a large gathering of Warring- ton Liberals. As one who had grown grey in the service of Warrington Liberalism—laughter)—let him congratu- late theca upon the great service they had done to them- selves by appointing Mr Parker as president af the asso- ciation. He had had a knowledge of past presidents for 4.0 years, and he could assnre them that all had done their very best for the cause. (Applause). Elo could allude to men who, in 1830 carried tlrma to a successful issue in the election of Mr Gordon McMinnies. And if they had been beaten still it was not because the associa- tion had not been composed of bands of earnest workers from the top to the bottom, but because the Pates had been against them. It was irn- possib'e to do impossibilities. They all recollected the time when Mr William Crosfield went into the fieht. A better Liberal candidate thee never had in Warrington, and there was no candidate who more deserved to win than ho did. Se was beaten by the forces of reaction, as was also Mr John Crosfield. Mr Arthur Houston was also a good candidate, and the Liberals never made a better fight. They all recollected Mr Percival Scott who came down and in e fortnight made the Tories of Warrington tremble to that extent that many of them were much concerned for a consider- able period of time afterwards. They bad always fought fairly and honestly, and if they had been defeated they bad not been disgraced. (Applause). The Liberal party had always been a good one. The forces had been against them but now they were with them, and they had nothing to do but to hack up the efforts of Mr Parksr, together with the efforts of the Council and eommittee,and give a good account of themselves at the next election. (Applause.) It was said they were dl5 organized, but it was not amongst the workers. Cer- tainly the Liberal party in the country had been dis- niganivd, but he felt that with such a president as Mr Parker, and with such a chairman of the executive, the Liberal party had a better chance of success than ever they bad. (Applause.) He would conclude by propoe- hie a hearty vote of thanks to Mr Crosfield for his hog- pitalitv. They knew his worth and loved him as a candidate and they hoped to have him as a candidate again. (Applause.) The motion was carried by acclamation, three &were being given for Mr. Arthur Crooned and three for hie sister. In reniy, Mr CROSFIELD said he thanked their old friend Councillor PiPrpoint both on behalf ef his sister and himself for the very cordial way in which he had proposed the vote of thanks, and the ladies and gentl cc men present for the equal eordiality and kindness wlth which they had received it. e 0 The visitors left the grounds aid were conveyed town in 'buses.

Isaac—Perkins. An interesting wedding was solemnized on Monday morning at Bold-street Wesleyan Church, the con- tracting parties being Mr Arthur Isaac, (second eon of Mr T B Isaac, Rockfields, Frodsham) and Miso Emma Perkins (Ettie), youngest daughter of the late Mr William S Perkins. The bride, who was given away by he brother Mr Albert Perkins, was prettily attired in a grey Irish poplin dress,trimmed with lace and chiffon. She wore a grey velvet toque to match, and carried a shower bouquet of lilies and chrysanthemums. The office of bridesmaid was fulfilled by Miss Lizzie Isaac, sister of the bride- groom. Her dress was a pretty flowered delaine, with large black picture hat, and she carried a shower bouquet of pale pink roses. Mr John Henstoek of Chester acted as best man. The officiating minister was the Rev W C J Neville,and Mr Frank Rickman, the organist of the church. played appropriate music. Later in the morning the happy couple received an enthusiastic send-off at the station, as they left for North Wales, where the honeymoon will be spent. They were the recipients of a large number of handsome presents among which were an aneroid barometer from the assistants of Mr J B Isaac and an oak inkstand from the messenger boys.

div.head: LIBERALISM.
div.p: LIBERALISM.

ICouncillor Tneteros observed that he had very much pleasure in seceding the resolution. Be bad seen a s good many presidents of the Liberal Asseniationete said, since he first took un active work in connection with the Liberal party, in 1880,and he felt that in Mr. Parker they had a gentleman who would occupy the position with honour to himself and to the party. He would, in fact, be second to none of those who had preceded him. (Applause). They were most fortunate in having a gentlemen to come forward at a time when it was common knowledge that the prospects of the Liberal party were none too bright. He was happy to say, however, that the dark days of Liberalism, in Warring- ton at any rate, were days of the past. They had before them that day a Pplendil array of workers, and he was proud te address them as men who took a deep keen and Intelligent interest in the political aft eire of the town and country. Such a gathering as they had that dayashowed that the Liberal party was not what it was said to be—entirely dead. It seemed to him that it was very much alive. It was not fair to ask Mr Parker to take up the position of president of the association unless they were determined to give him every possible help they could and make his duties as light as possible. (Hear, hear). They must all pull together with one accord with the one common object in view of working net only for the good of Warringten,but for the good of their country. (Hear, hear.) The Liberal party had done some great a-id desirable work for all °lassos of the community particularly tor the working classes, and it was to the Liberal party of the future they would have ,to look for any improvement in their condition. At any rate they had in Ur Parker a gentleman who would lead them forward and onward until the object thee had so dear at heart had ben attained. They were now start- ing on happier and brighter days for Liberalism, and let them hope that under Mr Parker's leadership they would achieve still greater successes than in the past. (Ap- plaune.) COUNCILLOR EVANS AND MR CHAMBERLAIN. Coencillor JATIU3 Elar,l9, said it afforded him great pleasure to support the motion. The cause in which they were all interested was what he might call the common cause—a cause in which he took as keen and as deep an interest as ever. He was a Liberal because he believed in the old Liberal traditions, the old Liberal principles. He had not had the pleasure of personally knowing Mr Parker, although he had been in his com- pany again and again, but from what he had beard of him be believed that:he was'a man of charaoterone that silent all prevailing Dower—character was ultimately bound to win. Whenever the Liberals had brought a Parliamentary candidate into Warrington, their Con- servative friends had scrutinised him and if there had been any holes they would have found teem. He was not complaining, for he held that men who sought the suffrages of the people ought to be men of character— (hear, hear)—and be also thought they should have a man of similar stamp for the position of president of the organisation. (Hear, hear.) With Councillor Tinnion, 1 who had just spoken, be believed that the mists were rolling away PO far as their Liberal principles were can. earned, and that being the ease he hoped they would all do their best to support Mr Parker in the position to which he was about to be elected. (Applause). When workingmen criticised the government they sem,- times did it roughly, and he recently hear(' a working- man speak very strongly on the recent action of Joseph and his brethren. (Laughter). He (Mr Evans) heard Mr Joseph Chamberlain when he earns to the old Public Hall in Warrington. Is was asked by the late Dr Hor- nell hew be liked Mr Chamberlain and be replied, " I don't like him." (Laughter). "No," said the deeter, " he said us on that occasion. Joseph did "—(A Voice : " He did "—and his (Councillor Evans's) opinion was that he was capable of selling them again. (Applause). From that day up to the present he had bad no confi- dence in him,and he had little confidence in the Govern- ment now that the venerable Lord Salisbury had left it. He had always respected Lord Salisbury because he was a Tory and professed to be one. Be (the speaker) would always be man enough te acknewledge that his Conser- vative friends had a right to their views but, if they r pleased, let him also have a bit of his own way. (Laughter). He hoped that when Mr Parker became their president he would lead them on to a better cocdi- tion of things than they were having at present. The Liberals had been told they had gone into nonentity ; in other words, that they had been "snuffed out." They did not look like tieing snuffed nut, and it would take a good deal to snuff them out. Be hoped the time would come when they would have the pleasure of seeing their friend Mr Arthur Crosfield more frequently amongst them in Warrington. (Hear, hear). H 9 dared say he bed many friends all over the world—(laughter)—and, perhaps, they might be better looking than those in Warrington. (Renewed laughter). LEITER FROM MR. ZIBA. ARMITAGE. Mr C J&CKSON Hoesaes (hon secretary) read letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr Ziba Armitage, Miss Bessie Dutton, J Mr Rymer Young, Alderman Roberts, the Rev John Yonge, Mr Frank A Roberts, Mr John Worrall, Mr Lawrence Weir Mr Seddon, Mr Thomas Birchall, and Alderman MIAs. Mr Armitage wrote from Seuthsea :—" The card of invitation to Mr Crosfield's 'At Home 'on Saturday reached me here this morning, and both Mrs Armitage and I greatly regret that we shalt be unable to put in an appearance at what will, without doubt, be an important and inter- esting event in the annals of our party. Please convey to Mr Crosneld and any others who may be interested to know it that we are unavoidably absent, but all ths same, cordially hope that there may be a successful gathering. There is everything which is favourable to us in the present position of political affairs. The Tories are playing into our hands, and nothing except our own failure to understand the times can prevent their defeat at the first oppertenity." . . . - -
- The motion was then put, and carried unanimously. MR PARKER AND THE EDUCATION BILL.

Mr PARKER, who had • hearty reception, said he felt almost over-burdened with the kind remarks which had been made about him. He had been taken a great deal by surprise, be did not mean with regard to the election of president, but with the fact that there was to be a tittle ceremony in connection with the proceedings of the afternoon. Everybody seemed to have known that he was to be elected president that afternoon except himself. (Laughter.) He had been under the impres- sion they were to meet to have a cup of tea, look round the grounds, and enjoy themselves ; ho had no idea ha was to be let in for anything of this sort. Too many kind things had been said about him, and he wondered if. when the Liberals of Warrington came to write his epitaph in convection with the assoliation, it would be in as kind terms as those in which he had been proposed. Councillor TINNZON : " It depends upon yourself." (Applause.) Mr Parker (continuing) said, it did partly but not altogether. He could offer them his best efforts but he could go no further. It would certainly not be for want ef effort if he failed in what was expected of him. Mr Cresfield bad said that they would like him to make a political speOeh ; he was certainly not going to do so that afternoon. He almost thought he was tieing spoken of as if he were a candidate at the working head of an organization. (Laughter.) During the last few years the fortunes of the Liberal party had been in a sett of ebbing tide. The times seemed to have been against them. The great principles which had divided the two parties had been • little confused and a little blurred. They had been divided a little amongst themselves, and for the want of great leading principles standing prominently out they had wasted a good deal of their time and energyin discussing personalities,who should be the leaders and whom they should follow. le was, how- ever, glad that principles rather than mei were coining to the front. (Hear, hear.) He attributed all honour te the men of Warrington and elsewhere who in these dark daya had stood by the party and the cause. (Applause). He thought now that the flowing tide was with them, and it was for them all to do what they I could in Warrington to carry that flowing tide to its fug , fruition, and to send from power the strongest Govern- ment and in some respects the weakest and most re- actionary Government they had had in modern times. (Applause.) There were several subjects Mr Crosfield had incidentally mentioned, two or three which were very dear to the hearts of many Liberals here, and no doubt is time they would in time came to the front and occupy the first place in the programme of the Liberal party. But there was one subject which at the present time dominated the position and held the field, namely, that of education, and he contended that they ought not to dissipate their power and strength—not forgetting the other subjects—but concentrate their energies upon the question of education. They should do everything in their power to see that the Bill was either altogether withdrawn or altogether altered. As president of the Free Church Council he leadftaken some part in the

Commissioners. The Penny Fare Question.

• At a meeting of the Stockton Heath Parish Council, held on Thursday last week, the Clerk (Mr Bradshaw) read the following letter which had bleu sent by Messrs Robert Davies and Company, solicitors, of Warrington, en behalf of the Council, to the Light Railway Commis- sioners :—" Market-place, Warrington, August 29th, 1902. Sir.—We appeared on behalf of the Stockton Reath Parish Council on the inquiry which was held as to this proposed Order, when the Corn- taissioners were good enough to express the Opinion that the demand of the Parish Council, /or a maximum penny fare between Rylands-street, Warrington, and Victoria.square, Stockton Heath. Vas reasonable. Your letter of the 21st inst to the Clerk to the Council was submitted to a meeting of the Council, and we are instructed to write you in reply. May we point out that under the Act of Parliament referred to in your letter by which the Warrington Cor- Potation Tramways were authorised, the Corporation have full power to make the fare over their tramways as low as they deem expedient. The only compulsion put upon them by their Act is against exceeding a certain maximum. Therefore, if tim Commissioners adhere to their decision to sanction the Light Railway upon the condition that a maximum fare of one penny is charged from Rylands-street to Victoria-square, we venture to submit that this deci- sion does not touch the existing statutory powers of the Corporation. The Commissioners clearly have juris- diction to sanction the Order subject to a condition. It OS open to the Corporation either to accept or decline, Sod their statutory powers enable them to accept. If they accept the Order it will involve charging on their tramway route a lower figure than their statutory Maximum, but in electing to charge this lower rate they are doing no more than exercising the powers 'fisted in them by the Act. The Town Clerk offered during negotiations preceding the inquiry to agree to the insertion of a provision in the order that no higher fare shall be charged for the route between Rylands-street. Warrington, and Victoria- square, Stockton Heath, than is charged on any other route on the Corporation Tramways for the same ois- Mace. If the Commissioners should still be disposed to abandon the condition inserted by them after the inquiry we are instructed to say that the Pariah Council would be satisfied to accept such a provision as was offered by the Town Clerk. If no provision as to a penny fare is inserted in the Order we are instruct- ed to urge that terms ought to be put upon the Corpora. tion that they will continue: to license the omnibuses Which now ply at a penny fare between Stockton Heath and Bridge-street, Warrington. We venture again to give you an outline of the grounds on which the Parish Council base their demand fcr a maximum one penny

rare : "1. There is an existing service of omnibuses over exactly the same routes running every fifteen minutes at a fare of one penny. The Corporation have intimated that they will refuse to license those omnibuses when their tramway is made. "2. The proposed Light Railway with the exception of a few yards is proposed to be made !entirely outside the Borough of Warrington so that the Corporation of Warrington is invading the district of an outside authority, and seeking to deprive the inhabitants of that authority of a benefit they now enjoy. The pro- Posed undertaking is not a public work of necessity. but is purely a profit-making scheme to augment the revenue of the Warrington Corporation Tramways. If the Corporation had applied to Parliament for an Act to enable them to extend their tramways (which at one tittle they resolved to de) the standing orders of the Houses of Parliament would not permit such extension except with the consent of the local authority con- cerned. 3. The Inhabitants of St-ckton Heath number about 3,000. A large proportion of these are people of !Mall means who go to work in Warrington in the morn- lag, return to Stockton Heath for their mid-day dinner, and go back to work in Warrington in the afternoon, Using the penny 'bus service for this purpose to a large fttent. A fare of 2d which the Corporation seeks power to impose means for such a person a weekly expenditure Of about 4s, a very important consideration to a man *arnine a sum!! 'Wary. —We are, sir, your obedient ser- vants, ROBERT DAVIES AND CO."
Thn CLERK informed the Council that the COM- missioners had acknowleged the receipt of the letter and mere giving it their consideration.

THE EXAMINER FRIDAY SEPTEMBER 26, 190" z MESSRS. CROSFIELD'S FIRE BRIGADE. Testing the New Engine.

' Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited, have recently established a fire engine station at their Bank IQuay Works, and equipped it with a new steam fire engine. The engine was put to an interesting test on Wednesday last week,in the presence of a large company. rho officials of the firm were present, as well as the Superintendent and Deputy Superintendent of the War- rington Fire Brigade and several others interested in fire extinguishing appliances from Crewe, Lsigh and other places. For some time:past, Messrs Crosfield's have had a fire brigade of their own but it was felt that the manual engine, useful as it had proved itself in ex- tinguishing small fires, was inadequate to cope with a large fire at the works. Accordingly Messrs Shand, Mason and Company of London, were commissioned to supply a steam fire engine which might be pulled about the works by the brigade but which would be eepeble of pumping water to the top of the highest buildings. It was in order to test this engine, which has been appro- priately called " Perfection," that an experiment was made on Wednesday. The operations were superin- tended by Mr Elliott, the represeatative of the engineers. Promptly at 330 a buzzer was sounded and immedi- ately workmen hastened from all parts of the works to the fire engine stetion, which is situated near the head office. A fire was lighted in the new engine and without a moment's delay the men exchanged their caps for helmets and harnessing themselves to the new en glee they dragged it out of the station and raced away with it to the river-side,a distance of a quarter of a mile. The idea was that the large warehouses tbere were on fire and the test was to see how the new engine could cope with such an emergency. On arrival at the wharf-side, a pipe was immediately placed in the river and other members of the brigade busied themselves in unrolling hose pipes and getting ready to pour water on the building All eyes were now centred on the en- gine and Mr Elliott announced that a steam pressure was obtained of Sibs within stnin, 45 seconds from the fire buzzer sounding. A steam pressure of 101bs was obtained in 6min, 25 seconds, and at the expiration of 7min 10 seconds the fingers of the pressure gauge showed 201b5 and 35 seconds later 301bs, and another 35 seconds sufficed to obtain Nibs pressure. Steam of 100 lbs pres- sure was obtained in Bmin 55 seconds at which pressure the engine was started and water was projected to the top of the building. It will therefore be seen that within 9 minutes from the alarm being given the engine had been taken a quarter of a mile and was playing a jet of water on the warehouses. Messrs Crosfield and Sons' new steam fire engine is a light machine of the patent " Double Vertical" pattern introduced by Messrs Shand, Mason and Co., the well known London firm of fire engineers, and now the moat popular type of fire engine among fire brigades of this country. The principal features of the engine are its twin doable ecting steam cylinders working directly upon a corresponding pair of double-acting pumps, these being placed vertically between the side frames at the rear of the quick-steaming boiler furnishing the motive power. Two piston-rods convey the movement of each piston to the correspouding pump-rod, and a special form of connecting rod is intraduced, the rods running from a joint in the headpiece of each pump to the pin of a double-throw crank-shaft. This arrangement mini- mises friction and facilitates the smooth working of the machinery, thereby considerably lessening the wear and tear • the absence of vibration considerably lengthens the 'life of hose and suction pipe ; while the design of the engine ensures a steady flow of water whether at high or low pressure. Other features of the Shand-Mason " Double Vertical " are its light- ness in comparison with power,the simplicity of design, and the rapidity and ease with which the pump valeee and other parts can be got at for inspection or cleaning 'or for overhauling when necessary. The boiler is of the firm's patent inclined water tube type which is capable of raising steam from cold water to 100 lb pressure per square inch in from 5i to 7 minutes while stationary,or Bto 9 minutes while travelling. The furnace door is at the side in preference to the re ir, the side position hav- ing important advantages, so much so that the Metro- politan Fire Brigade has in all its recent orders expressly specified this arrangement. Briefly the advantages are as follows :—the engineer being away from the hose and suction-pipe connections, and having all Ch. gauges and boiler fitzines within easy reach can perform his work better, the position is more convenient for clean- ing, oiling etc, the centre of gravity is kep, low allowing the engine to travel more easily and safely, the design of the engine is less cramped, and a lower position of the suction inlet is permitted which is very useful when working from a depth. The boiler fittings and feeding apparatus are complete sad well aeapted to their pur- pose, and bear several important improvements re- cently introduced. Alternative means of keeping the boiler supplied with water are provided to meet all possible contingencies. The lubrica- ting arrangements have been carefully arranged and are as far as possible self acing. The engine though remarkably light in weight is strongly built, steel entering freely into the consturucti ni of both carriage and frame. The parts of the machinery with which the water comes in contact are of gun-met 4 bronze or other non-corrosive metal. Pile engine is mounted on strong, higb, wood-spoke wheels wi,h steel axle, springs, and side frames, and being designed speci- ally for hand draught is furnished as ith a neat open hose boat in place '1 the usual full-size hose box floe to "double vertical "engines arrange I for horse draught and intended to carry several firemen. When fully stowed with the necessary hose and et.ler gear the machine can be easily and quickly drawn by hence The pumping capacity of Messrs Crosfield'a ring engine is 260 to 300 gallons per minute, and a powerful stream of water is easily proj mted to a height of 150 fee through a 15-16 inch jet-pipe or several slightly smaller jets simultaneously to a good working height This was demonstrated on Wedneelav to the satiefection of all present. At the outset three fin jets were got to work and nod fficulty was experienced in projecting the water to the top of the warehouse, which stands at a height of 7011. Smaller jets were then successfully tried, a powerful stream of dirty water from the river being steadily maintained. It was afterwards decided to test the supply from the Corporation mains. A con- nection was made with a six inch main and the water was pumped into a canvas tank. A satisfactory supply of water was Obtained but the pressure on the main wag rather low at the time. Notwithstanding this, no diffi- culty was experienced in forcing a jet of water to the highest buildings In the works. At the close of the proceedings which were intensel y interesting and eminently successful, tea was served to the visitors iii the dining room near the works. Mr Elliott congratulated Mr Gallon and his brigade On the excellent work they bad done. With a few more trials be felt sure, the brigade would be able to grapple with any emergency, although he trusted the firm would never have a serious fire to require the use of the fire engine. elle.CaoWe OF HEALTH.—AII sufferers from Dyspepsia,Liver Piles orgeadaches will receive sufficient of an infallible remedy for three days' treatment free. div.p: LOCAL REVISION COURTS. Newton Division. A MEMBER OF PARLIAMEN I'S SONS' CLAIMS AS LODGERS. Mr J T Foard, revising barrister, sat at S. Helens County Court on Monday afternoon to revise the lists for those parts of the Newton Division surroending St. Helens,and for the township of Rainford. Mr W Holland Owen, solicitor, and Mr W Mawdsley represented the Conservatives, awl Messrs W Shaw and t Moulding appeared on behalf of air Sam Woods.the Labour candi- date.—Air J R Lloyd, the St. Helens Conservative agent, appeared to support claims made for lodger votes by Messrs Arthur R Pilkington and W Nor- man Pilkington in respect of rooms at Rainford Mr Foard : These are in the family residence. I should like some proof of tenancy here.—Mr Holland Owen said there was a declaration which he thought would be sufficient —Mr Foard : I suppos3 it is a large house. How much is it rated P—Mr Smith : £320 —Mr Foard : According to the declaratien, there is only a bedroom in each case which is in the etclusive occupation of claim- ants. They claim for a bedroom and a study. Very often these declarations, although they are prima-facie perfectly sound, are unsound, because the persons who make them do not understand wflat is involved in the term tenancy. Arthur R Pilkington ha. a study on the ground floor, which is presumably a joint study. —Mr Lloyd said the claims stated that they In each case had the exclusive separate use, and las had come there to prove that.—air Foari : Is not this the same study ? —Mr Lloyd :No ; they have each separate roam.—Mr Foard: To your own knowledge P—Mr Lloyd : Yes.— Mr Foard : You have been in the rooms, I suppose ? Mr Lloyd : No. but I know these gentlemen very well. —Mr Foard : No, I must nave better proof upon these facts than is now before me. That won't do.—Mr Holland Owen said he wouli call the ciaimants.— Mr Shaw : Perhaps Me Lloyd can say they pay a certain sum per week for the rooms.— Mr Lloyd : Oh, no; I don't say the.—Councillor Arthur R Pilkington shortly afterwards attended, and said he had lived at Rainford Hal, all his life.—Mr Foard : But that does not satisfy the conditions of the franchise. When did you make arrangements to be- come the tenant and pay your father rent ?-11r Pilk- ington : I began to use the bedroola ten years ago.—Mr Foard Have you paid 103 a week since then ?—Mr Pilkington: No.—Mr Foard :I am afraid you don't. There must be a tenancy, or we should get on the list in that way a great many votes for one house. You must be either owner or tenant of the property to get a vote. Unless you can show me that you pay the rent, that you really have paid a rent, I cannot allow it. I think it improbable that you would pay it, or that your father would charge it. There most be a regular tenancy. —Dr Henry Baker Bates, of Junction-lane, Sutton, claimed a vote oa account of freehold land adjoining his boos'.—Alderman J Massey appeared for Dr Bates, and said he conveyed the freehold land.—Mr Foard : Is it rated at all P—Mr Massey : No, sir. It is for build- ing purposes, and freehold.—Mr Foard : But that won't do.—Me Massey : It is freehold land.—Mr Foard: What claim can you make for that ? It has no value at present. It is not rated at all.-11r Owen : The value is over tioe.—Mr Foard said that he knew of no case where land not rated could be described as a tenement. It was non-productive. The mere possession of land did not ipso facto give a qualificationdt most be a tene- ment worth £lo.—Mr Holland Owen : It being the ownership of freehold land he is entitled to be regis- tered as an owner.—Mr Foard There must be value. Mr Owen ; It cost over £loo.—Mr Foard : But if it does net produce anything it has no actual yearly valu No doubt it will be worth that in time to come. To take an extreme case, we might tax the sands of the seashore, and say it will be worth thousands of pounds for building purposes in days to come. I don't think the future taxable or rateable value can be taken into account hypothetically.

NEWTON DIVISION REVISION COURT. Mr. J T Foard held a Court at the 'Town Hall, Newton- lc-Willows, on Wednesday for the purpose of revising theyoters%list for the townships of Newton-in-Makerfield Earlestown, Burtonwood, Winwick-with-Hulme, Croft, &c. Mr W Holland Owen and Mr W Mawislay appeared for the Conservatives and Mr T Shaw, on behalf of the Liberals. The business at tho mornizg and afternoon sitting, was purely routine nothing, of importance transpiring.—At the evening Court, Albert McCoy, of Willow-road, Newton, applied for an occupier's vote. He was at present a member of the Manchester Police Force, and his mother and sister resided in the house, be coming home at the week ends. —The application was objected to by the Conservatives on the ground that McCoy was not a bona-fide occupier. —The Barrister upheld the objection, and said his mother could however, apply for the vote. Ernest J W Mullins applied for an occupiers' vote in respect of 11, Grant-street, Earlestowio. This was ob- jected to by the Conservatives on the ground of short date. The Barrister, after evidence showing that appli- cant had occupied the house the legal period, held that London and Ncrth-Western workmen were on sufferance, the rent being stopped from their wages and they had no rent book to keep. There might be a constructive tenancy if somewhat doubtful, but he would allow the vote.

COURT AT PENKETH. Mr J T Foard, revising barrister, attended at the Conservative Club, Penketh, on Tuesday morning, for the purpose of revising the voters' list for the districts of Bold, Cuerdley, Penketh, and Great Sankey. in the Newton Division, and bearing the claims and objections, Messrs W Holland Owen (solicitor) and W A Mawdsley representing the Conservatives of the division ; Mr William Shaw the Labour Party ; and Mr James Hough- ton, assistant overseer for Bold ;Mr James Wright, assistant overseer for (Merdley ; Mr Foster, assistant overseer for Penketh ; and Mr Joseph Sarin, assistant overseer for Great Sankey, were also in attendance. Mr. James Millington claimed a vote in respect to his ownership of two houses in Hood-lane,Great Sank,y He was supported by Mr W Shaw. Mr. Owen objected on the ground of the lease of tbe property. In reply to the Barrister, Mr Millington said h 3 had been in possession two and a half years' The Barrister : That will do. Yoa nee I not trouble further. Other applications were greeted, no objection being raised

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNIT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNIT.

Mr Foard attended at the Warrington Polies Court,on Tuesday afternoon for the purpose of revising the voters' list for the districts of Peulton-with-Fearnhead, Rixton-with-Glazebrook, Warrington, and Woolston- with-Martinscroft, and hearing claims and objections. Mr W H Owen and Mr W A Mawdsley represented the Conservatives, and Mr William Shaw on behalf of the Labour party. Mr H J Westbrook, of Messrs Robert Davies and Company. solicitors, Warrington, applied for votes on behalf of Mr Leonard Davies, Mr Vera Davies. and Mr Edward Graskell Davies for the Town Hall Ward in ref '- pact of property there lately left to them by the will of their father, the late Mr Robert Davies. They were granted. The Rev William Bracecamp, vicar of St Paul's Church, appeared and was allowed a vote for the Town Hall Ward. James Armitage Rushworth, 212, winwick-road, applied through Mr Owen for a vote in respect of some property be had owned since February 4th. Mr Shaw objected on the ground that applicant had not been in possession of the property the required sis months. He was four days' short. The claim was not allowed. Two lodger claims, those of Percy Houghton Bennett, of Padvate, and John Jackson, the Poplars, Penketh, were allawed. The former said be pail his mother 12s a week for the use of • sitting-room which he used as an office and a bedroom. Questioned by Mr Shaw, applicant said that RUM also included part of his food. Mr Shaw submitted that the 12i was for fond. The Revising Barrister said there was always a difficulty in assessing what rsallv wag paid in reenect of premises and °the- matters when they were conjoined. He would allow the vote, but it must not be taken as a precedent.
