div.head: WARRINGTON ACADEMY. -- Unveiling of alVlemorial Tablet by Principal Drummond.
div.p: WARRINGTON ACADEMY. -- Unveiling of alVlemorial Tablet by Principal Drummond.

Thera was an interesting ceremony at the War- rington Academy on Tuesday, when Principal Drummond,of Manchester College, Oxford. unveiled ' the tablet on the front of the building. Oae of the I best-known places *not only in the town bat in the country, this building will be better Marked out for , the information of residents an i visitors in the future by this tablet, which bears the following inscription :—`' The Warrington Academy was established in this building in 17.57, removing to larger premises in what is known as Academy-street in 1762. This tablet was erected in 1931 by the Warrington Society." It may be adJel that the_ tablet is of Wedgwood ware, bears a representa, tion of the fourader of the institution—John Sell° —and was designed by Mr A Warburton F.R.T.B.Ae a member of the Warrington Society. It has been wrought by Messrs Joshua Wedgwood end Sons, of Struria, and it is a fact not without interest that Joshua We lgwood himself was one of the trustees of the institution and that one at least of his sons was educated there. In view of the succession of Manchester College to the work begun at Warring- ton Academy, it was felt peculiarly appropriate that Dr Drummond should have consented to unveil the tablet. The weather was extremely wet, and the actual unveiling was done as briefly as possible. A' photograph of the interesting ceremony was aken by Mr J Dirties. It is intended, if the neces- sary funds are forthcoming to erect descriptive tablets on all the interesting buildings in Warring- ton.

—Mr WiLi.Lust LONG presided over a crowded gathering in the house, at which several interest- ing addresses were delivered. Amongst those pre-1 sent were : Alderman Thempson (Manchester), At. F Monks, 'Alderman F W Ntonks, Rev Morley Stevenson, Rev E W Lummis, Councillor Bennett and Mr E J Hall (han secretaries), Messrs J Lyon Whittle, Fulton Smith, J Fairhurst, W H Woolcmk Wll J Jenkins, A Ai Ker, T May, G Venn, A Crompton, J Birtles, Stuart Page, J A Ransome, M Ashton, B S Namcsmba, E V Walker, G Smith Junr J Monks and others.

The CHAIRMAN Said it Was his duty 83 President of the Warrington Society, to explain the object ot the gathering. It would be in the memory of most of them that some years ago, in carrying out some street improvements—very fortunately carrying out—the C3rporation removed a building which, although very good for commercial purposes was not at all in the spirit of that old mansion (the Old Academy). On toe removal of that building it was not known to what purposes the Academy might be devoted. However, a few gentlemen stepped forward, the Corporation accepted them as tenants, , and they took the Academy with the idea of pre- serving it as a building of great historical interest lin Warrington from a worse fate. Gradually the Warrington Society was formed ; and the object was as far as possible to cultivate something of the spirit, the life and the culture that was originally I possessed by those who occupied the premises !originally. As far back as 1757 the Academy was founded for the promotion of free thought and cul- ture in a broad and liberal spirit. The Chairman alluded to some of the eminent men who had been connected with the Academy, including Dr Priest- ley, Dr Enfield, Dr Taylor, the great theologian, and the Rev Gilbert Wakefield, and said that what would appeal to the ladies was the fact:that thia'was the home of Mrs Barbauld when she wrote about Warrington and the Mersey—a different Mersey to what they knew now, (Laughter). One of the chief things the Society set their bands to was to preserve the main features of the different old build- ings, and by means of tablets or memorial stones to mark them out for the benefit of the present and future generations. The present was the first tablet that had been erected, but it was proposed to mark in a similar way toe houses of Dr Aikin, Dr Priestley, Dr Enfield, and Gilbert Wakefield, the lodgings where John Howard, the prison philan- thropist, spent a great deal of his time, and the birthplace of Dr Percival. (Applause.) Any town might be glad to know that it owned the birthplace of such a man. He was tbe youngest fellow of the Royal Society, and the youngest president when he took the office. Cromwell's lodging were also in Warrington. Time would not allow him to tell of all the interesting houses, but he had no doubt if the present generation would only put their hands in their pockets and help them the society would mark in a similar way all these _pieces of note.

(Hear, hear, and applause.) John Seddon was the promoter of the Academy ; and he struggled hard in the earlier days of its inception to carry it through. With a man of less pluck the thing would probably have fallen through. The college was afterwards moved to Academy-street, and his (Mr Long's) great grief was that the place should have been allowed to be broken through as it had been. He thought something might have been done to preserve the orginal character of the street, and possibly even gas stoves could have been relegated to some less classic place. (Laughter and applause).

div.head: LETTERS OF APOLOGY.
div.p: LETTERS OF APOLOGY.

Mr E J HALL read several letters of anolozy for non- attendance. The Mayor who was staying in Hereford- shire, wrote that his sympathies were warmly with the society in Maintaining these interesting records of be: gone times, and people in their good old town. Mr Robert Pierpoint, M.P., wrote that he thanked the society for their courteous invitation to the Old Academy. He regretted he could not be present, as he was just waiting fo: a troublesome cold to allow him to go abroad. Letters bad also been received from Mesqrs Wedgwood and Sons, and the Rev William Blazley, an old fellow student of Dr Drummond. INTERESTING SPEECH BY PRINCIPAL DRUMMOND.

Priacipal Deumaioen then addressed the gathering. Ele"said the name of John Seddon, in whose honour they had assembled that afternoon, was one which was not highly distinguished in the annale of England,hut it was not without good reason that after almost a century and a half the people of Warrineton had agreed to do him honour. He was born not in Warrington, but be Caine here early in life. He was settled at the age of 22 as minister of Cairo-street Chapel in 1745. In the course of the fifties the question arose as to the necessity for academies. After the Act of Uniformity, other acts were passed which pressed very herd upon Dissenters' The object, be supposed, was to drive dissent altogether out of existence : otherwise he thought anyone would feel that the imposition of ignorance upon the Dissenters was abcut the most unwise course that ceuld have been resorted to, and if it were successful it could only pro- duce a very fierce and unwise fanaticism. But the Dissenters of those days °who were excluded from the universities and could only preach under restrictions meant to have the equivalent of a University education, and for many years one gentleman after another arose and opened an Academy In his own house, sometimes seeking, for purposes of concealment a very remote :and unpEopled district. The earliest was Dr Franklendie Academy at Rettimill, a little village in Yorkshire, where he was not very likely to be interfered with. After this a great number of academies were opened, but about 1753 or 1751 the suc- cession of these private academies seemed likely to come to an end. Two of the more important ones ezpired, and the question arose whether the time bad not arrived when an Academy should be erected by public subscrip- tion and kept open by public supper,. That was the origin of the Warrington Academy. Mr Jehn Seddon i took an extreme interest n the movement, and from thEi first exerted himself to the utmost to promote its inter- est. He gathered subscriptions from all over the country and wandered about from one place to another trying to collect them. At the same time he was very anxious that Warrington should be selected as the seat of the new learning. There Wa9 an earnest endeavour made to have the Academy at Ormakirk, and possibly it might have gone there, but they were unable to procure a suitable house, sad the result was that War- rington, to Mr Seddon'e delight, carried the day, and that house was taken for the purpose of the Academy ; Dr Taylor being summoned from Northwich to be the first Principal. (Applause). John Seddon was appointed the first secretary, and when the academy was opened in October 1757 he was appointed the first librarian. That did not end his con- nection with the building, for ten 3 ears later he was appointed the rector of the Academy. in order to obtain better discipline and be succeeded Dr Priestley in the capacity of professor of belles lettrel, so that in four different ways he was connected with the Academy in addition to the private assistance rendered by his zeal and energy in securing its presence in Warrington. Why should an Academy of that kind interest the citizens as a whole. Simply for this reason, that although it was founded by Dissenters, and even by a particular bode,it was founded on Catholic principles. It was never in- tended to be limited either in its teaching Staff or itg students to members of any single denomination. It was thrown open to all and not only Dissenters of different types but even Churchmen came under ite in- struction in those early edgy,. That showed the !Arne- ' mindedness which prevailed among the men of the 18th Century. They anticipated a principle which was now almost universally recognized. All our universities had been thrown open in the mannerin which the Warring- ton Academy was thrown open with the single exception of theological chairs, but the Academy at Warrington anticipated what he hoped would be the case—the open- ing even of theological chairs in all the great public in- stitutions. It was the principle of the Academy that instruction should be given in all the subjects of an arte course such as was pursued at the Universities and that

div.head: EXAMINER FRI AY SEPTEMBER 26, 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRI AY SEPTEMBER 26, 1902

there should be a faculty of theology. Naturally at first the professors belonged to the class of Dissenters, but they were laid under no obligation whatever la regard to their theological opinions, and so strictly was the freedom of the students respected that even one ot the friends of the College remarked that if it were possible it would be desirable that the teachers' opinion should not be known, even to his pupils. (Leughter). That seemed to be going a little too far. Their present principle was free teaching as well as free learning, and he believed the true principle was to say to the teechisr, " Dealt you can to And the truth. Speak freely and openly what you believe to be true. Give your students the best results of your thought and study, and leave them in absolute freedom to follow your teaching or reject it as may appetr to them in accordance with toe evidence." (Applause.) Teat was the course which the teleological faculty which had survived from the old Warrington days still sought to pursue. It was on account of that catholicity of principle he apprehended that the citizens of Warrington, without any regard to political or religious classification, were alike interested in the Old Academy. It represented a public movement, it was intended to be public and was governed throughout by a public aim and through a public spirit. Mr Seddon, to whom he had just referred, was largely instrumental in founding the Public Free Library in Warriegton and Was its first president. He ale) helped in the establishment of a Widows Fund, which still existed, and of which he was the first secretary. And so the Academy remained in that building for five years when it was found necessary to erect larger premises, and the Academy (which he understood hed been nulled dewe) was erected in Academy-street. Various difficul- ties arose, but not until after John Seddon's death. He died suddenly in 1770. Hs had done a good work for which he was most deservedly held in remembrance,and they had that afternoon erected a tablet in order teat he I might be remembered and honoured. The Academy , came to an end abut ten years afterwards,b at in order that it might not really cease, but be transferred only to new ground, the cause was taken up by a few people in Menailester chiefly, who founded the Manchester New College. That college teed various movements from place te place until it had reached he supposed, its final borne in Oxford, where a beautiful building had been erected with all passible conveniences and appliances neaessary for the ceriduct of a college. But one great change bad taken place. All the oil academies aimed at university educatign in its extent and its quality, and that weal*on uatil thirty-two years ago, when the ancient Universities were thrown open without restriction. At one time, therefore, what was now Manchester College had its own professional staff, and might have taken the place now occupied by Owens College, only that John Owens left money for purposes of foun ling a nollege on quite the same principles and the Manchester College was overshadowed. It was taken to London, and was there associated with University College for its arts teaching. On the removal to Oxford thirteen years ago the arts teaching was given up, and now it was a postgraduate college, devoted simply to theological teaching. But the old principles of John Seddon and others remained unimpaired. Fey imposed no obligations except what conecienee and regard for truth imposed on teachers or students. They had no formal creed. They required in their teaching to lose sieht at denominationalism and to teach theology as a scientific man taught science. Their desire was to obtain the best knowledge and form the most enlightenel thoughts and students might come from any deaoraina- tion and have the means of information laid before them And so what was best in a long-past generation remain- ed. Tneir limitations, errors, infirmities, had gradually dropped away and been foreotten. What was true and valuable in their high principles, earnest conscientioue- ness, fidelity to what seemed to them to be true—these things remained, and they in Oxford considered they were of such men the true and legitimate heirs. On that account, he supposed, they had done hint the honour to ask hien to unveil the tab'et, and this had been to him a I great pleasure. He hoped that all that was best and I finest in the culture and spirit of the past Academy would remain and grow in the good town of Warrington. (Applause.)
SPEECH BY ALDERMAN THOMPSON, OF - MANCHESrER.

Mr Alderman THOMPSON (Manchester), who was then called upon, remarked that when we looked at the results of throwing open Oxford and Cambridge we saw that the great prizes were taken as much by Dissenters as by Church people. Continuing, he said he took deep interest in the Academy for many reasons, and also in Warrington, owing to the very pleasant associations he had with it during the sixties and seventies of the last century. In fact he took as deep an interest in that historical institution as if he were a Warrington man. Ho believed in these institutions in these days of strain and stress, when they were compelled to live in large manufacturing centres, and saw towns prosperous, changes rapidly taking place, and new buildings being put up. In these circumstances sentiment was apt to be crushed out and die. Therefore, those who came for- ward and preserved some of the old relics and cherished some of the old assoziations were conferring an unspeakab'e benefit on the neighbourhood. In times gone by, when he was in business and bad sometimes a very anxious time of it, it was a pleasure to go to the annual meeting of the Chatham Society, to sit in the old building, and listen to the distant hum of commerce, and yet to be taken away to the doings of their prede- cessors. To him that was an unspeakable delight, and it would be so to them in Warrington, who bad gathered up those precious treasures and housed them. When, ever they came there or passed that place their thoughts would turn to the past and to the good men who lived in the town when it was like a village. (Applause). Of those assnciated with the Academy in the past such men as Dr Percival, Dr Barnes, and Dr Priestley exerted an influence which extended to Manchester, where they founded a Literary and Philosophical Society—a society that had done an infinite amount of good in its trans- actions and researches.—ln conclusion, the speaker expressed the hope that bis good friends in Warrington would carry out the object they had in view in preserv• ing buildings that had been occupied by good men in the past. (Applause.)

not very probably have founded the Warrington : Academy. He (the speaker) was proud of his position as minister of Cain-street Chapel, and to succeed his immediate predecessor the Rev W H Drummond, a worthy son of & distinguished sire ; the Rey F K Freeston, of Manchester College ; Dr Philip Carpen- ter, a name that appealed t 3 many hearts even yet in Warrington; and Dr Enfield, who was b4mself a tutor of the Old Academy. He felt par- ticularly proud that the list of his predecessors numbered John Seddon, He (Ur Lummis) had just been reading the account of John Seddon's activity in founding the Academy. He fought against great obstacles indeed, and had it not been for his energy and hopefulness the Academy would net have been established. (Applause). The proposition was passed with acclamation. Professor D EIIMIOND, in acknowledging the vote of thanks, recalled the following votation by one of the Peroivals in regard to John Seddon, which showed he was a man of remarkable parsonality :—" As a scholar preacher, and companion, he was almost without an equal." Mr F MONKS, chairm in of the Museum anl Technical Institution, moved a vote of thanks to the arohitect and to the contractors of the tablet, and also to Mr Long for presiding, Councillor BENNETT, in seconding, said they were all sorry that Mr Albert Warburton, the designer of the tablet, Was prevented from being present through serious illness, He pointed out that it was largely owing to the help of the Chairman that they were able to rescue the Academy from destruction. The vote having be pssred, the CHM &MAN expressed regret that the Rev Enfield Dawson—s direct descendant from Dr Enfield—had been unable to be present. _ .
Light:refreshments were then serves to the members of : the Society and guests.
fi ag s flying._ (Applause).

, A. vote of thanks was accorded to the ladies who had prepared the tea. During the evening an orchestra from Bewsey-road Church, conducced by Mr W Brotigh played • number of selections. SALVATION ARMY, RUNCORN. . . _ . • - - • - -

- . • . A service of thanksgiving for the mothering of the harvest was held at the Salvati ma Army Barracks on Sunday evening, when a sermon was preached by Captain 3 Cox. The decoration were vary pleasing and the room presented a bright and cheerful appearance. A service was also held on Bloaday evening.

PRIIIITIVE METHODIST CHURCH, EARLESTOWN. The annual Harvest Home CIOCICrG in connection with the above Church was held in toe schoolroom on Tears- day night. The programme was furnished by klr Harry BarrWe famous St Helens choir of sixteen singees,and no further proof of the high esteem in which this c 1011. is held in this district was nee led when the inside of the schoolroom was seen, every available seat being occupied. The programme was opened by a part song from the choir entitled 't Come Dorothy, come," Miss Ethel Parr afterwards rendered " Come back to me "for which she was deservedly applauded. After the choir had given "Shepherd of Souls," Mr Rigby effeotively rendered " The King's Champion," whilst ' several selections from the "Bohemian girt" excellently served by the choir evoked much enthusiasm, Mr F Price proved himself to be a very capable humorist by his description of Mr and Mrs Scroggin'e evening party which kept the audience in one continuous roar of laugh- ter. A quartette entitled "The merry chafers" tv Messrs Cotton, Berrey, Milne and Topping was followed by an excellent rendering of " The Soldiers of the Park." A humorous quartette " Toothache" described as being sung by " The Victims " brought the first part of the programme to a close. At the termination of a short interval the second portion was opened by a glee en- titled" All among the barley," followed by a " Sobbing quartette" " Poor old Man " by Misses Berrey and Parr and Messrs Cotton and Milne. Mr F Price afterwards caused much amusement with a comic song entitled" Achoo," rendering " Two Sweethearts" as an encore. " The torpedo and the whale' was given by Mr W Milne, assisted by the choir, after which a capital rendering of the'," Miserere Scene" from " II Trovatore " was given ; " Lenora " and" Manrico " being represented by Miss Barray and Mr H Berrey respectively. A part song " Lullaby of Life." by the choir, and a humorous sketch by Mr F Price were gone through, after which a splendid pro- gramme was brought to a close by the singing of " Good Evening" by the Choir, the National Anthem of course winding up the proceedinge.—Mr H Berrey conducted his choir, and Mrs Barrey officiated at the piano.

div.head: VOTES OF THANKS.
div.p: VOTES OF THANKS.
SPEECHES BY THE REVS MORLEY STEVENSON AND E. W. LUMMIS.

The Rev MORLEY STEVENSON in propeeing a vote of thanks to Principal Drummond said he was afraid there were very grave distinctions between the college over which he presided and the old Academy. There were grave disticctions of sects to begin with—(laughter)— but that ; he feared was unavoidable. Then, of course ttie curriculum and objects in view were very different but still there it was, and he did no: know that they could draw any comparison at all except in regaid to one little point which struck him. He had negtd it whispered—he did not know whether with truth—that in the days of the Old Academy there was one weak j point, namely, that the discipline was not always per- fect. (Laughter.) He hoped in that particular they might be able to bear favourable comperisoia with the Old Academy. (Laughter.) There were two points he would like to mention. As often happeued one of them had been taken up,haroely. by Alderman Thompson and consequently be would have to bow to the superior way in which be had expressed his (Mr Stevenson's) thoughts- He had intended to have said something about the enormous value of trying to preseive, in these Lanca- shire factory towns, anything which Was of a historical interest. Thera was no greater shock to one's feelings than to see one old place after another ruthlessly, but perhaps necessarily, destroyed, and he rejoiced from the bottom of his heart that that particular building had been rescued from that fate and he hoped it would be preserved for many years to come. (Applause). There was another point not unworthy of their attention. They, in these factory towns—where there was such a rush of life, where there was such temptation te materialism, to the making of money, and what was celled " your pile " and such like—found that it was ntcessary to plant, foster and keep those institutions whose business it was to promote culture. It seemed to hiuu that culture was, sometimes misunderstood. Taere was, of course, plenty of culture in what he might call the utilitarian sense. Their lads were keen enough to go whore they might learn their trade and anything which might advance them in their material position, and that was quite right. But what he meant by culture was that they should plant homes such as these where people, after they had learnt what was necessary for their material welfare, would be able to feel they could do something for the higher part—the intellectual and the spiritual. That that building might minister to that was, be was sure, the earnest hope of them all. (Ap- plause). They all felt a debt of gratitude to Principal Drummorrd for having come such a long journey-and given up his valuable time,and also for having sketched out far them in such an interesting way, and put so beautifully, the historical aspect of the house. In con- clusion, might they take a little parable from the room in which they were sitting ? The whole house breathed the spirit of the culture, thought and lemming of those , who had inhabited it in the past. They saw on the I walls pictures which spoke of those days, and they also I saw that the room was lighted by electricity. Might not that be a parable ? Might they not be able as they preserved the old culture and wisdom of their ancestors to throw fresh light upon them from modern thonght ? —and let that house shine forth within the town of Warrington as the home of culture and learning, and, if he might Say se, be an intellectual lighthouse. (Applause) The Rey E W GUAM'S (who, the Chairmen said, was a comparatively new corner to Warrington, hut had a claim upon them as a succ clam. to John Ssddon) seconded the vote of thanks, with which the name of Alderman Thompson was coupled. Mr Lammis observed that no more apt choice could have been made than that of Professor Drummond to perform the unveiling ceremony. It was not only his personal qualties, on which it would bs impertinent to lay stress, but he was also Presideat of the College which represented to-day the Old Acedarny. There were two institutions which had an historic connection with the Old Academy, one being represented by Dr Drummond and the cthet by himself. Manchester College stood in a filial relation to the Old Academy, while Cairo-street Chepeemest vener- ' able of all, might he said to stand in a maternal relation to it,for had not John Seddon been its minister he would

WYCLIFFE P.S.A..SOCIETY.

The half-yearly prize distribution in connection with sthis society took place on Sunday, when Ms) prizes were , awarded under the coniitions of the prize scheme. The meeting was well attended and was presided over by Mr C 11 Mills. Tne address was delivered by Mr W Williams of Manchester, who spoke upon the irreverence which was so characteristic of the present day, regarding that which was issued and good. This irreverence was shown for God's name and religious services. lir Flassall, of Warrington, gave an effirrient rendering of the solo" Thou didst not leave" (Messiah). Mr Payton , presided at the organ. The service was also taken part in bv Mr B Farrar (lion secretary), Mr D Owen and Mr WJLowe. PROFESSOR DAVISON AT WARRINGTON. Large congregations assembled in Bold-street Wes- leyan Church on Sunday, morning and eveuine, to hear the Rev Professor W T Davison, the ex-president of the Wesleyan Conference. The occasion was the anniver- sary in 'roam:Non with Bold-street Church,andithis is the third year in succession that the preacher at these anni- versary services has been the ex-Presi lent of the Wes- leyan Conference. As a cultured and devout scholar, Dr Davison bas gained a high reput atioo' and it was nor surprising that many in Warrington and district took advantage of the opportunity of hearing him on Sunday. His discourse at the morning service was based on the text " And the peace of God, which passetla all understanding, shall guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus." (Philippians 41., 7v.) These words, he said, were most familiar to us in the form of prayer. Many a time we had listened to them coming as the crown and the consummation of our Worship. They had tuned our souls to a more tender key. The preacher proceeded to explain that the words were a promise closely connected with the injunction which told them to be anxious for nothing "but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known ante God." In the busy city of lire with all its noises and distractions there WAS a quiet garden ' with shady nooks and sequestered re- cesses, which any man could enter who would go through the gate and trust his nitker. The peace of God was the celestial atmosphere He breathed. He gave it to His children to share His own blessings. It that seem too bold an assertion let them remember that the Lord Jesus Christ spoke thus. All God's gifts passed understanding. Let them take two examples—life and love. Did anyone mean to say that both life and love did not pass understanding ? The very existence we have at God's hands, the life of consciousness passed the , understanding of every one of us. Love—that pure fount of joy of father and mother and child and daughter and sister and friend and lover passed understanding. The more you thought of it the more you wondered at it. It passed the under- standing of man to conceive it or to produce it. They might as well try to produce a snowdrop by machinery as to produce peace by men's devices. They could not embrace the infinite but what if the infinite embraced us? That was where the blessing came in. That was the source of peaoe. It was a sea in which a man had to bathe. It was an atmosphere he had to breathe—a vast unfathomable sea where all our thoughts are drowned. Busy ammo men. it was a good thing for their thoughts to be drowned sometimes. It would be a good thing for some of them if their thoughts never came to life again. If they spent some moments in the presence of God they would not find the life outside altered. There would be the same noise, the same tempers and the came difficulties to be encennted, but whatever jarred or disturbed the spirit it did not so much matter if there was peace at home. They would experience many disappointments but if they took the words of the text with them, theirlives would be trans- lorrned.—The musical part of the service was 3 special feature. The choir under the conductorship of Mr Frank Hickmae, the organist, contributed several selec- tions. In the morning they gave careful renderings of " Senctus,"l Mrs Booth taking the solo, and the "To Deum "to a setting by Dr Dykes. The anthem " The Wilderness" (Sir J Goss) was also very capably sung. It included a bass solo by Mr Pownall, and a trio by Miss Hayward, Mr Berrey and Mr Page. The hymns were of a special character, on s of the verses in " Hail to the Lord's anointed " being tastefully given as a quartette by Miss Taylor. Miss Wilson, Mr Warburtoa and Mr White, while Mrs Booth, Miss Wilson, Mr Woods and Mr Warburton formed a quartette for a verse in another hymn. In the evening an augmented choir sang with great effect"o Father Whose Almighty power"and " Worthy is the lamb," (Handel). There was a very large congregation at the evening service Collections, taken in aid of the Church funds, realized about £2O.

THE NEW VVESLEYAN MINISTERS. WELCOME AT WARRINGTON. There was an interesting gathering in Bold-street schools, Warrington, on Monday evening, when local Wes,eyan Methodists assemblel for the purpose of ; extending a hearty welcome to the newly appointed ministers of the circuit, the Revs G H Carnson and R , Wilkins Rees. Mr Carnson comes from Birmingham to take up the superinteniency of the circuit and Mr Rees leaves Cossetharn Hill, Manchester, to take charge of Bewsey-road Cnurch. The proceedings on Monday , evening took the form of a social gathering. About 200 persons at down to an excellent tea, and afterwards a meeting was held, Mr J W Hayward, senior circuit steward, presiding. The attendance inclu- ded the Revs W C J Neville and John Gunnell, and Mr , George Weaver, junior circuit steward. Letters of apology for non-attendance were received from Miss Bessie Dutton, of Moore, Mr Robert Garnett, of Periketh, and Mr Menton, of Lymm. The CHAIRMAN delivered a short speech and heartily welcomed the new ministers, expressing the hope that their work in the district would.be successful. Speeches of welcome were also given by Mr William Silcoch, the Rev John Gunnell, Mr Wdliam Bennett, of Padgate, Mr Povey, Basysey-road, Rev W Howard, of Stockton Heath (formerly a Warrington; minister), Mr Wiloinshaw, of Penketh. Mr Lawton, ot Moore, and Mr Wadsworth, of Sankey Bridges. In reply the Rey R Wilkins Rees sai 1 he did not thihk ' he would please everyone. He was a man and not a monstrosity. (Lauaiter.) He was not infallible; he had been married 13 years. (Llughter.) He would try to do his duty, and whether his stay among them would , be for the heterodox one year or the orthodrx three ' years he would try to live In the affections of the people so that when be went they would not be inclined to fling the Doxology at his departure. (Renewed laughter.) He asked them to preserveharmony in the eirouit,f or the greatest difficulty of n minister was lo iestore it when discord had set in. They wanted the union of hearts and hands. Kind words from them would to more welcome than he should ever be able zo tell then,. They should not keep their kind words until the ministers I left. (applause.) The Rey G H Carlson referred to the fact that he had had no previous f xptrience hs a superintendent and urged his ne4rerBpllio their best for the advanc nnent of the work in the circuit. He had received letters from different parts of the circuit asking that they should always have ministers. He did not know how this was to be done, but he would consider the letters and do his beet, tie hoped that when the plan cams 04C it would be a model one. In alluding to the needs of the circuit, he said that Bold-street Crunch wanted renovating and also required an organ. liewsey-road were busy with an organ,so they had a scheme going. Latchford wanted a new school, and Stockton Heath wanted everyth ing— a site, a chapel, arid a school. Tao people of Autrobus would be glad to take up a scheme for the renovation of their chapel, and very likely something was ardhtod at Whitley and Appleton. He knew that if ho wont to Padgate and took his owe view of thing he would sty "Where is the minister's house ?" They had got a nice new house for the chapelkeeper. but no minister's house. Continuing the rev gnitlernan said he thought A superin- tendent ought to be the kindest man alive, and the most considerate man on the face of toe earth, and everybody else ought to be the same to him. (Laughter.) He thanked them for the hearty way they had received hirn He bad been dreaming about Warrington for seven years. He was told it was the best circuit in Metho- dism. (Applause.) One of the proofs that it was a good circuit from a minister's point of view lay in their good friend Mr Gunnell who had been in the circuit ' thirteen years. That he was so popular told him (Mr ; Carnson) that it would be an easy thing for Mr Rees and I himself to live, hero for three years andligo away with

div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLES rowN. BY A CORR ESPONDEN .

Barlestown had an off-day on Saturday 80 far as League matches were concerned and to fill up the gap they paid a visit to et Helens Recs. to play a friendly match. They took with them a fair num- ber of supporters, and although there was nothing at stake a very good exhibition of the game was given. Of course friendly matches are no criterion of the relative strength of the teams when points are in question, and consequently it would not be safe to say, seeing the result was a draw of two goals each, that the teams are evenly matched. Both sides played well and to all appearances there was a conscientious desire to do their best.

To-morrow (Saturday), the match at Esrlestown with Staleybridge Rovers will be full of interest and there should be an exciting game. The event is the second round for the Lancashire cup, and should Earlestown get through they will have the honour of encountering the second division team Burnley at Town Moor. At the opening of the season Esrlestown and Staleybridge met on the latter's ground, and Staleybridge won by 4 goals to 1. In that encounter Earlestown were not at full strength, and ic is hoped, with the match at home, on this occasion they will be able to turn the tables. Thera should be a big crowd of supporters to lend encouragement to their local champions.

There were loud complaints in Earles• town and Newton on Sunday anent the water supply. The quantity was alright, but the quality was beastly. It was so bad that the people refrained from drinking it, fearful that there might be a plot afoot to poison all the inhabitants. It tasted as if all the fish from New- ton Lake had got into the well, but enquiry showed that the unpleasant taste proceeded from the water haying come in contact with the brattice cloths used in connection with the sinking of the new wells. The cloths are thickly coated with tar. and although the evil was remedied immediately it was discovered, the offensive taste was not removed from the water until late on Monday.

div.head: VIADUCT INSTITUTE TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION CLASSES.
div.p: VIADUCT INSTITUTE TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION CLASSES.
Distribution of Prizes.

On Monday evening the prizes gained by the students of the ab yse classes during the sessions of 1900 and 1901 were distributed by Mr C W Emmett in the reading room of the Institute. Mr J W Emmett presided,and in opening the proceedings said it was so long since ha pre- sided at the distribution of prizes, he was at a loss to know what to say. When he entered the room their secretary was kind enough to ask him to preside, and as he was always very pleased t 3 help in any way he ac- cepted. Ho was pleased to see such a large number of IPriass ; it was the largest number he had ever seen. He 1 thea, Rs he said, for the encouragement of the students, i proceeded to give a short resume of his life, detailing bow he commenced as an ordinary apprentice, then a workman, afterwards a foreman, and latterly a superin- tendent, the position he now held. He was sorry to sae that Dr Handyside's modal had not been won for the last four years, but he hoped to see it won during the session. Mrs Emmett's prize of 24s had also not been- won this year. He announced with pleasure that Mrs Emmett had promised to give a special prize for cookery and needlework. (Applause). Mr C W Emmett before proceeding with the distribu- tion of the prizes congratulated the prize winners on their success. He would like to see more students gain these prizes. Some young men might perhaps say. "What benefit are these classes to mei have learned my trade and know as much as I shall probably need, thent why should I attendielasses?"This sort of reasoning might have held good many years ago,but to day this would no do. To get on at all tiles must have theory as well as practice. It was not sufficient to know that a certain wheel did ceitain work, they must know why it chid the work. We in England, made a machine which did its work well for a number of years. We let it go on working year after year without any alteration what- ever. In America they were different. As soon as one machine was set to work men were engaged to watch Ws progress and to suggest any alwlration which would materially increase its value, taeroby keening up to date and leaving England in the lurch. To keep peace with them we should have to study and work hard. He would like to suggest that when any student was think- ing of taking up any single subject, say mechanics, he would do well to consult his teacher as to what wsnald be a good subject to take in conjunction with the one already entered for, one that would materially help him in the study of his subi e,t. (Hear, hear.) He then proceeded with the di3trilutioa of the wiz") Et and certificates.

At Ph l clon Mr C Rawlins (a student) prnonsed a vote of thanks to Mr C W Emmett for his advice and kindness in dist.ributint, the prizes. Mr J Graham seconded. A vote of thanks to the Chairman was accorded on the motion of Mr Bradley eoonded by Mr Birchall.

div.head: TOMBSTONE INSCRIPTION AT GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: A TOMBSTONE INSCRIPTION AT GRAPPENHALL.

The Rector's Objections. " Truth " says ; —An ex-army schoolmaster (Mr E Jones) living at a place called Grapoenhall, near War- rington, lost a son in a battle in the Transvaal. The son was a non-commissioned officer in the R.H.A,, and was buried on the veld where he fell. rfne lath sr had buried a daughter in the churchyard at Grapeeahall, and he had P.t, ocher times het two other children, one buried at Aldershot: and the other at York. After the death of his son in South Africa be desired to inscribe his name on the tombstone in the Parish Churchyard, and bear- ing in mind the deaths of four children in places so far apirt,he proposed to add the first verse of Mrs Hernias' poem, " The Graves of a Household" : They grew in childhood side by side : They filled one home with glee ; Their graves are seve-ad far and wide By mount, and stream, and sea. The use of these lines was vetoed by the Rector of Grappenhall on the around that they were • ridiculous and inappropriate ! ' The reader will, I think, agree that this height example of critical discernment, to say nothing of kindly feeling, on the part of a beneficed clergyman deserves to be placed on record. A 'ST. HELENS FOOTBALLER'S INJURIES. Since Saturday afternoon Oliver Allaby, half-back of the St Helens Recreation Football Club, who was injured in the match with Earlestown, has been somewhat seriou‘ly ill. Allaby, who roe ides at 18, Eldon-streetsbas played for the St Helens Rocs since they adopted Association, six years ago, and for the last three or four years he has bean capt sin. He came to the ROCS from Garston Copper Works. On Saturday he collided with Limond of H arlestown, and received injury to his face and head, which has , since turned to congestion of the brain

div.head: WARRINGTON PARISH CHUdOH.
div.p: WARRINGTON PARISH CHUdOH.

Opening of the Chapel and Organ. Warrington's venerable ?arise Church has for some time been undergoing extensive alterstions,the necessity of which has long been felt. The major nart of a scheme of restoration has now been carriedout and on Thursday last week, services were held to celebrate the opening of the new side chapel and organ. The prin- cipal interior alteration has been the entire reconstruc- tion of the organ, and its removal from the west and of the church to the arch between the Soldier Chapel and the tower. This will la. a great advantage both to the choir and organist, for it can readily be imagined how difficult it was for the choir to lead the singing when the congregation interposed tetween them and the organ. The rebuilding of the instrument was entrusted to Messrs Alexander Young and Sons, of Mancheeter,but the work has not yet been quite completed. The organ will be blown by an electric motor. On Thursday the motor supplied was not powerful enough, and men had to undertake the task of blowing. It is intended net the rough pitch pine supports of the organ shall form the ground work of an elaborate oak gallery with fan-vaulted ceiling, which it is hoped to erect when I sufficient funds are raised. The plaster has been removed from all parts of the walls of the church, leav- ing the stone work xposed. Tee Boteler Chapel has been reseated, an altar has been erected, and the chapel will now be used for dagy serviles. The children's gallery at the west end has been removed, and replaced with pews on the general level of the church. The exterior of the chureh has received considerable atten- tion in the nature of re-pointing and the repair of the pinnacles &e. The total cost of the work will be £2.500 and it is hoped to be able to carry out further improve- ments which will entail the expenditure of an additional £5OO. Messrs William and &gar Owen, architects, have superintended the alterations. Thursday's services commenced with the dedication of the side chapel and a celebration of the Holy Communion at 730 a en, which was well attended. A special form of service was used, the Heuer (Rev Canon Willis) "pronounoieg the Dedication after weich Holy Com- munion was celebrated.

A good congregation assembled in the afternoon,when the opening of the organ took place. A. short service was conducted by the Rector, special dedicatory prayers being offered. The sermon was preached by the Rev A A Markham, vicar of St Jude's, Liverpool, and formerly curate-in- charge of St Clenaent's Mission, who took for his text the words, "Lord, I have loved the habitation of Thiee house and the place where Thine honour dwelleth." After expoundingithe text the rev gentleman went on to speak of the work which bad been done in connection with the Parish Church during the last fourteen years. , The great parochial building work began, he said, in 1891, StjPeter's Church had been built and consecrated and a great load was lifted from the minds of church- people in that parish. Then it was that they were able I to turn their thoughts to their own most pressing needs and the year 1891 saw the erection of their first mission, building—St George's Mission. No sooner was that I finished than they were face o face with the great I school question and so the year 1892 saw the building' of Ellesmere-street schools and in 1894 the schools at I Fairfield were erected. Then there followed a breathing' space, and they afterwards set to work once more and the year 1897 was occupied with the building of St Clement's Mission. It certainly was s very great work. These four buildings alone represented an outlay of £15,000, butsee what it had all meant. It had meant a thousand school places two great mission establishments supplying places for a united congregation of some 500 people, with Suaday schools numbering some 1,400 children, and large bands of communicants—living centres of parochial work under the shadow of the Parish Church. It was natural after these things had been done that they ehould turn their attention to the I Parish Church,and a scheme was launched for the raising of £3,000 which was required for the renovation of the, fabric of the church and for the organ. Though,no doubt that scheme was received with the courteous scepticism with which all the schemes had at first been met, yet the great scheme succeeded. The band of God was upon them, the people had a mind Co work, and so they were present that day to celebrate the conclusion of the major part of that scheme. What had been done to the exterior of the church spoke for itself. The atmosphere of Warrington had contributed very largely to the decay of the stonework and steps had to be taken to renovate it. He was told that in the repair of the fabric alone some £1,500 had been spent. The interior of the church certainly looked more dignified. The church was larger and more open and he thought they were glad to see the pointed stones instead of the plaster. The improvement really suggested how much more might be done in the beautifying of the church. Surely it reminded them that the chancel was still a dingy spot, of how paltry SOME of the surroundings of the sitar were, of the stucco frames which enclosed the ten commandments. How feeble, how poor, andthow paltry the chancel still remained.VThere were two great works of which he would like to speak at greater length. A side chapel had been arranged and that morning was dedicated. Now there were many people who perhaps saw no reason for such an arrangement, but he would venture to say it was a practical necessity in any church where the Prayer Book system was carried out. Surely the memory of those dreary daily services had not yet faded from his mind. A handful of people in that vast church—it was very dreary. He supposed there must have been considerable useless expense in lighting far more of the church than was needed. It was a practical necessity that there should be a small portion of the church set apart for the small congregations at the daily services. He knew that a side chapel was also a very great aid to devotion. They were glad that the church doors should be left open all day long so that people might come and go as they wished, and it was useful that •there should be some side-chapel where people who came for devotion might go,mahindered by visitors or by cleaning operations, Co be alone and undisturbed—a quiet corner in a great church Speaking of the organ the preacher said it was twenty six years since it was erected in the church at a cost of £2,000, and beyond a sum of £lOO, spent half-way through that period, he believed no money had been spent on the instrument at all. Considing the extra- ordinary complication of its action caused by the strange position it was placed in with regard to the doorway, it was wonderful that the parish had escaped for more than a quarter of a century with an outlay of about £lOO for keeping that elaborate piece of machin- ery and mechanism in good order. It was a good thing that the bold step had been taken and the organ had been removed to the east end, and the difficulties which were inherent in.. its old position _were now

things of the past. Possibly there Were a few -people who regretted the step and who had a love for an organ 'in a western gallery, perhaps with memories of some vast Continental Cathedral. He would venture to remind them that there were two kinds of music employed in the service of God in church. The first was that which the choir rendered alone as a musical offering to God which the congregation offered vicariously through the lips and hands of those skilled in the heavenly art. Every church had its anthems, and they also looked for an occasional setting of the canticles, for the singing of those parts of the Communion service which were directed to be sung, and perhaps occasionally for the rendering of some musical service, cantata, or the like. It was almost impossible with the organ at the west end for the choir to sing. any music of this character. There was also music which the congrega— tion and choir offered together. They looked for their hymns and perhaps even for congregational settings of the Eucharistic service. With the organ at the west end there was no doubt that the organist was able to lead the congregation but the more successfully he led the congregation th 3 less he led the choir and, in fact, when the congregation was singing the choir was almost a useless appendage and the reason for its existence was gone. Any alliance between the organ and choir in the old days for the sake of loading the con- gregation was quite impossible and they (the clergy) well remembered how. sitting between the choir and congregation it was their endeavour from time to time to try and direct Mtn one unison the three con- flicting times which were frequently heard. All this was now a thing of the pest. Continuing the preacher said he often thought the organist was one of the chief ministers of any church. He had a very high and im- portant task, not only to lead the congregation and choir, but surely it was entrusted to him by his art to iuternret to them the words they were singing. Ho coull also vastly help their devotion. HO voluntaries camo as it were to supply the atmosphere in which they were to worship; his playing over of the hymrns would not merely suggest the time they were to be sung to, but it would tell them of the character of the hyrdrns and the way they had to sing them. The ministry of the organist was very wonderful and they might be glad that at that church it was in safe hands. He trusted that the work, the conclusion of whioh they were called upon to celebrate that day might be for the edification of all the worshippers. and for the advancement of the beauty and the dignity of the service in that Church which they loved so well.

A collection was taken on behalf of the Restoration Fond and the service concluded with the Benediction. Mr BERTRAM LI7ARD SELBY. Organist of Rochester Cathedral, then gave an organ recital which proved to be a rare musical treat. As is very frequently the case with new instruments a little ciphering occurred, but notwithstanding this Mr Selby handled the organ in masterly style and his recital was listened to with the greatest pleasure by the congregation. The pro- gramme wal as follows :—lmprovisation, Luard Selby ; Introduction to act 111. " Die Meistersinger " Wagner ; Pastorale, Bach ; Minuet, Claussmana ; Caprice, Gail- mant ; Sonata (No. 6). Mendelssohn. At eight o'clock there was a choral evensong, and a large congregation assembled. The canticles were Bunnett in F, and the choir gave a very creditable rendering of the anthem" 0, give thanks," (Elvey). Mr Selby gave an organ recital, the following being the pro- gramme :—Solemn March, Lnard Selby ; Autumn Song, Schumann ;" Priere," Ciaussmann; Al egretto in 11' sharp ml, Guilmant ; Improvisation ; Prelude and Fugue, Mendelemohn. There was an entire absence of ciphering and the recital was highly enjoyable. Mr B Poole eff.ctively sang " Honour and Arms " (Handel). The collections for the day, which wore in aid of the Restoration Fund, amounted to over £23.

div.head: REFORMATORY SCHOOL AT NEWTON. ---- Prize Distribution.
div.p: THE REFORMATORY SCHOOL AT NEWTON. ---- Prize Distribution.

The distribution of prizes gained by the boys who are inmates of the above school, during the year ending December 1901, took place in the schoolroom on Tries. day afternoon. The Rev Canon Peurhyn,rector of Win— wick, presided and amongst those present were Coun- cillor It Dart, of Liverpool, Revs T R Matthews, and J Ryder, Captain Withington, Messrs R S Blew, E W Cropper, J Lowe,and a number of ladies. The report of the official inspection showed that on the Eitb February 1902, there were 142 boys in the school, 67 on licence , land two had absconded. All parts of the buildings were clean and in good order. The incandescent light had been supplied in the schoolroom and other day roorns.The general standard of the examination of the boys was good. The provision for physical training and recreation was on first rate lines. The free gymnastics were on the best principles,every boy got the advantage of them and the effect in improving the lads' physique was marked. The report was a record of • year's thoroughly good work. .The appearance and manner of the boys bad improved markedly of recent years, and it was pleasing to learn from the results in after life that this improvement was not superficial merely. After a few brief remarks by the Rev Canon Penrhyn the prizes were distributed by Councillor Dart, who gave the lads some sound words of advice stating they must attend to their work, and if they asked God's help they would do well in the future. If they were tip top they would be wanted, they :might depend upon it and to be tip top they must kncw not only how to do their work well, but to be trustworthy. He warned them against self- fishoess. They must realise that those who could do most for others were the happiest of boys and men. He wanted them to use the opportunities there to the very full, so that when they left they might do the things they had learned well. (Applause.) The prizes con- sisted chiefly of books, handkerchiefs and belts, and were awarded for religious knowledge, history, arith- metic, geography, farming, gardening, joinerin4 and for athletics. During the afternoon a couple of vocal items were given by the boys, and the band played selections of music.

GOLBORNE COLLIER FINED FOR THEFT. At the Warrington Occasional Court on Monday, John Browne, collier, of Go'borne, was charged with stealing six cabbages, the property of Edwin Johnson, of Turret Hall Farm, Croft, on Saturday afternoon. P.C. Johnson found the prisoner coming from a field with the cabbages in his possession, and locked him up.—The Bench inflicted a fine of lOs and costs, or 14 days.
THE FIGHr AGAINST CO-OPERATIVE STORES. ACTION BY CHESTER TRADERS.

The threat of a boycott on the part of Chester trades- men in consequence of the Co-operative Society affecting their trade was, apparently, no mere flash in the pan. Several tradesmen have not been slow to interest them- selves in.the movement, with the result that on Tuesday a meeting of tradesmen and property holders was held. It was of a private and preliminary character, and with a view of arranging a conference between the heeds of the different trade societies in the city. However, the fact shows that private traders in the city have felt,and are feeling, the effect of the Co-operative Society upon their business. The Co-operative people regard the pro- posed boycott with indifference, although if it is to be fought tooth and nail some of the society's individual members are likely to suffer. Already one grocer in the town has dismissed an employee because his family dealt with the Co-operative Society.

Seldom has a Britith warship had a more ad- I comm;ssion. which will undoubtedly ii venturous and successful commission than the one She' which the Terrible has just concluded. She arrived of at Portsmouth at the end of last week to be paid f off: and on Tuesday the officers and crew were en- 1 tertained at a public banquet in the Connaught Hall, to celebrate their great and doughty deeds in South Africa and China. Between 800 and 900 persons sat down, including General Sir John French: and the mayoress presented the crew with a silver souvenir beaaing the inscription : "Naval Brigade, South Africa, 1899-1900, North China, 1900."
